Uniform Title: Niśvāsakārikā Manuscript: IFP Transcript T0017A Description:
IFP Transcript T0017A constitutes the first part of the *Niśvāsakārikā*. The remainder is contained in transcript T0017B, which will be added in the future.
Notes: Revision 0: December 16, 2013.
Country of Publication: India. || Śrīḥ ||
Oṃ.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter of the Niśvāsakārikā.
As those gods are established— Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Śiva themselves— the wise, devoted to that [path], understand it accordingly.
That which is the supreme even of that is the highest limit;
it consists of the letter A, the letter U, the letter M, and the Bindu.
Śiva is beyond that, and beyond him is that which is higher than the high. (3)
The letter *a* is remembered as Brahmā, the letter *u* as Viṣṇu, and the letter *m* they say is Rudra; the Lord himself is the seed-syllable (*bīja*). (4)
Since Nāda is to be known as Śiva, all-pervading, and higher than the highest;
for even those principles which exist as higher than the highest belong to Him alone. || 15 ||
The goddesses who are to be understood in their true nature, as well as those presiding over the *bindu* and *nāda*, were addressed.
The Goddess said:
"And those which are the imperishable syllables..."
"How do they, by resorting to oneness, go to the supreme state? The Lord said:
"The syllable Om, conjoined with the Bindu, is remembered as the mouth of the Vedas. (7)
The letter *a* belongs to that god Śiva, the Supreme Self;
through the union of the letters *a* and *u*, the syllable *oṃ* is proclaimed. (8)
The letter *ma* arises when joined with the two lips;
and the moon (*i*) is situated above that *ma*. (9)
One should know it to have four parts, adorned with the fourfold knowledge:
namely, Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and likewise Śānti.
These are declared to be the digits (kalās) of the wise Bindudeva.
When the letter 'ma' is touched by the syllable 'oṃ', it indeed resounds.
Then the drop (bindu) quickly touches the head of the letter *ma*;
the twenty-four digits (*kalās*) are traditionally taught as beginning with *ka* and ending with *ma*.
(4) They say that [the letters] situated in the three places should always be known as established;
the characteristic of the deity Bindu is the form of a siddhārtha. 13.
O Goddess, that which is common to all tantras has been proclaimed by you as having a form resembling the letter *ma*, situated at the top of the syllable *oṃ*.
Resembling a half-moon and situated beyond the Bindu is that which is even more supreme than that— the Sadāśiva who has the form of Nāda.
The Nāda exists pervading that which is beyond the highest, beyond the highest, and beyond the highest;
there is nothing higher than this, nor anything beyond Śiva.
By knowing the God who performs all actions, a man is liberated;
[he is] the beginning, the middle, and the end, with three, five, and the visarga. 17.

In the Grandfather (Brahmā), they are established in the principle of the Self (ātmatattva) residing within the body; from the fourth [element], and likewise from the one beyond it, they are taken up as far as the seventh. (18)
One should point out that which is the supreme of him, as well as that of Keśava;
that which is the beginning and the end, and that which is below and the eleventh.
One should designate the five specific [letters] beginning with ‘ā’ as portions of Rudra.
For whatever the nature of each [letter] may be, it consists of that very essence.
All letters from ‘ya’ to ‘kṣa’ are established within the principle of Śiva (śivatattva).
The Goddess Mātṛkā, who is established within the syllable Oṃ, is said to be all the deities. 22.
One is liberated from all fetters and goes to the stainless Śiva.
The Goddess said:
O God, that which has been described as the syllable Om, the embodiment of all deities.
"How then, O Lord, is it said that the Lord is meditated upon by yogis who contemplate reality?
The Lord said:
"Mind (citta), consciousness (cetas), as well as thought (cintā), the object of thought (cintya), and the thinker (cintaka) are distinct. (24)
Having understood this pentad, one should thereafter practice yoga.
The Goddess said: "What indeed is the nature of the mind (citta), and what is the nature of the thinker (cetana)? (25)
What kind of thought is said to be, and how is the object of thought related to the thinker?
O Supreme Lord, tell me all of this again according to the truth. (26)
O Mahādeva, wielder of the trident, source of grace, I have a doubt. O Īśvara, [grant] attention, mindfulness, consciousness, intellect, and the various modes of cognition. (27)
Thus, having understood [the matter] in these five ways, the Supreme Goddess is remembered as the Puruṣa. 28.
Therefore, one should apply oneself to yoga; otherwise, never at any time.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord, O Supreme Ishvara, even now there remains a doubt regarding yoga. (29)
What kind of yoga would it be in its true nature? Tell me that, O Lord. (p. 8) The Lord:
Thus has this supreme yoga of yogis been fully explained.
It is proclaimed to be of two kinds: that which has become the mark (*lakṣabhūta*) and that which is unobservable (*alakṣya*).
Having correctly perceived the mark, the knower should indeed apply himself to that which resides therein. (31)
Having become absorbed in that and being intent upon yoga, one is liberated;
free from the senses, one experiences neither pleasure nor pain.
But that which has become motionless and steady is declared to be the unmanifest (alakṣa). This yoga, which is both supreme and most excellent, has been explained to you. (33)
To whoever has become absorbed in that [state], one should impart the yoga:
"Oṃ; intellect, mind, ego, and the living soul (jīva) as the fifth. (34)
(9) Resting in the state of the Fourth (turya), the Praṇava is firmly established;
for the Praṇava is bound to the Bindu within the domain of the Nāda of the Suṣumnā. 35.
Abiding in the emission at the end of the sixteen, liberation is held to lie beyond that.
This very Lord consists of speech; He is the imperishable fivefold portion of mantra. (36)
It is proclaimed by all the established doctrines that the supreme station of the Imperishable (Akṣara) is situated there;
it abides as its own nature and is renowned by the name Brahmā.
When it is uttered aloud, Brahmā is the presiding deity therein;
when it is uttered in a whisper, Viṣṇu is the presiding deity therein.
One should remember [the mantra] with the mind without uttering it aloud; there, Śiva is the presiding deity.
The self is the meditator, the mind is the meditation, and the object of meditation is the pure Maheśvara.
O Goddess of gods, one should unite the self through meditation within that very body with the Supreme Lord, who possesses supreme sovereignty and is all-pervading. (40)
Having made the Praṇava partless and devoid of its vowel-matras,
and having placed Śiva at its end, that [mantra] joined together bestows the state of liberation.
He for whom this supreme rarity has thus arisen as a distinction shall go to the highest abode, accompanied by hundreds of millions of his kinsmen.
O Goddess, even if one has reached every possible state or is joined with all sins, he is necessarily liberated, for [this power] is capable of bestowing grace upon everyone. (43)
This, O Goddess, is that supreme [teaching], which must be guarded with great effort;
behold, O Queen of the Gods, how one is liberated by this means that is free from all constraints. (44)
(11) I shall further explain its higher and lower divisions;
it is to be known by yogins through vision, touch, movement, and meditation. 45.
For even by mere remembrance, the supreme state is attained;
O Goddess, I shall describe that which is difficult even for the gods to obtain. (46)
That which consists of the thirty-eight kalās and is "Śivo'm" is indeed the embodiment of the Vedas; it is certainly the savior from the ocean of worldly existence.
The Goddess said:
"Tell me, what is this procedure for the auspicious syllable Om like? Again, a doubt has arisen: how is it that Śiva is remembered as 'Om'? (48)
When the Lord, [consisting of] all the principles and so forth, is above the *dvādaśānta* of the Deity; (p. 12)
And Śiva is likewise ordained as being endowed with the three and the five. || 49 ||
The Goddess said:
"In which locations are the thirty-eight kalās established? Tell me their names according to the distinction of their places."
Siddhi, Ṛddhi, Dyuti, Lakṣmī, Medhā, Kānti, Svadhā, Sthiti, Rajā, Rakṣā, Arati, Pālyā, Kāmā, Saṃyaminī, and Kriyā. (51)
You are intellect, the creator, the one who dwells in the village,
the deluder, darkness, delusion, hunger, sleep, death, illusion, fear, and old age.
Manifestation and foundation, knowledge and likewise peace;
Śaśinī, Aṅgadā, Iṣṭā, Marīci, and Jvālinī. (53)
The half-moon and the spear, along with the digits, belong to the Knower. || 54 ||
The power that ceases the half-moon and does not go upward, which I have described as abiding in the *nāda*, one should designate as the *vyāpinī*. 55.
The utterance of the Praṇava for him is [as follows]:
that sound which is always heard arising from the dual [state] of the produced Nāda is indeed the upward-moving [current], situated both within and without the Nāda. (57)
When the Śakti is being observed, that splendor which is perceived is indeed the all-pervasive one, situated both within and without the Śakti. (58)
In brief, the thirty-eight kalās of the Praṇava have been declared;
they should always be known by those who follow the Śiva Tantras. (59)
That great God who is omnipresent and heard of by all, is indefinable, nameless, equal, and established everywhere. (60)
The contemplation that "it exists" is indeed its first stage;
even by the gods, that contemplation of what it is which exists was not understood. (61)
A notion regarding that very [reality] has arisen; it is designated as "Power" (Śakti).
It is perceived directly in all worlds and is seen to be present everywhere. (62)
But that which is its state as fruit is directly perceived everywhere;
it is heard constantly, O Goddess, and is renowned by the name "Nāda. (63)
The other [aspect] of that state is called cessation;
it is declared to be the half-moon, pervasive and situated externally at the end. 64.
For indeed, by means of conjunction, whatever syllable is enjoined elsewhere obstructs all yogins; it is renowned as the "Half-moon" (ardhacandra). || 65 ||
Knowledge is that which is born of yoga and meditation; it is the auspicious conduct, the fire, and the ritual action.
He who is to be known as the most supreme abides within all the senses and other faculties.
O Lord, you previously declared that the Goddess is the partless *praṇava*, situated everywhere within all the stalks, lotuses, and so forth. (67)
Furthermore, O Lord of the Gods, for what reason does the Supreme Lord [act] toward those who possess blemishes?
Abiding in the form of mantra, he sustains all beings.
Having first grasped the form of the mantra, knowledge subsequently manifests;
the root of the world is known as the bond of the bound (paśu), consisting of both the bound and the bond. (69)
And Maheśvara, whose form is mantra,
compassionate toward all beings and resplendent like ten thousand suns, became the cause for its uprooting.
The Lord, together with Śiva, the imperishable, has entered the form of the mantra out of compassion;
she is Vyāpinī, whose form is space, Anantā, Anāthā, and Anāśritā.
The form of the God is renowned as the Praṇava, joined with the Brahmans; it comprises Īśāna, Puruṣa, Aghora, Vāma, Sadyojāta, and the others. (72)
He is the Lord of the moving and the unmoving, the source of immeasurable qualities; he is the Praṇava, the manifest God, the sovereign lord of all sciences.
Indestructible and perfectly complete, the Bindu of splendor is Supreme Śiva;
the Lord Īśāna, the Lord of the Lords of Mantras, has the Praṇava as his body.
Having known the great [power], the Lord...
[is] the master.
O lady of excellent vows, as many vowels and consonants as there are situated within the Praṇava,
so many hosts of gods become manifest to you.
These [energies] reside within the Praṇava; in reality, they abide in the Praṇava.
The Praṇava is the soul of all dharmas for those whose minds are attached to the Praṇava.
The *praṇava* is the support of all, yet it is itself without support; it possesses infinite forms.
Within the *praṇava* is the entire universe, as well as that which is beyond sound and the rest. (77)
The Praṇava is the life-breath of the vital breaths, devoid of all means of valid cognition.
Maheśvara, whose self is the Praṇava, is the lord of the creators beginning with Brahmā;
yet Śiva is the supreme reality whose nature transcends even that collection of mantra-forms. (79)
Understand in accordance with reality that the entire world, from the realm of Brahmā down to the earth, originates from the Praṇava, and that the entire world is dissolved into it.
But the form which exists at the beginning is exactly the same as that at the ends of the kalās;
for it is remembered as the Praṇava because of its eternity and its inner nature, as previously stated.
O virtuous one, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Śiva, and Śānta perform the *praṇava* (salutation) for Him; therefore, He is remembered as *Praṇava*. (82)
Pure, all-pervading, and eternal, Śiva is established in the Praṇava;
he is the supreme, pure, primordial body of knowledge belonging to the Supreme Lord.
Whatever is contained within the Praṇava, established in light, serves to purify both the form and the formless; it is also the cause of liberation.
The supreme god, the Praṇava, who pervades all, is established as the remainder of the names of the gods and the entire world; he is the creator of all creators. (85)
The Praṇava is the soul of all dharmas, residing in the hearts of living beings;
consisting of three mātrās and a half-mātrā, the Praṇava is beginningless in its origin.
The *praṇava* is Maheśvara, who dwells in the hearts of all beings;
he is indeed to be known, to be sacrificed to, to be meditated upon, and to be recited. (87)
The Soul of the Universe, the Source of all Existence, the Means of Attaining the Bindu, and the Means for Individual Realization—the Praṇava should always be meditated upon as such. (88)
Sovereignty, mastery, and likewise greatness—O Goddess of gods, O fair-faced one, these are attained without doubt through mere meditation alone. (89)
When meditated upon, the Lord of All, the Divine, bestows omniscience;
all deities reside in the heart, and their abode is within the vital breath (prāṇa) in the heart.
All lights reside in the heart, and this Praṇava is situated in the heart;
joined with these three, it is established within all beings.
(21) The goddess Citta is superior to the mind (cetas); she knows herself in reality.
Citta is declared to be the body, while Cetā is proclaimed to be the power (śakti). || 92 ||
When one perceives oneself as devoid of these [faculties], as if fallen asleep from poison, even so, O Goddess, is consciousness perceived when it is deprived of them. (93)
Form, touch, and likewise sound—these three aspects are present everywhere;
the Praṇava is supreme, subtle, and devoid of all means of valid cognition.
The origin of all principles consists of the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas;
among these, the Praṇava is to be known as the charioteer of the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña).
That which is consciousness within this body, the Lord who dwells in all beings—that is to be known as the syllable Om (Praṇava); it stands filling everything.
That supreme, subtle Prakṛti, whose essence is Śiva, performs [this].
O Goddess, she is proclaimed as fifty Praṇavas through a single division. (97)
This should be constantly known by yogins who follow the knowledge of Śiva, as it is found in the Vedas, Sāṃkhya, Purāṇas, Pāñcarātra, and Itihāsas. 98.
Likewise, other Smṛtis declare various things in succession;
all yogis proclaim that the single syllable "Om" is Brahman.
"They speak without knowing," thus [it is said that] Māyā is of the nature of Śiva. The Goddess said:
"O Lord, the fifty Praṇavas have been understood by me through your grace. (100)
Within that, O Lord, the phonemes reside, as well as the Bindu and the Nāda.
(23) O Maheśvara, I wish to hear further; I have a doubt. 102.
Īśāna, Puruṣa, Aghora, Vāma, and likewise Sadyojāta;
the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas), the Guardians of the World (Lokapālas), and the Weapons, in their proper order. 103.
"Tell me the extraction of the mantras for these [deities] without distinction.
The Lord said: "Listen, O Goddess, to the supreme secret, the most excellent true essence of the mantras. (104)
O lady of beautiful countenance, I shall now declare all the mantras within the Praṇava; that which was proclaimed first as the letter 'A' is indeed the end. (105)
The second [syllable] is indeed *dha* from *dharmādi*, and likewise the *cchādanāni*; one should conceive the third as the lotus (*padma*) together with the anusvāra, and it shall truly exist. (106)
One should assign the nine Śaktis using the seed-syllable *cathrtha*;
the letter *ma* is declared to be the pericarp of that lotus eternally.
In this regard, the syllables beginning with *u* have been briefly described;
O Goddess of the Gods, one should arrange them ending with *oṃ* and concluding with *puṣkara*.
Those letters beginning with *ḷ* and ending with *e*, which have been declared, should be known as the filaments of that beautiful lotus. (109)
Having thus performed the placement with effort, one should place the form as before:
Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and likewise Śānti.
O Goddess of Gods, Śāntyatīta and the others are proclaimed as the five Brahmans;
beginning with Vāyavya and ending with the letter Śa, they are established. (111)
The limbs of Śiva should be understood as they have been described in brief:
the syllable *ṣa* shall be the eye; she is proclaimed to be Gāyatrī. (112)
O fair-faced one, in this tantra, Kṣassāvitrī should always be known;
O Goddess of the gods, having worshipped Sadāśiva, who is called Haṃsa. (113)
The supreme syllable is the transcendent deity, endowed with all tantras;
having meditated upon him, the Lord of Gods, one should worship him according to the prescribed sequence.
One should place the embryo in the first [square], the universal monarchs in the second,
the world-protectors in the third, and the weapons in the fourth.
The eight universal monarchs (cakravartin) are indeed those beginning with the letter *ka* and ending with *ja*;
those beginning with *jha* and ending with *ta* are proclaimed to be the world-protectors (lokapāla). || 116 ||
The weapons, beginning with the letter *tha* and ending with the letter *bha*, are joined respectively with the vowel *a*; these are proclaimed as the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśas*). || 117 ||

One should join the world-protectors with the *bindu* and the weapons with the *visarga*; for all of them, however, one should proceed according to the ritual sequence of perfumes and incense with the *praṇava*.
O Goddess, all these actions that have been described must be performed with effort in their proper sequence and in every way by means of the *praṇava*. 119.
O noble lady, all duties must be performed without conceptual differentiation regarding those principles (tattvas) proclaimed to begin with earth and end with Śiva. || 120 ||

(27) By means of the *praṇava*, however, the worship, the performance of the fire-offering (*homa*), and all ritual actions— including recitation (*japa*), meditation (*dhyāna*), and so forth— of all [deities] must be performed. (121)
One should offer oblations three hundred times in sequence with the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
This sacrifice to the Mātṛkās is difficult to attain even for the gods.
This sacrifice to the Mātṛkās has fulfilled its purpose for you; with doubts severed, stainless and free from fever, he attains union with Śiva. 123.
O Goddess, that which is designated as the Supreme Imperishable was explained by me from the very beginning;
O beautiful one, such a sacrifice for it has also been proclaimed by the Lord.
This division of the mantra of the Praṇava has thus been declared;
thereafter,
[one should perform] that which consists of victory.
In a very short time, he shall conquer timely death;
for one month it is said to be a hundred years, and for two months... [126]
Through the procedure of recitation and worship, one attains perfection in a single year. || 127 ||
Henceforth, O Goddess of the lords of gods, I shall explain the wheel of ritual placement (nyāsacakra) in its proper sequence, beginning from the east until everything is completed. 128.
Thus, with a well-concentrated mind, one should perform the placement according to the sequence of the classes of consonants;
the letter *kṣa* alone should be employed sevenfold.
Endowed with the seed-syllable of Rudra and accompanied by the six limbs. || 130 ||

Having placed the syllable *juṃ* at the beginning and ending with the letter *sa*, O beautiful one, some [call] that *mṛtyuñjaya*; among those, it is summarized as consisting of sixty-four [syllables]. (131)
The knower of yoga should perform recitation (japa) in sequence with the exhalation;
established in the wheel, the knower of the path should constantly practice meditation. || 132 ||
The host of mantras should indeed be known as resembling pure crystal;
through meditation and the mind, [this is realized]—of this there is no doubt. || 133 ||
When a yogin seeking victory over death enters the field of time (kālakṣetra),
he should contemplate the *saṃpuṭa* [mantra] and a second one above it.
Having acted thus, O Goddess of Gods, one should always traverse the path;
one recites [the mantra] one hundred thousand times.
(30) "O Goddess, this [teaching] concerning the Cakra-Mṛtyuñjaya has been told to you by me, through the power of obstructing death by means of the destruction of the sense-objects. (136)
One is liberated from all diseases and becomes equal to Amṛtīśa.
O fair-faced one, I shall explain the initiation in the wheel once again.
Having withdrawn [the breath] free from all agitation,
one should perform the ritual of universal withdrawal in brief.
O Goddess of gods, sprinkling and protection are prescribed by means of the supreme syllable;
likewise, the "seizing" (laṃbhana) of bound souls is for the sake of purifying the consecration of those to be worshipped. 139.
Everything must be performed by him; having observed the sequence with a focused mind, he should meditate according to that very order. 140.
O Goddess of the gods, having meditated upon the wheel as it exists specifically within the body of the bound soul (paśu), one should perform the ritual actions in their proper sequence. (141)
Starting from the first leaf until everything is completed, one who is not discerning [should proceed]. || 142 ||
Having joined [the breath] at the heart-cakra, one should commence the fire-oblation (homa) there;
one hundred and one oblations should be offered in sequence, culminating with the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti).

Having joined [the disciple] by means of the path of the channels, he who enters with a concentrated mind—there, the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) should be offered; then one should join him again to other [practices]. || 144 ||
Having drawn [the breath] in this manner by means of *pūraka*, one should cause it to enter the wheel in the heart; O lady of good vows, it should be joined to the channels in this sequence.
This procedure for the sacrifice, however, one should not give to just anyone. || 146 ||
He attains equality with the gods and comes into my presence; of this there is no doubt. This entire secret essence, O incomparable one, has been told out of love for you. 148.
One should carefully draw an eight-petaled lotus, having inscribed the mantra with diligence.

In the heart-cakra, one should perform all this according to the previously stated procedure; whatever is desired, the practitioner of mantra should worship that, and there is no doubt that he will attain success. 150.
O Goddess of gods, by means of non-conceptualization, he shall become a partaker of the fruit of accomplishment.
O fair-faced one, having first performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the deities in the heart-cakra, [one should proceed]. (151)
O Dear One, one should perform the arrangement of the mandalas as before;
O Goddess, this is declared to be the most secret [teaching] and must not be given away. 152.
Having examined [the recipient], one should bestow [the teaching] upon them, but not upon an atheist or a slanderer;
rather, like a seeker who has mastered the meaning through the intellect of logic and inference, one should uphold the instruction. 153.
If accepted, it would not succeed; therefore, one should avoid it.
Whether he possesses the three qualities or is endowed with qualities, the teacher remains so in every state. (154)
It should always be worshipped by those who know the principle of Śiva;
the ritual placement (nyāsa) was previously taught by me in the Sūtra known as the Uttara.
(34) That very thing is to be known therein; those alone are proclaimed as the mudrās.
One should not act otherwise, O Goddess; this is the command of the Supreme Lord. 156.
But he who, out of delusion, fails to understand this unsurpassed ritual for the purpose of destroying death, shall instead partake of only oily fruits. (157)

One who knows the procedure for nourishment, who understands the application of the rules for ritual placement (nyāsa), and who knows the reality of the movement of the channels (nāḍī)—he shall conquer death. (158)
Exhausted by burning and dehydration, he departed with half his body;
with a head split open by a hollow pipe, he was carried away by the excellent wind. || 159 ||
Whoever, through such distinctions as these, knows the reality is to be known as liberated; all others are impostors who know only the self. 160.
He who understands the principles and the supreme pervasion of those principles is not stained by merit or demerit; he is capable of bestowing grace upon all. (161)
Whether he be a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra, when he knows reality,
no distinction whatsoever exists, for he is indeed like fire within fire.
Just as milk poured into milk, or water placed into water, no distinction can be found; so too, when one is permeated by the Lord, reality becomes unified.

For just as all rivers, once they have reached their resting place in the ocean, cannot be distinguished by their individual flavors or essences, [so it is with those who have entered the state of the Tathāgata]. (164)

In the same way, O Goddess, whether one belongs to a caste and stage of life or is an initiated animal-sacrificer (paśu), if they are endowed with the state of Śiva, these two are equal; of this there is no doubt. || 165 ||
He who, relying upon the Śiva-tantra, should perform a division [of the teachings],
that man shall cook in the thirty-two terrible hells. (166)
A man who undergoes penance for five days of Brahmā and five days of Keśava, as well as three days of Rudra, is purified.
Therefore, with every effort, one should always remain undiscriminating;
for the discriminating person goes downward, while the undiscriminating person conquers.
This supreme pervasion of the principles has been told to you, O Goddess; it must be kept strictly secret by you and not given to one who has not received initiation from another. 169.
From the unsurpassed [state], one [attains] ten, twelve, six, or three castes;
or rather, it may be in truth itself when the goal has been realized through worship. 170.
One should not record [them] among merits and sins; this, O Goddess, is declared to be the truth. (171)
And it is stated in the *Cicchakti-āgama* according to this rule, O virtuous one:
"All those [mantras] should be known as *praṇavas*, bestowing the fruits of both desire and liberation. (172)
This Mātṛkā sacrifice has been told to you, O beautiful one;
by performing it, whatever is desired shall indeed be attained. || 173 ||
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the section on the Knowledge-portion (*jñānakāṇḍa*) of the *Niśvāsakārikā*.
The Lord said: "I shall fully explain the heart-lotus, which is situated within the ten knots (*granthi*)."

Thus, having understood that the mantras emerged from the mouth of the Supreme Lord in five ways and are established in five ways, one should then commence the ritual action.
The syllable *ha* is declared to be the mantra that is the sovereign lord of all;
it is the impeller among all mantras and the increaser of the power of one's own energy. || 25 ||
"Abiding in the mantra with its attendants, the imperishable Lord is the essence of mantra"—

Just as there is sap in herbs, as there is radiance in fire, and as there is gentleness in the moon—in short, as it resides within the pericarp. || 17 ||

and that Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is indeed Viṣṇu, the twenty-fifth Puruṣa. (19)
Having known the single syllable, which has four divisions, is adorned with four morae, transcends the fourfold fetters, and is the Bindu, one shall go to Śiva. || 20 ||
That white form which is seen there, situated at the corners of the eyes, is the form of Brahmā; they declare it to be the sāttvika aspect.

Beginning with Ananteśa and ending with Śikhaṇḍin, they are proclaimed [as the nine]; Kālāgnirudra is the ninth, while Sadāśiva is the tenth.
This is the primary characteristic of the deity Bindu, known as Śiva;
it should be understood by wise practitioners, sages, and those desiring liberation. || 52 ||
The first point is called "void" (śūnya), and the second is the "supreme void" (paraśūnya);
therefore, they say that the third alone is the profound state of ultimate reality (tattvārtha).
Akṣobhya is the supreme drop (bindu), the sixth, beyond doubt;
the seventh is the "more empty" (śūnyatara), and the eighth is the appearance of emptiness (śūnyābhāsa). (54)
The ninth is the Nirābhāsa (the non-manifest), while the tenth is the Ābhāsaka (the illuminator).
The eleventh is declared to be Sukānta (the beautiful end), and the twelfth is remembered as Suśiva (the most auspicious).
The thirteenth is Sunāda, the fourteenth is named Tāra;
the fifteenth is Varābhāsa, and Dhruva with Bindu is the sixteenth.
Ten times seven are said to be the imperishables established in the principle of Vidyā;
and Śiva is the one who is imperishable—thus, in sequence, there are eighteen.
One should diligently know that Bindudeva is both supreme and non-supreme;
by means of the single-rooted ladder, one should ascend to the highest state.
The Goddess said:
How can there be the non-utterance of the *bindu*, or how might its utterance occur?
From the void, a voider void was spoken; thus, eighteen [voids] were taught in succession. || 59 ||
Thus have the principles been proclaimed according to their distinct names;
that shadow which rests upon the eyes emerges from the middle of the eyebrows.
"O Blessed One, you should tell me: what would be the characteristic of such a person?
O Goddess, listen; that which you have asked is a supreme secret. (61)
Therefore, O Goddess, I shall fully explain that unsurpassed nectar of the *lakṣmā*, which is designated as the single *bindu*. (62)

That which is beyond utterance is to be known as Śiva; it is remembered as the unmanifest (avyakta). Devoid of phonemes, it is nothing whatsoever; therefore, it is called the immovable (kūṭastha). || 63 ||
Possessing a body endowed with color, [the Self] is within the range of perception from Brahmā down to a blade of grass;
having produced everything through its nature as a dense web, it departs.
O beautiful one, this is said to be the utterance of the deity Bindu;
therefore, one should utter it joined with others in all ritual actions.
At the time of initiation, during recitation, in the fire sacrifice, and likewise in the ritual worship of the letters,
[the mantra] joined with the nasal drop (bindu) should be employed for the successful accomplishment of all rites.
O fair-faced one, that which I have described to you regarding the invocation by means of the word "Śūnya" should be understood through the division of the elements, beginning with earth. (67)
(78) Its production occurs through one [element], O beautiful one;
* * * * * one hundred and one oblations should be offered; one should unite reality with reality. 68.
That which is devoid of the sixth vowel and consists of the first of the seven principles—
the entire path without exception— should be offered as an oblation by means of the single seed-syllable.
The full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) should be offered for every hundred homas;
one should cause the syllable to be pronounced with a protracted vowel, joined with the nasal bindu.
Then, when [the mantra] is joined with the bindu, the preceptor must perform the nāda;
at its conclusion, the Goddess, one should again offer the full oblations (pūrṇāhuti).
In this way, one attains union with each reality (tattva) by means of that very reality; of this there is no doubt.
Now, I shall describe the target (lakṣa) of that shadow which rests upon the eye. || 72 ||
By the mere knowledge of which one is liberated from the bondage of birth—
all that has been proclaimed in other treatises is here fully set forth. (73)
But the news is told, O Goddess, and this is indeed evident:
"Bindu, Bindu," O Mistress of the Gods, so say all the yogins. (74)
They do not recognize such a direct perception as that which proceeds by way of the wrong path, even though it faces the sword. 75.
With divine vision, one should behold the supreme orb of light;
covering the face, it remains resembling the color of lac.
Resembling the rising sun and appearing as if produced from saffron dye,
it stands like a mass of smokeless embers gathered into a single heap.
O Goddess, he who practices the supreme *lakṣa* [recitation] day after day is not afflicted by diseases within six months. (78)
Strengthened by the splendor of Śiva, he performs even the purification from the murder of a Brahmin without the ignition of fire; of this there is no doubt. (79)
Through the yoga of constant practice, within six months for one who is well-disciplined,
there arises the fulfillment of all desires, even those sought after by the gods.
Within a year, the master of yogis, whose self is disciplined and who is permeated by Śiva,
perceives directly whatever occurs within the three worlds.
Enveloped by this body within the midst of his own splendor,
he creates and withdraws the universe at will, like Śiva, attaining mastery over his own desires.
I shall now tell you how a *lakṣa* will come about even in the midst of that splendor; listen now, for it is not otherwise. (83)
That lakṣa of power (śaktilakṣa) exists precisely within the midst of that fire;
it should be known and understood by them as the beautiful lakṣa of power, O most auspicious one.
For those desiring the accomplishment of the first, which is representation-only, and the second, which is the Great-Lakṣa of eighty lakṣas, [the time required] is that of molten iron. 85.
Just as it has been seen through direct perception and likewise through divine vision,
I shall proclaim the supreme true nature of yoga, which is itself direct perception.
Pressing the breast with the left hand, one should extend half the hand;
all the fingers should be extended, and one [finger] among them should be released. || 87 ||
O Goddess of the Gods, one should fix the target (*lakṣa*) there at the center of the swing;
having established it directly in front of that, one should draw it back through practice. (88)
One should meditate with a single gaze; whenever it wavers, one must certainly steady it. Very gradually, one should draw that focal point toward the face.
One should contemplate [the moon] entering, resembling the milk of a white cow, with an exceedingly cool touch to the face, incomparable and unsurpassed. (90)
O Goddess, as soon as its taste is obtained, one attains perfection; there is no doubt about this.
Endowed with intelligence and splendor for just one month, there is no doubt. (91)
His body will especially arise; there is no doubt in this matter.
Like Śakti, the state of omnipresence belongs to the lord among practitioners (sādhakeśvara).
Even though he had not yet entered the hall of a hundred thousand [verses], he was fortunate and pleasing to behold;
there is no doubt that he was a knower of all scriptures, like the Lord of Speech himself. (93)
O beautiful one, the characteristics of this [mantra], which is like direct perception itself, have been told to you;
now hear in brief the perfection that comes from its divine vision. 94.
O Goddess, when it is seen motionless, pride is dispelled and it brings joy to men;
one should recognize this as the Great Lakṣa, which bestows all perfections.
Whatever exists in the three worlds becomes directly manifest to him;
the yogi, freed from old age and death, blazes like fire. (96)
Whatever he touches with his hand, whatever he beholds with his eye—
all of it blazes like fire, becoming as difficult to touch as it is for even the gods of the Thirty-three.

One who knows yoga is not stained by things edible or inedible, nor even by those who have committed the five heinous sins; he is likewise never stained by such evils as the killing of a Brahmin. (98)
One should observe the remaining group situated in three positions like a garland:
in the case of direct perception, they are white and yellow, as well as blue, black, and white.
One should observe such qualities as these within the midst of the white;
just as a gem pierced by a thread shines brilliantly in its purity.
Thus that garland shines, strung upon the threads of the *nāda*.
O Goddess, this true nature of reality has been declared to you. 101.
Now I shall describe the supreme characteristic of the *bindu*;
it is situated above the forehead in the center of its mandala. (102)
Resembling a water bubble, as pure as clear crystal,
smoke-colored, O Goddess of Gods, and blazing with many rays. (103)
O fair-faced one, this *lakṣa* increases day by day;
within a single month, whatever direction the lord of yogis gazes upon, [it becomes his]. 104.
The yogi perceives the bindu, which resembles lightning and is like Śiva, as it flows; he should contemplate it through the movement of the fourth state. There is no doubt in this matter. 105.
Through the path of the uvula and the palate, into the expansive and auspicious heart-lotus—this should always be meditated upon by yogis for the sake of conquering death. (106)
By the very flow of the iḍā, everything is certainly nourished;
O lady of beautiful hips, it is remembered as the bringer of all accomplishments through its various modes.
This divine characteristic, which brings about all accomplishments,
consists of the knowledge of hearing from afar, mental cognition, and vision. (108)
There is no doubt that it is born within this well-formed body; all those forms previously mentioned are established herein. (109)
O Goddess, that which is characterized by direct perception is remembered as the bringer of all accomplishments;
for accomplishments exist everywhere within the illuminations of reality for one who is well-disciplined. (110)
O Goddess, this supreme essence of knowledge must not be given to one who is wickedly clever, deceitful, cruel, or who treads the path of injustice. (111)
To one who is self-controlled, peaceful, and devoted to the worship of Śiva,
and who follows the path of Śiva— one should [approach] that teacher who has reached the further shore of reality.
This knowledge should be imparted to one whose devotion to the Guru is always greater than that toward Śiva; otherwise, it should never be given at any time. (113)
The Goddess said:

"O Mahādeva, O Lord, explain to me according to the proper method the path of the digits (kalādhvāna), which consists of four parts and comprises the entire universe of moving and non-moving beings. (114)
O Lord, I shall explain the path of Kalā in brief; listen to me as to how creation proceeds through Nivṛtti and how it occurs through Pratiṣṭhā.
O Goddess of the Gods, I shall explain the Vidyā pertaining to Śānti in brief; and I shall also explain, in brief, that which pertains to Śāntyatīta. || 116 ||
p.
88) However, for the *nivṛtti* [kalā], one should offer oblations in the sequence beginning with Earth;
O Goddess of Gods, its emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) is declared to end with *prakṛti*. || 117 ||
O Maheśvarī, having first performed the *pauruṣa* [oblation], one should offer the *māyātattva* last; however, at the time of initiation (*dīkṣā*), the oblation for *pratiṣṭhā* must be offered.
Beginning from the Vidyā up to the principle of Sadāśiva,
the practitioner of mantras should perform oblations for the Vidyā at the time of initiation during the Śiva-sacrifice.
One should offer oblations into the Śānti fire according to the sequence of the Śiva-tattvas;
O Goddess of the Gods, one should then gradually bestow the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) into the Śāntyatīta fire.
Having performed the illumination from the syllable Oṃ, as well as the salutation (namaskāra),
the short Haṃsa shall be Nivṛtti, while that differentiated by the long vowel shall be Pratiṣṭhā.
The Guru should indeed join it with the *vidyā* and the *bindu*;
joined with the *visarga*, it is proclaimed as *śānti*. || 122 ||
It is joined with the syllable *haṃsa* and the utterance *ukāra*, endowed with the ending *vauṣaṭ*,
conjoined with the crescent moon (*ardhendu*) and the nasal sound (*nāda*), and accompanied by the syllable *ū*.
O Goddess, this has been fully explained as the cause for that which transcends peace (śāntyatīta).
Therefore, one who desires union with Śiva (śivasāyujya) should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
In the Nivṛtti [kalā], the eight and three principles (tattvas) are to be offered by the preceptors;
however, in the Pratiṣṭhā [kalā], only seven are to be offered by those who are composed in mind.
In the Vidyā [tattva], one should offer the three principles preceded by Vidyā into the fire;
above that, the Śiva principle is declared to be in the Śānti [tattva].
(90) O Goddess, this is the path of the *kalās*, declared to be the pervasion of emanation (*sṛṣṭivyāpti*).
Having known this, one is liberated and can liberate others; of this there is no doubt. (127)
The Goddess said:
"The vowels and all the gods alike are dependent upon the *bindu*. By what is that *nāda*—which possesses the brilliance and resonance of the *bindus*—distinguished? (128)
Īśvara said:
Within its pericarp, the seed-vitality (bījajīva) is proclaimed;
resembling a thread of lotus fiber, it is pierced by the void of sound (nāda). (129)
The Goddess said:
"O Lord, you have described the partless Bindudeva Maheśvara;
I now wish to hear how he is both with parts and without parts."
Furthermore, O Lord, there is doubt regarding Bindudeva Maheśvara. O Ishana, tell me here of his higher and lower division. (131)
O Goddess, listen, O beautiful one, as I shall fully proclaim that supreme secret of the Lord Bindu, which is both with parts and without parts. 132.
The manifestation of the fifty principles, which effects the continuous cycle of bondage and liberation,
exists in this principle of withdrawal (saṃhāra-tattva) as the manifest form of Svayambhū himself.
The God residing on the Yoga-pīṭha is proclaimed as Sakala (with parts);
but that which transcends it, O Goddess, has been described to you as Niṣkala (without parts).
The Goddess said: (p.
92) Of what nature is his body, and by what seeds is it said to be known?
I desire to know this, O Blessed One; you should deign to speak.

The Lord (Īśvara) is so called because he is described as being under the control of Īśāna and others; likewise, in the word "mantra," he is the Great One who is worshipped through the majesty of his qualities, beginning with all the principles (tattvas). || 136 ||

The fourteen vowels, that which transcends the vowels, that which transcends the *kalās*, and that which transcends the senses—these, together with the neuter letters, should be known as the fifteen syllables. (137)
But another, beyond the three pentads, is liberated in the state of the Bindu as the sixteenth;
he is to be known as Śiva with parts (sakala), for that Śiva creates the Kalā.
Restrained by the end of the *bindu*, [the sound] issues forth from the mass of sounds (*śabdakūṭa*).
The *bindu* expands within the knot (*granthi*), and from that, the emergence of sound occurs. (139)
The five [elements] are the outflow of the aggregate, well-perfumed by the seed-source;
consecrated by the water of power, it is the great sprout of the radiant drop.
The Goddess said:
"What is the meaning of the name 'Binduteja' (Light of the Bindu), and what is this 'bindu' that is spoken of here?
Īśvara replied:
Therefore, O Great Goddess, through your grace, I shall explain that to you.
This Bindu is the Blessed One for you, the one who leads all the world;
it abides in the midst of Sound (Nāda), and its nature is neither origination nor dissolution. || 142 ||
Neither the lunar mansion nor the seed is its creator;
it is never diminished, nor does even the slightest part diminish, nor is it ever censured, yet it increases nowhere. (143)
Existing as both unmanifest and manifest, he is extremely subtle yet not merely subtle;
like the wind, he moves eternally with his ten forms.
The protector of the eight worlds, with eyes like lotuses, he is this very Lord Bindu, the teacher of all the worlds and the universe. 145.
He is the fierce one who brings about the end of the eon, filling the seven continents and so forth;
he leaves only the seven oceans remaining and is the destroyer of the twelve suns. || 146 ||
The entire world here exists as a single egg, like a lump of clay, with its foundation in the netherworld and its surface crushed by the bodies of serpents. 147.
With the subtle balance of yoga, Śiva weighs this entire world of the moving and the unmoving— just as one might weigh a jewel with the half-and-half space between the chin and the armpit. (148)
Whirling the machine of the potter’s wheel that is saṃsāra through his māyā, he is Time, and he is indeed Death; he is Indra, Varuṇa, and the Moon.
He is indeed Anala, Nīla, Āditya, and Ākāśa in succession;
he is Brahmā, he is Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Īśvara as well. (150)
Hrī, Śrī, Smṛti, Dhṛti, Medhā, Kānti, Sarasvatī, Prakṛti, Puruṣa, Niyati, and Kāla. (151)
This Lord is Māyā and Vidyā; from the Bindu, this entire world [proceeds].
He is likewise the Veda, Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Buddhism, and Jainism. || 152 ||
Whatever treatises there may be, all have issued forth from the Bindu;
one should know that everything consists of the Bindu—mind, consciousness, and form. (153)
He is the most excellent, consisting of all the immortals, the bearer of the burden of all scriptures;
he is immeasurable, subtle, unmanifest, and eternal.
Whether walking, throbbing, sleeping, eating, or even waking, for those whose nature is permeated by Śiva, the Bindu-deity is their eternal self. 155.

Then, with his body divided as Ardhanārī, he is remembered by you as Sakala (with parts); then, through the yoga of the absorption of his partial portions, she is remembered as Niṣkala (without parts).
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter of the Niśvāsakārikā. The Goddess said:
"O Blessed One, I wish to hear the definitive explanation of the sound of Nāda."
It is proclaimed to be of two kinds, distinguished as gross and subtle. || 1 ||
O Maheśvara, how does the nāda become gross or even subtle?
How is it to be known within the body in its true essence? Tell me this.
O Goddess, listen; I shall explain to you that supreme secret which you have asked about—
the unsurpassed knowledge of Nāda.
That sound which is heard perfectly full from within the body—
therein Prakṛti has arisen, clothed in a great net.
One should report that he stands there in the midst of that resonance;
the person born there has transcended all qualities and is stainless. (5)
The third, however, was the great sound, abiding like the resonance of a bell;
within that, Rudra was born, the Lord and leader of the three worlds.
That which is declared to be the peaceful, supreme cause, the sound,
stands like a mass of moonlight, resembling a staff for striking the wicked.
Within that [egg] arose the Lord, a mass of splendor belonging to the Great Soul—
he who is the perfected Śiva, subtle, perfectly tranquil, and facing in all directions.
For he is indeed immeasurable and inexpressible, yet he is proclaimed to be the essence of sound (nāda);
and that very same [reality] is celebrated by the knowers of truth as the state of dissolution (layastha). || 9 ||
The supreme deity is beyond the state of dissolution, indefinable, and free from affliction;
knowing this, the man of knowledge is liberated even while enjoying sense objects. (10)
"This supreme secret knowledge has not been told to just anyone.
The Goddess said:
"What is this Nāda? What is its measure? What is its form? From where has it issued? (11)
"For what purpose and by whom was this uttered, and how does it proceed?
The Lord said:
"O fair-faced one, this is my supreme form, known as Nāda."
It is constantly contemplated by yogins who desire the state of no further rebirth;
because it is all-pervasive, no measure of this liberation can be apprehended. (13)
Because it is beginningless, there is no origination; and because it is eternal, there is no fixed destiny. It is like conventional reality—unutterable and devoid of words and syllables. (14)
That is attained with ease; I shall tell you the means for it:
having covered both ears of the practitioner with the two thumbs. (15)
Then he hears that sound, which has a resonance like the roar of a thundercloud;
O Goddess with long eyes, from hearing this sound— || 16 ||
Having severed the bonds of the fetters, he attains supreme nirvāṇa;
this subtle body of mine is designated as "sound. (17)
This wonderful [teaching] has been made manifest for the purpose of removing the bonds of the bound soul (paśu); beyond this, there is no other object of meditation to be taught. (18)
And this supreme, unutterable, and stainless potency of his is not obtained by the Goddess when I am not pleased. (p. 101) 19.
He who correctly discerns this attains identity with it;
thus has this supreme and most difficult-to-attain Nāda been explained to you. (20)
Now hear of that irreproachable state where this [self] attains dissolution;
it is the fourth stage, known as the Turya, which transcends this [third].
One should perceive the fifth state as space, situated in equilibrium;
it is immovable, indefinable, infinite, unborn, and undecaying.
Without beginning, middle, or end, one, without returning,
free from conceptual proliferation, mental in nature, beyond the senses, and free from affliction.
Extensive, uninterrupted in its middle and ends, facing in all directions,
stainless, pure, circular, lofty, pervasive, and eternal. (24)
The ether known as Sadāśiva is declared to possess such qualities;
this subtle, imperishable supreme ether is the seed of the universe. (25)
Here, the *nāda* (sound) attains dissolution when all activity has ceased;
having reached the dissolution of desire, it indeed attains that state which is beyond calculation even here.
By His will, these beings become once again embodied in sound; thereafter, those whose bodies are sound abide in the station of universal sovereignty.
By the will of the Lord, they perform the act of bestowing grace upon the worlds;
having thus assumed their office, [they do so] through the expenditure of this time.
"They again attain the state that is unattainable by nature, which is empty and free from the ego. Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the *Niśvāsakārikā*.
O Lord Śiva Mahādeva, tell me specifically the definition of Śakti and the nature of Śakti.
Is this power in the cause said to be different from it, or non-different? (1)
Whether by way of identity or difference, I ask this concerning my doubt:
if the power were not different from those two, tell me what the distinction between them is.
Or else, there might be another power [distinct] from Śiva; therefore, he would not be the uncaused [cause].
Through the state of being either non-different or different, there arises the doubt as to whether he exists or does not exist. || 3 ||
(104) The scriptures have various differing conclusions; one who is of a doubting nature perishes.
Therefore, O Supreme Lord, speak without concealment so that I may be free from doubt. 4.
The Lord is the non-different cause; His power is characterized by presiding over [the universe].
He is omniscient, conscious, pure, and the illuminator of all principles. || 5 ||
Abiding therein among all principles, it should illuminate those various states according to their qualities and defects, among living beings who are both pure and impure.
Likewise, the power that pervades all beings, as well as their essential nature and the senses,
eternally abides within them all.
Just as the quality of burning exists in fire and the state of coolness in water, so too do these six qualities exist within the non-dual reality, for they are the powers of the Lord. (8)
Just as there is the supporting of the earth, just as there are rays in the sun,
and just as there is space in the sky— such are the powers of the Lord.
Just as fragrance is in the earth, form in fire, taste in water,
touch in the lordly wind, and sound [in ether], so too are the powers of the Lord.
Just as rays belong to the sun, or as the radiance belongs to gems,
so too is the beginninglessness of power (śakti) and the possessor of power (śaktimat) accepted here.
Just as the radiance of jewels, fire, the moon, and so forth, is inseparable from the sun,
so too do the powers (śakti) residing within one's own body belong to the supreme Śiva.
Whether undivided or divided, characterized by the nature of being a property-bearer (dharmin) or a property (dharma),
[the Lord] establishes the activity of the property according to His own will. (13)
When the substratum (dharmin) does not exist, the property (dharma) cannot attain establishment;
when the substratum is maintained, that property is said here to have a valid cause.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the Niśvāsakārikā.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord, O Maheśvara, even now there remains a doubt regarding knowledge and the object of knowledge."
Tell me in its entirety the distinction between reality, both supreme and non-supreme.
How do the principles (tattvas) perform the various activities within the bodies of embodied beings?
And how do those principles experience dreams while lying down? || 2 ||
Whether standing or walking, speaking or even laughing, what principles reside in breathing? They reside in the long breath (*dīrghaprāṇa*) while one is active. (3)
And what principles (tattvas) are proclaimed for him during the middle and the conclusion [of the rite],
while he dances and sings, filled with passion and longing for compassion?
And who abide in the signless (animitta), and who indeed remain in the state of contemplation?
What is the destiny for those attached to ritual actions when they give up their lives? (5)
Tell me by what these principles are impelled to perform their activities;
and how are the principles known to exist in eight or nine forms?
How is there equality among the groups ending in the final consonants, and how is the taste uniform? And how is it that those devoid of internal organs are established within the body? (7)
(108) "O Mahādeva, please graciously explain this secret.
Īśvara said:
Listen, O Goddess, to the supreme secret as to how the principles (tattvas) are situated within the body.
And hear how they perform their activities when presided over by another— the true nature of knowledge, the distinction between the principles, and that which is supreme and inferior.
Exaltation, agitation of mind, as well as the prowess of the sun, intoxication with joy, and delusion—these, O beautiful goddess, have been described. 10.
All this has been declared as full of essence and should be understood by those who contemplate reality;
likewise, there is the upward stream, the power of experience, and those on the left and right.
Steady up to the ears and tranquil, the supreme partless [reality] has been described;
with speech placed upon the lower lip, one gazes without a causal object. (12)
Laughing, the state residing within the heart shines forth in eight ways as it is described; having thus known these eight ways, this indeed is the characteristic of emptiness.
The palate [is characterized] by the taste of joy; cough, breath, and the hanging tongue;
joined with the sound "huṃ" and the mind—this is declared as the eightfold [mantra] rich in aesthetic power (kalā). 14.
One should observe the face for sweetness, the *halāhala* (poisonous) look, brilliance, fear, terror, trembling, and whether it is joined with anger or compassion. 15.
O Goddess, it is fragile like a child's [toy], turned away, and beautifully shimmering;
it is scattered by fire and wind, and its song is accompanied by the sound of tinkling ornaments. 16.
That which is named Kṣapaṇa has been declared as the supreme knowledge. One should recognize the states of Āghūrmita, Vighūrmita, Suṣupta, and Supta. (17)
O beautiful one, awakening is indeed the cessation of the continuity of the dream-impact;
these qualities at the end of destruction are to be understood by those who contemplate reality. 18.
Gentle and steady movement, as well as leaping and shifting;
the sound "huṃ," harsh speech, and the eight Vedas in the throat and lips. (19)
O Goddess, pervasiveness has been described; now understand the nature of sound as well:
the deity is with parts (sakala) in the udāna breath, and partless (niṣkala) in the supreme state when [the breath] is agitated. 20.
One should understand that in the void of thought, the piercing of the heart has been described by me;
in the secret [teaching], however, the essence of the *kalās* is known as the impurity of *vikrama*.

O lady of excellent hips, one who knows the knowledge should understand that "harṣe" (in joy) signifies "kṣepaṇam" (casting forth); likewise, in the case of "unmāde" (insanity), you should comprehend it as "kṣayam antam" (the end of destruction). 22.
Then, in the state of delusion (moha), there is that which is guttural-labial; this indeed is the first group of eight.
Above that is the union with the manifest (sakala), the unmanifest (niṣkala), the sustainer, and the trembling one.
That which is without appearance is said to be "emptiness"; it should be scrutinized with effort.
On the left is the principle of Kalesvara, and on the right is Bhujamalin.
O Goddess, the mendicant (kṣapaṇa) should be known through the application of the heart up to the ear;
O lady of excellent hips, he is the end of decay, partless, and characterized by the body. (25)
In the principle of Śānta, the second characteristic of differentiation has been declared to me:
the *sakala* [form] is in the path of the mouth, while the *niṣkala* [form] is in the left path.

In the state of emptiness, when there is distraction regarding the support, it is conceptualized as the absence of intrinsic nature; in the signless state, however, one who is rich in creative power perceives [reality] as being remembered as a stainless void. (27)
The destruction [of defilements] is to be known through laughter; one should observe it within the mind itself.
O you who abide within, I shall explain to you that internal radiance which brings about the destruction of what resides in the heart. (28)
The Lord Īśāna is established in the throat and lips; there is no further [higher] stride.
Thus, the eightfold impurity (malāṣṭaka) is to be understood through the threefold division of knowledge.
O lady of excellent hips, the third supreme division has been described:
the deity with parts (sakala) resides within the heart, while the partless (niṣkala) is unperceived.

One should know the palate to be empty; one should perceive existence within its own nature. When it is illuminated, one should know it as endowed with the digits (kalā); when the void is agitated by the breath, [it is known]. // 31 //
O Goddess, one should know that the *pralamba* [breath] is the *kṣapaṇa*; it is proclaimed as *svarita*.
O lady of excellent hips, one should recognize the *kṣapita* by means of the sound *huṃ*. (32)
Likewise, O Goddess, that which is joined with *na* is proclaimed as the gutturo-labial;
this, O beautiful lady of the gods, is declared to be the fourth division.

O beautiful lady, in the sweet [note] one should know the eternal state within the totality; having reached the station of Ananta, it is characterized by the meaning of emptiness in the laughable [note]. (34)
When one is afraid, Kāleśvara is to be known; when terrified, Khamala is remembered;
when trembling, Kṣapaṇa is proclaimed—thus it has been told in due order. (35)
The other is the abiding reality, compassion, the eightfold nectar;
this is indeed declared as the fifth division in its proper sequence.
In movement, they call it the support of three steps; in that which is fragile, the partless supreme; in pervasiveness, the void—this is your Bhujamālin. (37)
O Aparājita, one should always understand that these elements— earth, water, fire, air, and space— are distinct entities, even when they exist together within the body.
O lady of excellent hips, maintain the thread within the house until its end;
O beautiful goddess, [recite] that which is produced from the throat and lips, joined with the sound of the *jhaṅkāra*.
The six varieties have been explained in due order according to their application:
in the state of Aghūrmita, there is the support of Kalās; in Vighūrma, it consists of the Niṣkala (the partless).
They say that in deep sleep it is empty; one should perceive it as being veiled.
But in the dream state, time arises from mental construction, while at the end of the dream, it is remembered as the pure void.
O Goddess, [the syllable] *kṣa* is for destruction in the case of obstacles (*vighāta*), and *kṣaya* is for the end of the lineage (*santāna*).
Then, for awakening (*vibodha*), there is *kaṇṭhoṣṭhya*; thus, the seven [syllables] are in sequence, with *subheda* as the seventh. (42)
In the case of a gentle [sign], they say the movement is gentle; in a fixed [sign], it is indeed the supreme, partless state.
One should know the swift [movement] to be empty, and one should observe its own course. (43)
In the act of leaping, the deity is known as Kālatattva; in the act of moving, he is remembered as Khamala.
In the utterance of the syllable *huṃ*, the deity is Kṣapaṇa; he should reverse all of this.
At the end of the *kṣaya* [syllable], *jharjhara* is proclaimed; one should observe it in that which is called auspicious (*śubha*).
In speech with broad syllables and bright vowels, the gutturo-labial [sound] is situated everywhere. (45)

O Goddess, having thoroughly understood this supreme reality—which is stainless due to the distinction of its eight divisions and free from parts—by means of the prescribed method, it is truly known. (46)
Thus, for one who knows the distinctions of consciousness, there is no doubt regarding liberation. (p.
117) In that which is called Haṃsa, there is Bindu and Nāda; in the Half-moon is Nirodhikā.
The pervasive one and the upward-moving power reach the great state of peace;
all that is imperishable within the imperishable should be understood in its proper sequence.
He who knows this in its true essence shall become that supreme goal.
Thus, indeed, O beautiful one, has the eightfold division been explained to you. 49.
Furthermore, I shall later explain it in nine ways as it truly is.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter of the Niśvāsakārikā. The Lord said:
Henceforth, I shall proclaim the unsurpassed knowledge of sound,
which resides within sentences, within the heart, and is established even as it is being imparted.
In the three locations, the entire deity brings about the destruction of the bonds of bondage;
one should know Śiva as the follower, while the prowess belongs to the Queen of Knowledge (Vidyārājñī). || 2 ||
O Goddess, that which follows the breath should be designated as "niṣkala" (partless);
it is divine, born of the *apāna*, and devoid of the limits of the navel and the ears. || 3 ||
It is eternally situated in the midst of the void, liberating one from all bonds within;
it is the palate located between the ears and the navel, curved like the stalk of a lotus.
That which is designated by the name Kalāḍhya is the creator of all forms;
it casts both of those [principles] into that reality (tattva), the tranquil reality (śāntatattva), along with all the others.
The mind should always contemplate everything together with the states of space,
as the fire of the upward-moving breath (ūrdhvavāha) blazes forth within the body in brief.
(119) Well-applied and perfectly tranquil, it removes the fetters of the *kṣapaṇa* [ascetic];
[one should place it] from the heart-lotus to the navel region, and between the ears and the palate.
For in these aforementioned locations, the auspicious destruction that ends the bonds occurs;
it is in the udāna at the station of immobility, and in all stations, O beautiful-eyed one.
Everything should be consumed with the word "sarva"; the eighth word is "kūṭastha.
O Goddess, this group of eight words has been proclaimed for the sake of welfare.
Nor should the supreme good be given away; there is no knowledge higher than this.
The meditation on emptiness is difficult to perceive, being without beginning or end and devoid of intrinsic existence.
Therefore, with every effort, one should characterize [reality] through both existence and non-existence;
by this it is known, O fair-hipped one, that my state resides within him whose being [is thus realized].
(120) For the sake of protecting non-existence, I have composed this discourse on existence for one whose mind has abandoned non-existence and turned toward existence. (12)
One wanders in saṃsāra as long as one does not find the true state of being, even through the words of the meaning of Śruti and Smṛti, or through the beauties of poetry and rhetoric. (13)
One who is deluded by reflection on the treatises of grammar goes to a downward state;
non-existence leads to emptiness, and that which is empty is called non-existence.
Liberation is said to be non-existence, while bondage is the conceptualization of existence.
Through non-existence, the mind becomes eternally motionless within the void. (15)
Then the embodied soul, going toward Nirvana, proceeds to the abode that is free from all affliction.
I contemplate that which is without state or word, inaccessible, the pure emptiness of nirvāṇa, the vast sky above, all-pervading.
By which [means] a person who has practiced the non-dual void is not born again here in a womb;
the net of bonds is severed, primordial nature ceases its activity, and he is withdrawn from the state of creation. || 16 1/2 ||
Behold that which is solitary, become void, and free from the impurities of worldly existence; behold this state here declared by those liberated from all bonds as the void of Nirvana.
This is void, this is void; from the void, the void is both supreme and inferior.
And that which is empty even from emptiness—that emptiness is indeed free from affliction. || 17 1/2 ||
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter in the Jñānakāṇḍa of the Niśvāsakārikā.
The Goddess said:
O Knower of the Vedas, Sāṃkhya, Purāṇas, Pāñcarātra, and Itihāsas!
And likewise for other yogins, as well as those who abide even on wrong paths. || 1 ||
Having deluded them with their circle of breasts, they show them their own bodies;
and they too say here: "What other way could there be here? (2)
"There would either be partiality in this [teaching], or liberation would exist everywhere.
O Lord, I have this doubt; tell me that which is the truth. (3)
Īśvara said:
O large-eyed one, both you and I are the root of all people;
as Mātṛkā in the form of Śiva, we are the tree born of the intellect.
a) From the realm of Brahmā down to the very foundations of the earth, the entire world of moving and unmoving beings— all have originated from my seed and emerged from your womb. (5)
The five [languages] beginning with Vedic that are proclaimed on earth as the great sciences are:
Sanskrit, Prākṛta, Apabhraṃśa, and Anunāsika.
Whatever verbal expression exists, whether divine or non-divine, is born from your progeny;
you are the goddess who is eternally proud, always devoted to egoism.
Since everything is established in you, transformations arise from you;
therefore, the world perceives me as subject to transformation, though I am free from change.
Those who are deluded regarding the fundamental knowledge do not attain the supreme goal;
for all living beings die even while consuming food of the six flavors.
Having consumed the root of the *mṛtasañjīvanī* plant, they do not die;
just as a jar exists within a lump of clay, or a cloth within its threads. (10)
The phonemes, existing in the form of power (*śakti*), attain manifestation by the will of Śiva.
The Goddess said:
"Having recited the root-knowledge (*mūlajñāna*), the yogis, being disciplined, meditate upon it. (11)
Having all their desires fulfilled, they enter the auspicious state; O Maheśvara, liberation is attained through renunciation and through the practice of ascetic conduct.
O Lord, that liberation which is obtained through contentment by those veiled by ignorance is likewise obtained through knowledge;
you are the illuminator of that knowledge.
O Lord of Gods, tell me how worship, knowledge, and the object of knowledge may come to be; O Lord of Gods, I have a great doubt regarding this. (14)
The ignorant desire liberation through the practice of renunciation and non-renunciation, through contentment and self-restraint, and indeed through the emaciation of the body. || 15 ||
The wise seeker of liberation should endure cold, wind, heat, fire, the ten [senses], and the eleven [faculties], as well as hunger, thirst, and rain. (16)
"Celibacy, austerity, charity, compassion, patience, and non-violence—this speech is not for the sake of birth, nor does it lead to pervading the world, nor to liberation. (17)
Liberation does not come through charity, nor through austerities, nor through the Vedas and sacrifices;
liberation comes through knowledge alone for the embodied soul when it is completely freed.

Even one whose senses and mind are restrained—what could he do with knowledge that is so difficult to attain? He would be like a charioteer mounted on a well-trained chariot who lacks the power of sight. (19)
The Goddess said:
Those Brahmins who are exponents of the Vedas, those who know the Sāṃkhya, those who know Yoga, and those who are learned in the Pañcarātra—[if they associate] with other sinful people... 20.
They speak thus, O Mahādeva; I shall declare their knowledge:
it is like fire cast into fire, or water poured into water. (21)

Just as a lump of clay is devoid of pleasure and lacks consciousness when struck by a staff or a stone, so too should Nirvana be understood as being entirely free from both pleasure and pain. || 22 ||
"O Lord, this has been told to you by me just as it was known to me.
Īśvara said:
All are likewise afflicted, being utterly ignorant of the reality of liberation. || 23 ||
I shall tell you; listen to what liberation is like:
it is where there is the destruction of the living soul, devoid of happiness and devoid of consciousness. (24)
For them, liberation is like the dissolution of a lump of clay; it is not truly called liberation.
Their liberation consists of the belly of Māyā, whereas for him [the enlightened one], it is consciousness remaining in its true state.
One should remain like a corpse, free from the duality of deep sleep, through both dishonor and liberation, being devoid of conscious awareness. (26)

Thus, even though this essence exists, for one whose mind is attached to sense objects, it remains [unrealized] within this auspicious great knowledge of Śiva, the city of supreme realization. || 27 ||
The Lord is omniscient in mind, all-pervading, subtle, auspicious, and imperishable;
indeed, that state of equality with the nature of the Master belongs to the knower. (28)
He shall be omniscient and complete, all-pervading and imperishable;
there is no arrival of sufferings, and therein happiness is uninterrupted. (29)
The state where all attachments have ceased and which is tranquil is designated as "liberation.
Liberation belongs to both consciousness and its absence; it is not merely the release from delusion.
When consciousness is pervasive and free from delusion, it is designated as liberation;
having become Śiva, the stainless one, he remains devoid of passion. || 31 ||
That wise one, whose mode of being is self-dependent, who is seated in bliss and bestows happiness,
becomes either bodiless or embodied according to his own will.
Becoming more gross than the gross and likewise more subtle than the subtle, he enjoys sovereignty over all worlds according to his pleasure. (33)
They are indeed free from obstruction, devoid of passion and greed;
having attained the supreme, attributeless Śiva-knowledge that fulfills all desires. || 34 ||
Having become the Great Self within the Uneven One, he creates himself within himself;
pervading everything, they remain established, abiding within all beings.
There is nothing unknown to her, nothing unseen, and nothing unresorted to;
there is never any movement of hers that has not already reached all the worlds. (36)

Through their intuitive discernment, they always grasp the objects of reality—both the transformations of primordial nature (prakṛti) and that which is devoid of qualities as well as the qualities themselves. (37)
Having been sustained by the Cause, they grasp their respective objects;
and all those qualities of sovereignty abide in the eternal Śiva. (38)
Even among those who have been initiated and who know the reality, he alone—endowed with immeasurable power, omniscient, and indeed the giver of all—is [the true teacher]. (39)
He is remembered as the doer of all, the lord of all yogas, and equal to Śiva;
he possesses the power of hearing from afar, as well as knowledge, reflection, and vision.
Free from the forms of mind, intellect, ego, and the causes [of perception],
the slayer of Bali is self-dependent in all his undertakings.
Dhāraka, Preraka, Adhiṣṭhātā, Kalarava, Damana of all beings, Mana, and Unmana. (42)
The Lord of All, the Soul of All, the Master of All, and the Great Goal; he is ageless, immortal, imperishable, and the agitator of all. || 43 ||
Whatever qualities belong to those born of eggs—the suffering of conception, birth, and old age—all these arise from ignorance; there is only one true happiness, which is absolute.
Just as the pure fire, though produced by friction while residing within wood, does not enter the fire-drill again once the time for its extinction has arrived; [so it is with the Self]. (45)
Once it has attained the state of clarified butter, it cannot become curd again;
likewise, having realized perfect knowledge, one does not become a bound soul (paśu) again. || 46 ||
Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the Jñānakāṇḍa of the Niśvāsakārikā.
The Goddess said:
"Without having attained supreme perfection, even one who has been initiated and is endowed with knowledge..."
Having understood the true nature of the scriptures, one is nonetheless tormented by the sufferings of death.
O Lord, O Supreme Sovereign, tell me: what would be the cause for [the fruits of action] regarding living beings while they are acting, since their destiny is imperceptible?
The Lord is two finger-breadths above; that is the place where He resides during salutation.
That trident, by the force of the wind, is upon the right breast.
For seven nights, people listen to [the teaching] by name and by self,
including the short, long, and protracted vowels, as well as the *sādhārita* and *sakauśaka*.
From the moment of vibration (*spandana*) until the end of the month of one's own fortnight,
the *Tantriṇī* conjoined with the eighth [vowel] is known as the nectar (*amṛta*). (5)
Nandā, Bhadrā, Jayā, Riktā, and Pūrṇā—these are the five worldly [tithis] that recur every three nights; now hear from me regarding those belonging to Śiva.
The lunar day (tithi) is Amṛtā, and by its very nature it is the second; the asterism (nakṣatra) is Abhijit, and above that is Jayantikā.
The moment known as Piṅgala consists of the two stars Brahmā and Viṣṇu;
it repeatedly sweeps around like a wheel with the moonlight of the cluster of the Dhruva star.
When the sun of immeasurable lifespan has risen and shines intensely, licking [the vital breaths], then one falls under the power of death at the completion of the year; of this there is no doubt.
Having understood this, the wise person should perform acts of giving, recitation, and meditation on the day of immortality; all of that shall become a bestower of liberation. (10)
Whatever action one performs under the lunar mansion named Abhijit, or during the Jaya-lagna, or under the asterisms of Rudra and Vaiṣṇava, all that bestows the attainment of liberation.
Whatever action a man performs during the Piṅgala Muhūrta,
having understood the day of the week and the lunar date, all that bestows both success and liberation.
The two fortnights consist of truth and untruth, and the third is the fixed one;
when conjoined with immortality, liberation is granted by one of these two.
Through recitation and the yoga of meditation, success shall be achieved in a single day;
for thus indeed does one who understands this supreme secret [attain it]. (14)
He shall become equal to Śiva and rejoices together with Śiva;
his dead body shall not decay—this is the supreme conviction. (15)
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter in the Jñānakāṇḍa of the Niśvāsakārikā.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord, those who were created by you in the past have been separated from their respective rites."
The Brahmins, endowed with the eight forms, perform sacrifices through various rites.
Why are those very people who have been initiated by various performers with abundant sacrificial fees not liberated by those same mantras? (2)
If you truly speak the truth, that [the Vedas] lead the castes to union [with the divine],
then why do those Vedas, which are composed of the very same castes, not grant liberation? (3)
The masters say: some know it as the *praṇava*, others know it as the syllable *ma*;
it is the arrangement of fifty letters, the Puruṣa whose form is the *bindu*.
A certain sixteenth digit of the moon, possessing the luster of nectar,
is the source of trees, shrubs, creepers, and medicinal herbs.
The glorious one, the best among all sustainers of beings, is like nectar and the speaker of nectar;
some say he is the syllable "Ya," while others say he is the life-breath and so forth, facing in every direction.
In all things, the All-Knowing Creator acts wherever He proceeds;
the wise declare that the letter 'ra' here signifies fire.
The withdrawal of all principles is renowned as being like the fire of time;
that consumer, whose fuel is food and drink, is called the individual self (jīvātman). (8)
Some praise Indu, who is honored by gods and asuras;
others call him Vibhū, who is worshipped by Śakra. (9)
All those who bow before you [bow] to the syllable *la*, the supreme state, which resembles the kunda flower dripping with nectar and is as cooling as the rays of the moon. (10)
