They say that the seed-syllable of Varuṇa, which is eternal and bestows life upon living beings, is supreme;
yet others say that the seed-syllable of space (Vyoman) is unsurpassed.
Space is the support of all beings, providing them with room;
some say this is the best, being established as half of half of fifty.
The letter *ma* is the supreme reality; standing with his arms raised, he is the Puruṣa consisting of twelve syllables, which the elders learned in the three Vedas possess. (13)
He is Agni, the lord of sacrifice, the sacrifice itself, the utterance *vaṣaṭ*, and the *svadhā* offering;
he is the Sun, the end of all, who shines in the east.
The waking state, preceded by the letter 'A', which sets all phonemes in motion, is the *Ṛgveda*, the *Āhavanīya* fire, and is said to be the *Sāttvika* quality. (15)
The letter *A* is proclaimed as the Brahman of the earth-element among all beings;
the letter *U* has Viṣṇu as its deity, is characterized by passion (*rajas*), and has the nature of liquidity.
For this Dakṣiṇāgni is remembered as consisting of the Yajurveda;
they call the inner self within the dream state the supreme abode.
The syllable *makāra* has Rudra as its deity and is proclaimed to be characterized by *tamas*.
The *Sāman* is indeed the *gārhapatya* fire; it is characterized by the quality of *tamas*. (18)
They call the state of deep sleep the supreme state;
indeed, the letter *ha* without measure is the fourth [state], that supreme state. (19)
The *sañjīva* [breath of life] is the essence of the mantras of the Atharvaveda for all embodied beings;
it transcends the *guṇas*, and by knowing that supreme peace, one attains immortality. (20)
The stainless, divine space, all-pervading, the immutable Lord—this is the supreme Brahman, the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta), which is the eternal Self. || 21 ||
Some call this the manifest Śiva, the tenfold seed-enclosure;
it is remembered as the abode of all vidyās, the "Vidyālaya."
(139) Regarding that, others speak of what is expressed through the syllables of the three principles;
some, relying on the knowledge of the Savior (Tāraka), [speak of] the Lord of a million [verses]. || 23 ||
The Lord of the Sixty-nine, the Destroyer of Keśin’s Noose, and likewise the Withdrawal of the Fifty Seeds—this is considered the supreme cause. (24)
They say that Sadāśiva, the sound, is the cause of all beings;
he alone is Śiva, existing in five states, both with parts and without parts.
Likewise, other people who know the knowledge of Śiva conceive of it in this [place] as having the curved form of a serpent—unutterable and free from affliction. (26)
First, among all the scriptures, this is written but not recited;
thus, it is devoid of salutation with joined palms, chanting, and meditation. (27)
p.
140) Devoid of the instruments [of perception] such as smell, form, taste, touch, and sound, and with the mind free from volitional constructions—that indeed is the supreme state. || 28 ||
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Śiva—
thus the Praṇava is proclaimed to have five aspects and five deities.
Śiva, whose form is fivefold, consists of one mātrā, two mātrās, three mātrās, and likewise more than that, as well as that which abides in half a mātrā and half of a half-mātrā.
Those who know the Vedas and those who propound Sāṃkhya, being thus deluded regarding these matters and confused by the section on knowledge (jñānapāda), do not arrive at a certain conclusion.
Deprived of the supreme reality and devoid of primordial origination, those deluded ones do not understand that the *ṛc*s alone possess the pervasiveness of the mantra. || 32 ||
(149) By means of pride in the Purāṇas and Vedas, and likewise by the Smṛtis,
men whose souls are well-sprinkled with gross states of being are devoted to the knowledge of cattle. (33)
They defile the Śaiva knowledge of Śiva, which brings about the destruction of all [suffering];
being firmly established in their own position, they revile the positions of others. (34)
Not knowing the pervasion of the *varṇas*, nor likewise the pervasion of the *tattvas*, and not knowing the supreme reality (*paratattva*), they desire the fruits of gross knowledge. || 35 ||
For this reason, O Goddess, in that [state] letters do not grant liberation;
all those of unsettled minds dispute with one another. (36)
"In this way, they mutually revile one another through formal debate, frivolous chatter, and cavil.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Manner of the Delusion of Knowledge," in the Jñānakāṇḍa of the Niśvāsakārikā.
The Goddess said:
It is traditionally held that among the principles of Pradhāna, Ātman, and Īśa, action alone is innate.
For what purpose does the Lord perform creation—that which is born of Pradhāna? (1)
O Śaṅkara, how does this bound soul (paśu) become one who has accomplished his purpose?
Is the body derived from primordial matter (pradhāna), or what is its ultimate nature? || 2 ||
What is the characteristic of one who is awakening, and how do the awakened and the unawakened differ?
Among Pradhāna, Puruṣa, and Īśāna, whose is agency, and of what kind? (3)
Having reached the state of the *kalala*, how does the person remain?
O Lord of the Gods, for what purpose is there bondage, and what indeed is bondage? (4)
What is the nature of bondage, or who is bound by bondage? Is the individual soul (paśu) joined with primordial matter (prakṛti), and is he separated from it? (5)
And how is the creation of the principles (tattvas) brought about, and what is the nature of the differentiation of their functions?
[Tell me] truly of that which possesses qualities and that which is without qualities, as well as the various types of yoga.
O Lord, tell me all this again in due order; O Goddess,
embodied beings have been submerged in the beginningless stream of existence.
Like a boat for crossing over, this triple principle (tritatva) is taught;
it has been explained to you, O Goddess of Gods, as the supreme primary quality.
The individual soul (aṇu) is devoid of qualities, yet it possesses form; though all-pervading, it is powerless and imperishable.
Its conduct is downward, its nature is insatiable, it experiences the qualities (guṇas), and it remains within the sphere of bondage. || 9 ||

The individual soul (puruṣa) is traditionally held to be powerless, a creator of cattle, possessed of passion, ignorant, other [than the Supreme], not all-knowing, incomplete, and indifferent. || 10 ||
Such a thing characterized by these attributes would be a state of non-awakening;
[for the true Self] is devoid of qualities, all-knowing, the agent, independent, and has everything as its sphere of experience. (11)
Complete, imperishable, peaceful, subtle, powerful, supreme, and formless—this is declared to be the characteristic of the Supreme Goddess as she is being realized. 12.
The eternally awakened and pure Self, whose form is the intellect of the cause;
He is infinite, immovable, eternally satisfied, and without support. || 13 ||
The immutably established, the Lord, the Master of all, of measured luster;
the beginningless, the one, the unshakable, the conscious, the sustainer of all—Śiva. (14)
O beautiful-eyed one, the Smṛtis indeed declare that the Pradhāna alone is omnipresent, designated as the "field" (kṣetra), and insentient. 15.
And for all [beings], the one Puruṣa is traditionally held to be the conscious enjoyer of the field;
because it is insentient, the Unmanifest does not act of its own accord.
Since volition also lacks independence, it is a union of both;
the conjunction of these two states is a great cause of delusion.
Existing in the form of dissolution and origination, these two are beginningless and unperceived;
both consciousness and unconsciousness are likewise without a lord.
They undergo manifold division through the desire for the differentiation of syllables;
Īśvara, presiding over that [differentiation], [governs] the two, namely Pradhāna and Puruṣa. (19)
Having extracted the entities from the principles in their proper sequence,
the Lord, having perceived the name and the object, creates the emanations born of Pradhāna.
This [treatise] on the waters is proclaimed for the sake of liberating the bound soul (paśu) from its fetters;
for even though the bound soul is solitary, it is rendered powerless when colored by innate fetters.
And because it does not perceive the existence of the principles beginning with the Unmanifest (avyakta), it is non-existent;
for, due to its lack of awakening and its reliance on the qualities of the unmanifest, it remains unawakened. || 22 ||
Having attained that state, he experiences the arising of the fruits of pleasure and pain;
for although the Lord is capable of bestowing grace upon the individual soul (paśu) alone, [he does not do so]. (23)
The Lord indeed does not act impulsely, for he would otherwise destroy what has already been accomplished;
since he lacks any external cause, he does not perceive [an object] within the self of the person. (24)
Therefore, Maheśvara brings about the conjunction of its causes;
they call the unmanifested the instrument (karaṇa), and the effect possesses ten characteristics.
Under the influence of another, it performs the purpose of the Puruṣa in many ways;
therein, however, the purpose of the Puruṣa is proclaimed to be pure consciousness alone. || 26 ||
The person (puruṣa) is designated by the name "the totality of the principles" (sakalatattva);
for through the knowledge of the principles, bondage goes to complete destruction. (27)
And due to the destruction of the bonds, he does not enter into saṃsāra again;
for the person who has turned away from saṃsāra, there is no further falling away. (28)
He becomes one who possesses absolute happiness and is born indeed as independent. || 28 1/2 ||
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter of the Niśvāsakārikā. Now, O Lord, [I shall explain] the correct and concise determination of the three principles.
For the sake of compassion toward living beings, this marvelous [teaching] is being fully revealed. || 1 ||
That which was called "the unmanifest" is now described as the manifest sense-faculty;
that which is self-cognizable yet not [externally] cognizable is understood as the unmanifest by implication.
The elements consist of that [Self], and that [Self] consists of the five elements;
the manifold diversity and the unity of the origin of the elements are thus proclaimed. (3)

a) That which begins with the earthly element (pārthiva) and extends up to Āśiva— this entire collection has been declared by the knowers of reality to be *prākṛta* (of the nature of primordial matter) in manifold ways. (4)

The ordinary elements, being undifferentiated, are not sung as having the distinction of being divine or non-divine, nor as pure or impure, for they do not possess such a nature by their own inherent essence.
The principles (tattvas), even though they are composed of consciousness and primordial matter, attain purity;
yet, when pure, they bind those embodied beings who are ignorant.
But for the ignorant, those who are intent upon the effects of existence and perform virtuous deeds,
these auspicious principles bind embodied beings.
Whatever is taught as being composed of modification is undoubtedly declared by those who know the meaning to be *prakṛta* (derived from primordial matter). (8)
Because it is all-pervasive, because it is both subtle and manifest, and because its qualities are unproduced,
many regard the immutable Supreme Self as the Void. (9)
Some declare the vital breath (prāṇa) to be the supreme Brahman, others fire, and still other people the moon; thus they instruct one another.
With reference to the effects of beings, [this] was spoken out of respect for their inherent nature and qualities;
it was not stated for the sake of conventional usage, nor from the perspective of ultimate reality. (11)
One, two, three, four, and five are the qualities of the specific elements beginning with space, as conceived by the sages in their proper sequence. (12)
Here, that which is singular, possessing immeasurable qualities, empty, and imperishable is proclaimed;
yet it is further described as being twofold through the distinction between the supreme (para) and the non-supreme (apara).
That from which sound proceeds is called the supreme void;
from that, the subtle element of sound (*śabdatanmātra*) arises—that is the primordial, supreme state. (14)
The distinction between the two spaces has been made by means of the method of the single reality;
it is the supreme concealed by *māyā*, yet devoid of even the highest *māyā*.
Neither pure nor impure, devoid of both purity and impurity,
it is empty of the innate and colored fetters, possessing an unmanifest form.
That which is reckoned as space—unborn and imperishable—is composed of entities both gross and subtler, and takes on forms through existence and non-existence. (17)
This form of sound proceeds having the nature of the state of milk;
from sound comes the perfection of the body, and its cause is characterized by space.
(151) It proceeds in two ways by way of the nature of knowledge and ignorance. Knowledge creates the body; this is the realization of the Puruṣa and the Unmanifest. (19)
And for men whose existence is destroyed by the presence of delusion, there is perversion;
though consisting of knowledge, they resort to a perverted basis for the sake of the [five] categories. (20)
This [element] manifests sound in two ways for living beings as ordained;
for it awakens those who are deluded to the void that has sound as its quality. || 21 ||
It is taught that it brings about purity for one thing and impurity for another;
this entire world is of the nature of mantra and is remembered as consisting of the sound of mantra. (22)
That which consists of the void of sound is declared to be the Void, known as the Unmanifest;
from that, as soon as it has arisen, the mantras are impelled by the vital wind.
It manifests through the two ears; therefore, it is remembered as the gross [element].
That which is of the nature of sound, beginning with space (śūnya), is designated as possessing immeasurable power. (24)
This is said to be the Supreme Śiva with attributes (saguṇa) or as impure;
thus, the elements along with their own qualities are mutually unreal.
In due course, they come into being and manifest all phenomena through great grossness and subtle pervasiveness on every side.
Existing both as the pervaded and the pervader, they are one yet manifold;
for this [reality] consists of all the principles (tattvas) and likewise consists of equanimity.
The body composed of the five elements is declared to be material;
yet he who abides as all-encompassing knowledge is this powerful body.
It is taught that [the body] consists of the elements and is the cause of excellent enjoyments and pleasures;
this aggregate consisting of the five elements is designated as the "unmanifest" (*avyakta*). (29)
Having understood that all things arise from [the mind], one is completely liberated from bondage. || 29 1/2 ||
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter of the Niśvāsakārikā.
The Goddess said:
O Blessed One, I desire to hear [the distinction] between those whose intellects are awakened and those whose intellects are unawakened.
Tell me, why was it not previously taught by me in the seven crores of great tantras?
How is one to be known as unawakened, and how does one become awakened? Tell me truly of the process of awakening for one who is seeking knowledge.

Listen, O Goddess, to the supreme, pure [reality], and that which is impure, enveloped by the qualities (guṇas). That reality is proclaimed as pertaining to the Person (puruṣa), unborn, yet within the sphere of worldly existence. (3)
Though formless, because it is unawakened, this [Self] plays with enjoyments whose nature is māyā,
due to its conjunction with the unmanifest (avyakta), like a child with toys.
The insentient, which consists of the qualities (guṇas), is enveloped by that sentient one who is devoid of qualities;
the manifest is enveloped by the unmanifest, and that [unmanifest] is likewise enveloped by Him.
It does not perish while that which is perishing is being destroyed; it is born along with that which is being born.
Through the manifest states produced by human effort, the imperishable appears as if accompanied by its own properties.
On this earth, men of unrefined intellect speak of this person—who is unborn and undecaying—as being "born," even though he has been so for all time. (7)
(155) One indeed goes to destruction, while another experiences sensation;
here, yet another remains as the Lord, liberated from suffering and unperceived. (8)
O blameless one, although this bound soul (paśu) is essentially one, it exists in three forms: the unawakened, the awakened, and likewise the awakening.
When one does not perceive the difference between the self and primordial nature, he is then called "unawakened" by those who know the truth; such a person is a bound soul (paśu). || 10 ||
The Puruṣa, when not yet distinguished from the unmanifest, is called the "becoming-aware" one;
he who is eternally awakened, the Lord of Pradhāna, is remembered as the Sovereign of the Puruṣas. || 11 ||
Because it is not awakened by the natural qualities (guṇas), it binds itself;
from that, passion arises, and through attachment to that, the fettered soul (paśu) perceives what is inauspicious.
Stained by passion, one subsequently pursues sense objects;
being addicted to them, one wanders here among beings merely through thought. (13)
As he meditates on sense objects day after day,
emaciation, overcoming his strength, proceeds irresistibly.
Then, for one overcome by desire, fierce anger arises;
in the deluded embodied being, the destruction of the intellect ensues. (15)
Through the destruction of the intellect, the fourfold group beginning with the senses proceeds;
through attachment born of ignorance, the person goes toward taking refuge in the unmanifest.
Due to taking refuge in the unmanifest, birth and again terrible karma proceed for the embodied soul—even though it is devoid of qualities—through attachment born of delusion. 17.
(157) With straight qualities born of virtue, and with his body composed of both the past and the future,
the Infallible One moves upwards and downwards like a water-wheel. 18.
Who am I, and of what nature am I? Am I the doer, or is there an action? It is said by the wicked that one is powerful; who here experiences sufferings, and for whom? (19)
The Goddess said:
What is the cause of pleasure and pain that they are experienced so suddenly?
To whom do these forms—childhood, youth, old age, and so forth—belong? (20)
Who is it here that is born or dies, or who even exists? Or who, having abandoned the house, departs from these bodies? (21)
O Blessed One, you should explain this task in its entirety. (p.
158) Īśvara:
I shall relate these [matters] concerning a man who has been carried away by illusion.
Through association with ignorance, it deludes one so that even while seeing, one does not see;
it is accompanied by disease, birth, old age, death, and suffering, along with all its adjuncts. (23)
Even though he knows this, that deluded soul does not experience agitation;
thus he remains enamored by the qualities born of the Unmanifest.
Even another who has forcibly drawn his sword is overcome by forceful illusion;
that entire retinue is born and grows only for the sake of suffering. (25)
And by means of the rope, its gross nature perishes;
this is another quality of the Puruṣa who is free from bondage. (26)
Now listen; I shall speak of the arising of qualities in the one who is becoming enlightened.
His innate state of ignorance [is removed] through the impulsion of the Lord’s grace. (27)
This state of awakening arises for the embodied soul;
through that engagement, this wise one becomes free from the suffering of the great sleep.
The beast beholds before him the inexhaustible ocean of worldly existence,
completely filled with hot water and agitated by waves in the form of the snares of desire.
It is intensely thick with great delusion, covered with bubbles of passion,
defiled by desire, hatred, and the like, and agitated by the wind of mental activity.
It is bitter-sweet with the turbulence of desire, terrifying with the roar of anger,
strewn with the whirlpools of the womb, and thick with the mire of illusion.
(160) It is frequented by the great multitude of disease, birth, old age, and death;
it is characterized by pleasure, pain, and fear at their appointed times, and is bounded by the limits of time. 32.
It was filled with flocks of beasts and swans crying out here and there;
from food, blood, flesh, phlegm, and semen are produced in succession.
Beings arise from the white [seed]; therefore, the world consists of food (annamaya).
That food is consumed by embodied beings through morsels, mouthfuls, and gulps. (34)
He gradually establishes the full vital breath within the thick inner receptacle;
therefore, he divides that food and drink which have been consumed into two parts.
Having entered into the midst of the food, [he should place] the food separately and the water separately;
having placed the water above the fire, he should place that food upon the water.
p.
161) The vital breath (prāṇa), itself abiding above the flame, gently fans the fire;
the fire, being fanned by the wind, makes the water exceedingly hot. || 37 ||
That food is then cooked on all sides by hot water;
once cooked, it becomes twofold: the waste matter (kiṭṭa) separately and the nutrient essence (rasa) separately.
The ears, eyes, nose, tongue, teeth, penis, anus, and nails, along with phlegm, sweat, feces, and urine, are known as the twelve seats of impurity. (39)
All the channels are connected on all sides to the heart-lotus;
moreover, the vital breath places the subtle essence at their openings.
The vital breath (prāṇa) fills those channels again with that essence; once they are completely filled, it thoroughly nourishes the entire body from all sides. || 41 ||
Then, situated within the center of that channel, it is cooked by the heat of the body; and while being cooked, it undergoes two further stages of cooking. (42)
From all around the skin, marrow, and bones, the sinews are produced;
likewise, blood, body hair, flesh, head hair, and fat arise. (43)
The channels, fat, pus, marrow, and phlegm—these arise from food, as does semen, which is the essence of procreation. (44)
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter of the Niśvāsakārikā.
The Lord [said]: "And because the white [semen], conjoined with the vital fluid (rasa), is the source of the body's origin."
When, during the period favorable for conception, the flawless semen is situated within the womb; (1)
Then, rubbed by that wind, it becomes one with the female blood;
at the time of the emission of the semen, the *jīva* is joined with its cause. (2)
Whichever latent disposition, through its ripening, extends toward the enjoyment of a particular enjoyer,
he finds delight therein alone, being previously colored by that very disposition.
Or even if he is capable of discernment, he should not carry out what has been scrutinized;
becoming one whose mind is fixed on that and absorbed in it, he enjoys enjoyments like one who is hungry.
Having transcended the living soul, as well as the rising and falling of states of existence,
one who has transmigrated enters a womb according to the constraints of destiny and the distinctions of karma.
That white and red [elements], united together, become the *kalala* in one day;
by five nights, the *kalala* attains the form of a bubble (*budbuda*). (6)
After seven nights, the bubble then becomes a mass of flesh;
after fourteen days, from that mass of flesh, blood and flesh then become firm.
Like sprouts from a seed, from the *peśī* it becomes fivefold in twenty-five nights;
and again, in just one month, it arises in five ways.
The neck, the head, the shoulders, the spinal column, and likewise the abdomen—
all these indeed arise from Tamas within two months.
In three months, all the limbs and joints are fully formed;
in four months, the fingers and toes are produced in their proper order.
The mouth, the nose, and the two ears are produced in five months;
likewise, the rows of teeth, the tongue, and the nails and so forth are produced. (11)
Within six months, however, the lips and cheeks are produced;
the wind, the penis, the generative organ, and the navel likewise come into being. (12)
All the joints are formed within seven months, along with the complete major and minor limbs, the head, and the hair. (13)
Furthermore, with all its parts fully differentiated, it remains fully matured for another eight months,
endowed with the five objects of the senses.
Through the potency of the mother’s food and by means of the six kinds of tastes,
bound to the root of the navel, it grows day by day.
Then, when this subtle body is complete, the individual soul (jīva) regains consciousness;
it perceives pleasure and pain, as well as the dreams of its previous existence. (16)
I have died and been born again; I have been born and died again.
While being born, thousands of various wombs have been seen by me. (17)
Now that I have just been born and have already received the sacraments,
I shall perform there what is most beneficial, so that a future conception may not occur.
Remaining in the womb, he thought: "Once I have emerged from the womb, I shall study the knowledge of Śiva, which brings an end to saṃsāra. (19)
Thus, intensely tormented by the great suffering of the womb,
the living being remains there under the power of karma, not contemplating the means to liberation.
Just as someone trapped on a great mountain peak remains there in suffering,
so too does the embodied soul, enveloped by the fetal membrane, remain miserable within the womb. (21)
Just as falling into the ocean brings terrible suffering,
so too at the end does a man become distressed, his limbs drenched by the fluids of the womb.
Just as one placed in an iron cauldron is cooked somewhere by fire,
so too, cast into the womb-cauldron, he is cooked by the digestive fire.
Whatever suffering arises from being pierced incessantly by needles the color of fire—that very thing would be a blessing in the womb. || 24 ||
There is no dwelling anywhere more painful than dwelling in the womb;
it is filled with a body that is exceedingly terrible and crowded with manifold sufferings. (25)
Thus, indeed, this suffering of the womb has been fully described for living beings;
for all true creatures, whether moving or stationary, great suffering is recorded as existing within the womb. (26)
The suffering from being crushed by the mechanism of the birth canal is ten million times greater than that within the womb;
and as the embodied being is being born, intense fainting occurs.
The body is covered by thirty million sheaths, with the pits of sleep and the like;
it is endowed with gross and subtle forms, both visible and invisible. (28)
Through those same millions of channels, that impure perspiration situated within flows outwards. (29)
Thus, this house of the body has arisen for the eternal self, which is impermanent;
it is impure and constructed by the karmas of that pure [self].
In the month of the womb there is great suffering from the pressure of the vaginal canal;
in childhood there is suffering due to ignorance, and in youth there is suffering from the instruction of the teacher. (31)
Furthermore, in youth there is suffering from the disease of desire and from envy, as well as through activities such as agriculture, trade, service, and the tending of cattle. (32)
In old age, one is tormented by decay and diseases;
at death there is great suffering, and even greater than that is the agony of longing. (33)
There is great fear of kings, fire, water, heirs, thieves, and enemies; the acquisition and protection of wealth are difficult, and its loss or expenditure brings further suffering. (34)
Miserliness, envy, meagerness, the fear of grass and disease, great danger,
and engagement in improper acts— suffering always increases when fuel is added.
In sovereignty, for rulers of the earth, there is the suffering of mutual rivalry and the suffering of mutual subjugation; furthermore, there is the suffering of internal and external turmoil. (36)
The transience of powers, their rise as well as their fall,
their mutual greatness, and even their devouring of one another— (37)
Through mutual excesses and falls, there are the occurrences of the flooding of enjoyments;
they are cut and split by weapons and tormented by diseases. (38)
One who is not devoid of passion never abandons the body through suffering, even when his own limbs are pierced by weapons and his senses are impaired. (39)

One who is enamored by its essential nature and qualities would not be able to abandon it; for whom, then, is passion—not itself the object of attachment—characterized by the bliss of sense-objects? (40)
By that [karma] with which animals, humans, and gods are joined, they go to their destruction;
neither medicinal herbs, nor the taking of wealth, nor mother, nor kinsmen [can protect them]. (41)
The high-souled ones are able to rescue a man oppressed by Time, who has perfected his asceticism, recitation, and mastery of yoga. (42)
Having fallen under the power of timely death, it decays along with those men who are indolent;
yet it does not decay for the great-souled ones who have attained perfection in yoga through excellent means, austerities, and recitations.
"Even timely death is digested by the wise, not by lazy men;
'O father! O father! O beloved! thus do they cry out in extreme distress. (44)
Like a frog being crushed by a serpent, a person is tormented by death, even while embraced by kinsmen and surrounded by loved ones. (45)
Sighing long and hot breaths with a parched mouth,
he rolled repeatedly upon his bed at its four corners. (46)
Overwhelmed, he is tossed here and there from limb to limb—from his arms to his feet;
from the bed to the desired ground, and from the ground back to the bed, and again to the earth.
Naked, devoid of modesty, smeared with urine and excrement, he begs for water, his throat, lips, and palate parched. (48)
But when reflecting on wealth, whose will these be once I am dead?
Thus, with his five limbs exhausted and dragged by the noose of Time, he is tormented. (49)
While all are looking on, he dies; his throat makes a rattling sound, and like a grass puppet, the life-force gradually enters from one body into another.
I, who take delight in this impure body, which is subject to momentary destruction,
filled with various diseases, and adorned by the serpents of the sense-objects. (51)
They are liberated from the intoxications of pride, which steal away discipline and conduct;
yet they are repeatedly tormented by the fevers arising from desire and anger.

O Queen, alas, I am deeply distressed in this world that is exceedingly thick with hair [of worldly entanglements], agitated by the fear of old age and disease, and completely filled with anxiety and sorrow. (53)
How can I find delight in this body, which is bound with skin, a foul-smelling mire of fat and blood, and filled with feces, urine, and semen? (54)
Just as a reflection appears in mirrors, or as a form exists in a painting,
so too this body is merely a pleasing appearance devoid of intrinsic reality.

In the ocean of the knowledge of the boat, which is turbulent with the whirlpools of the three qualities (*traiguṇya*) within the lineage of Mahāmāyā, and which is crowded with crocodiles of grasping at [false] principles (*tattva*), [56]
Beholding this ocean, he became overwhelmed with fear; after sighing deeply for a very long time and lamenting, [he spoke]. (57)
Oh, how great is the ignorance in this world, submerged in traditionless darkness, its mind distracted by the sovereignty of sons, home, and other such things! (58)
You alone are the mother and you are the father; you indeed are the wife and the sons. You are wealth, you are friends, you are kinsmen, and you are truly the home.
This delusion of the world was ordained by someone long ago;
now, children, wife, family, and wealth appear to me like enemies. (60)
But when one performs that action through oneself— arising from speech, mind, and body—
one experiences its corresponding fruit alone in another birth. (61)
By whatever means, through various actions, they have gathered wealth from here and there;
having relied upon these for enjoyment, they are therefore made miserable.
Those kinsmen who are dear to him do not become his companions at the abode of Dharmarāja; they do not follow those who depart.
A living being is born alone and indeed dies alone;
alone he experiences the fruit of his good deeds, and likewise his evil deeds.
Having understood this, one who is undeluded, seeing the world as being within the belly of Time (Kāla),
resorts to supreme detachment and seeks the goal of the self.
By what means shall I easily cross, before long, this ocean of impurity— a formation of such extremely fierce form? (66)
Charity, sacrifice, austerity, self-restraint, dispassion, knowledge, and right conduct are remembered as being like a boat for crossing over this ocean of saṃsāra. || 67 ||
Whatever fruit has been acquired through actions such as giving and sacrifice, that too undergoes complete exhaustion through his enjoyment. (68)
(Through its enjoyment, even this [merit] comes to an end without remainder.
From sacrifice comes the attainment of heaven as a fruit; upon its exhaustion, there is a subsequent state.
Because of their karma and because of their heavenly state, there is therefore a return once again.
Endowed with such qualities as these through deeds such as giving and knowledge, this destination has been clearly perceived; yet all of them are subject to decay. (70)
For one who has properly performed austerity, heaven alone is the supreme fruit; however,
knowledge and the imperishable renunciation of action pass away.
Even though it has been renounced, [the result arises] due to lack of understanding... || 72 ||
The practice of detachment is one, and likewise, the practice of knowledge is another.
A great distinction has been proclaimed even by the immortals who know the truth:
those characterized by their virtues [are superior]. (74)
Having fallen under the influence of the primary cause (pradhāna), one returns again to a downward state;
yet through knowledge, there is no return, and that [knowledge] is indeed the agent of liberation.
From the acts beginning with giving (*dāna*) and ending with detachment (*vairāgya*),
the ritual actions prescribed by the Vedas are led through the four stages in due order.
Those desires, characterized by renunciation, yoga, and so forth, have their fruits already attained.
When acts such as giving, sacrifice, and vows are offered before the deity,
that indeed is the ritual of renunciation (sannyāsikī kriyā).
Whatever action is performed after having ascended to yoga—those four types of action which have been specified as consisting of the three qualities (guṇas)—[are described]. 80.
179) I shall further proclaim the fruit of these [rites] again in due order:
whatever merit has been acquired through non-violence (*ahiṃsā*)... || 81 ||
The remaining mode of existence, consisting of the qualities (guṇas), remains alone and uncorrupted.
Due to the power of their remaining impressions (*vāsanā*),
they all then experience the fruits [of their actions] with such a very body,
whether in heaven or in hell, wherever and in whatever manner it may be. (84)
Regarding those performed actions for which no fruit was intended, as well as ritual acts prescribed by the Veda; p. 180) [these too...]
Those who perform renunciation of actions already performed... [86]
Or when the unmanifest has been completely exhausted, it does not exist through destruction. || 87 ||
And when the qualities (*guṇa*) are not yet exhausted, how [is this] regarding these eyes?
Yoga, moreover, is of two kinds: with qualities (*saguṇa*) and likewise without qualities (*nirguṇa*), according to the division of gross and subtle by Śiva, the Supreme Self. (89)
Having attained the qualityless yoga through the qualified [yoga], those seeking liberation [attain their goal]. || 90 ||
Furthermore, by means of their qualities and supreme tranquility, they indeed attain universal sovereignty;
having enjoyed those supreme pleasures consisting of the qualities, they finally [attain liberation] therein. (91)
And even though they do not desire it, they return once more to an inferior state;
for those perfected through the yoga of knowledge, suffering remains characterized by exceeding intensity. (92)
What indeed could be more miserable than falling downward?
Therefore, one should practice that yoga which is preeminent and endowed with the conceptualization of the sciences. (93)
The yoga consisting of the qualities (guṇas) and characterized by bonds is not intended for liberation;
now I shall explain the definitive teaching on the yoga of knowledge (vidyāyoga). || 94 ||
O Goddess of gods, listen even though it is without support; I shall tell you:
that which is the dust of the wind is proclaimed as the *trisareṇu*. || 95 ||
p.
182) One should know that a half-mora consists of four atoms (*aṇu*), and two atoms constitute one mora.
The state of the mind is to be known as an atom, and the state of speech is two atoms. || 96 ||
Know that there is a triad of atoms at the tip of the tongue; the wise know this as the emitted *mātṛkā*.
Short, long, and protracted—these are declared to be the three measures (*mātrā*).
Furthermore, the goddess who has transcended the leap is proclaimed as the fourth part.
A blue jay utters one mātrā, while a crow utters two mātrās.
The peacock indeed has three measures; this is the conceptualization of the measure.
That which is proclaimed as the pause (virāma) is situated at the end of the resonance of the bell. 99.
Without that [sound], one should draw the food-like sound situated in the heart into the cavity of the throat;
by means of the very state residing in the heart, one reaches the beginningless and imperishable Nāda.
When that unmanifest half-measure is contemplated, it is then remembered;
one should contemplate it with the mind as long as it remains in the heart and does not issue forth from the navel. (101)
"This is the certainty of the scripture: that which is called the Imperishable (akṣara) is said to be situated in half of a half-mora. (102)
The yoga of knowledge (vidyā-yoga) is to be understood as one thing, while the yoga of liberation (mukti-yoga) is otherwise;
this is declared to be the definitive determination of that yoga of knowledge. 103.
This knowledge is accepted as the cause of liberation;
this entire exposition of the meaning of Sāṃkhya knowledge has that [liberation] as its primary goal. (104)
Having understood this, O Goddess of gods, she spoke thus to the teacher:
"O Blessed One, [save me] from this intense cycle of existence, which is crowded with the whirlpools of ignorance. (105)
Save me, who have followed you, O refuge for those who seek shelter!
Through your grace, may I obtain all the supreme nectar of wisdom. (106)
I desire to know completely and exactly,
with the eye of knowledge, the destruction of worldly existence and the distinction between the Person (Puruṣa) and the Unmanifest (Avyakta).
"Having understood [this], you who enjoy the qualities of absolute liberation (kaivalya), please speak out of your grace.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter in the Jñānakāṇḍa of the Niśvāsakārikā. [Thus spoke] Īśvara.
Henceforth, O Goddess, I shall describe the arising of the qualities of one who is eternally awakened,
and how his mind becomes established in the supreme state.
Having investigated and become discerning, possessing great intelligence regarding the three principles,
he who seeks that which transcends the principles remains devoted to service to the Guru. (2)
One who desires liberation through yoga must again restrain the *liṅga*; O Goddess, without the restraint of the *liṅga*, one does not attain success.
Just as the mind of embodied beings constantly moves toward the objects of the senses,
so too does it move toward that state which transcends the senses and is not of a single form.
The mind, which should not be known as a guardian, seizes forms from every side;
and when the form is led away, it follows after it.
When existence has been exhausted and the solitary intrinsic nature remains, then, O Goddess, it ceases;
otherwise, it does not cease.
The mind turns away from forms; it cannot be described anywhere.
One should not say anything about that, O beautiful one, for who would ask? (7)
When that supreme Brahman is to be contemplated as being devoid of all mental constructs (saṅkalpa),
then the wise man should abandon both mental construct and speech.
Through the relationship between disciple and teacher, that [knowledge] is understood and does not cease;
therein alone the intellect, wisdom, insight, memory, and discernment find eternal delight.
He who indeed knows that which is unutterable, free from doubt, devoid of vowels and consonants, auspicious, peaceful, supreme, and subtle— he is a knower of Śiva.

Those fools who speak thus regarding all things, from the imperishable (akṣara) and so forth down to the perishable (kṣara), in their gradual sequence, have not reached the further shore of Śaivism. || 11 ||
(187) Free from the fifty syllables, devoid of the perishable and the imperishable,
and having abandoned the *bindu* and *nāda*, as well as the entire collection of mantras without exception; || 12 ||
Where trembling is observed in the teeth, lips, palate, and tongue, how can there be immortality for it? It always exists in a state of flux.
As long as speech is uttered and as long as the eyes function, so long is that [reality] to be known as with parts (sakala); otherwise, it is partless (niṣkala). || 14 ||
Whatever is perceivable by the eye, or even that which is heard from hearing—all this, including gods, asuras, and humans, is impermanent. (15)
How can there be liberation in syllables? How can there be a flower in the sky? How can there be oil in sand? How can there be a bow in a rabbit's horn? (16)
Thus, O Goddess, the characteristic of one who is awakened has been fully explained. (16½)
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter in the Jñānakāṇḍa of the Niśvāsakārikā.
The Goddess said:
Śiva is to be known as fivefold: as Sakala (with parts), Niṣkala (without parts), as well as Sakalaniṣkala (both with and without parts), Sūkṣma (subtle), and Bhinnakala (of distinct parts). || 1 ||
What is the nature of the deity as *sakala* (with parts) and as *niṣkala* (without parts)? Tell me the third division, namely how it is both *sakala* and *niṣkala*.
Tell me the divisions of the subtle and the divided; [O] Lord (p.
I shall explain this to you: Śiva, who consists of five divisions.
By the mere knowledge of whom one shall not undergo rebirth again—He is the Supreme God, the Great Lord Maheśvara, who pervades the sky and consists of the five mantras. || 4 ||
Pierced by thirty-eight digits (kalās), possessing the form of the light of the unmanifest (amajyotis),
he who is called "the manifest" (sakala) is indeed the Lord himself, the consort of Umā.
For the individual soul (puruṣa), while always abiding within the entire primordial nature (prakṛti) and impelled by the Creator,
would pervade the whole world and would pervade all embodied beings.
And because he is established everywhere, he is remembered as "Sakala" (the Whole);
he is the non-conceptual, equal state wherein one is joined with the mantra. || 7 ||
By all the syllables and words of the mantra, he is designated as "sakala" (the manifest);
he abides within the gross and subtle elements of all embodied beings. (8)
Because he pervades both Pradhāna and Puruṣa, he is remembered as Sakala (the Whole);
O gods, because of his all-pervasiveness, he is proclaimed as the Kalā-tattva.
Because he is the abode of all arts (kalās), he is therefore known as Sakala;
Sakala performs creation and bestows the perfection of mantras. || 10 ||
He destroys all obstacles and brings about liberation at the end;
for he is immeasurable, indescribable, incomparable, and devoid of form.
It is said that there, the subtle and partless [state] is supreme among all principles;
within the body, which is delimited by the principle of the physical form, resides the resonance (nināda) of all embodied beings.
That which transcends the power of sound (nāda-kalā) is called the partless (niṣkala);
it is liberated from the manifest (sakala) and devoid of both the point (bindu) and sound (nāda). || 13 ||
The reality situated in the sky is partless, devoid of both the expressible and the inexpressible;
it is liberated from both knowledge and ignorance—the partless, supreme state.
In the sky, which resembles crystal and destroys old age and death, dissolve yourself into the partless [Brahman] with your mind for the sake of attaining liberation. 15.
Consisting of both *bindu* and *nāda*, it is within the range of the senses of sight and hearing;
here, the object of vision is known as the "half-pure," which is both with parts (*sakala*) and without parts (*niṣkala*).
One should know that form to be both with parts and without parts;
it is the subtle element of sound, the syllable Om, which is heard but cannot be described.
And it is not perceived by means of form; the object of knowledge is both with parts and without parts.
But when, having joined the "with parts" (sakala), one joins the "without parts" (niṣkala), [then it is realized]. (18)
Then the wise should know Śiva as both with parts (sakala) and without parts (niṣkala);
he who resides in the body is to be known as with parts, while he who is devoid of a body is without parts. || 19 ||
He is to be reached through the yoga of action and other means; He is to be known as both with parts and without parts.
He is the fourth, consisting of space, beyond sound, and beyond the reach of the senses.
The stainless form known as Sadāśiva is here said to be subtle;
because it is subtler than even an atom, it should be meditated upon as free from all affliction.
Extremely profound, beyond the subtle vital breath, and devoid of defining characteristics,
it is subtler than the most minute atom and is situated in the center of the heart.
He causes the entire world to breathe forth; he is indeed proclaimed as the subtle one.
He always perceives that which is situated in the void by means of the foremost syllables and words of the mantra. (23)
That which is to be known is subtle vision, for the purpose of illuminating the yoga of knowledge;
it arises from the destruction of evil, from yoga, and likewise from the accumulation of meditation.
He beholds Śiva, who is subtle and merged within the light of the heart; he is situated within all, established in samādhi, and perceivable by the internal organ. 25.
It is not seen by the eyes; it is meditated upon by yogis.
It possesses the forms of earth, water, fire, air, ether, the kingdom (of the senses), the self, the moon, and the sun.
That Śiva is the self of all dharmas, yet he may exist as divided into parts;
his form consists of the phonemes from 'a' to 'kṣa', which are the essence of the kalās of mantra.
That which exists in manifold ways is called "entirely differentiated" (sakala),
because the intellect is established through the syllables and words of mantra, as well as through the meanings of those words. (28)
Śiva, whose aspects are differentiated by words denoting distinct meanings, is thus to be known in ten ways; furthermore, he is to be known in five ways.
Sevenfold, then four, eight, and again four;
then Śiva with his limbs (Sāṅga), the Gāyatrī, and the other five beginning with Sadyojāta. (30)

Having understood that the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas) and the Guardians of the World (Lokapālas) are non-different from that one, all-encompassing Śiva, yet exist in a state of differentiation, one should, being well-composed, effect their union.
He shatters the mass of bonds; therefore he is remembered as Bhinnakala.
Thus, O Goddess, has Paraśiva been described to you in his five states.
"Knowing this, one is released from the bonds and goes to the imperishable Śiva.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter in the *Niśvāsakārikā*. (p. 195) || 33 ||
The Goddess said:
O Śiva, it is precisely because of qualities such as omniscience that you are praised everywhere;
therefore, O Blessed One, I desire to hear of them—please deign to speak.

O Goddess of all-knowing primordial deities, he is the Lord (Īśvara) of the bound souls (paśu), the fetters (pāśa), as well as the principles (tattva), their emergence and dissolution; therefore, he is called the All-Knowing One (sarvajña). || 2 ||
He is said to be one who is perfectly endowed with all sovereignty, who is both the support of all and himself without support, who is omnipresent and complete, and who is utterly fulfilled.
Because it is beginningless, its own nature is the self of all, and its sphere of activity is firm;
since it awakens [beings] by its own power, it is therefore proclaimed as "Awakening" (bodha). || 4 ||
He could create the entire world, the three realms with all that is moving and unmoving; because he is the Lord of Gods and independent, he is called "Svatantra" (the Independent One). || 5 ||
Because he is eternal, free from old age, and all-knowing, and because he is unimpeded by yogic powers, Śaṅkara is therefore called Alupta (the Undecaying).
Someone knows that supreme [reality] which is without beginning, middle, or end;
and because its power is unimpeded, it is therefore called infinite.
These limbs of Maheśa should be understood with diligent effort;
one is liberated from all sins and attains the stainless state of Śiva. || 8 ||
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter in the Jñānakāṇḍa of the Niśvāsakārikā.
The Goddess said:
"O Maheśvara, as for what was stated by you—that [the body] is devoid of the six veins—"
Therefore, tell me that, O Lord of Gods, as to how it may become inferior in color. || 1 ||
O Goddess, listen; I shall declare to you that supreme secret which you have asked about, which is difficult to obtain even for the gods. (2)
O Goddess of the gods, this should be understood with effort in five ways:
the distinction of the phonemes must be known, as well as the distinction of the principles (tattvas) according to their true nature. || 3 ||

Furthermore, the classification of his vital airs (vāyu) belonging to that God of gods has been proclaimed, as well as the classification of the states of the deities; in brief, there are five divisions.
O Goddess, when the Teacher of the World, the God of gods, is devoid of these distinctions, then Śiva is said to be free from the six phonemes.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord Śaṅkara, how is there a division of castes and a division of principles?
Furthermore, [explain] the division of the winds and the distinction of the deities of the castes."
O Lord, when one is devoid of these, what is the nature of that true being?
Tell me this, O Lord of Gods, for I have a great doubt in this matter.
O fair-faced one, listen with a one-pointed mind, having become absorbed in that and identified with it, as I shall tell you these things exactly as they are. 8.
(199) O fair-faced one, listen as I explain the distinction between the castes;
how they are concealed and how they are lost, that I shall tell you. 9.
When the letter *a* is elided, the syllable *oṃ* is deprived of Śiva;
therefore, O Goddess, when that fifth [letter] is elided, it becomes endowed with him.
When the sixth is deficient by the fifth, it is proclaimed as such;
O Goddess, when the sixth is deficient, the letter *ma* is seen there.
Therefore, O Goddess, when he is lacking, how could he be like the moon? For when he is deprived of him, Śiva is devoid of his six colors.
But the *niṣkala* is that which is devoid of the phonemes (*varṇa*) of the entire *tattva*;
it is not by elision, O lady of beautiful hips, that the form of the curved plowshare (*vakra-hala*) exists therein.
(200) O Goddess, when [the body] is deficient in reality, I shall explain that very thing to you;
the seven realities and so forth have been fully described by me regarding this body. (14)
The Supreme Lord (Parameśvara) should be fashioned as devoid of six principles;
for five principles are situated above, and he himself is established as the primordial source (Aya).
O Goddess, when one is deprived of those and becomes devoid of the six syllables, listen to this which is being told regarding the further classification of his vital breaths (vāyu). || 16 ||
Listen now to the order in which they are situated:
Udāna is established in the upward direction, while Apāna is positioned below. (17)
There, the *prāṇa* is situated in the center; the *vyāna* is in the sphere of connection;
the *samāna* is there, all-pervading; and among them, O Dhanañjaya, is the *dhanañjaya*.
(21) O Goddess, when the God of gods, the Teacher of the World, is devoid of all these, then Śiva is said to be free from the six syllables. || 19 ||
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, as well as Rudra, Īśvara, and Śiva himself—
when [the reality] is devoid of Śakti and Nāda, it is free from them and is partless (niṣkala).
White, red, yellow, black, crystal-like, and beautiful;
when it is devoid of these colors, it becomes one that lacks the six colors.
When it is devoid of these phonemes and only a single *bindu* remains established,
then at the end there is the supreme peace, which is devoid of the form of phonemes.
Therein neither vowel nor consonant exists, nor form, nor indeed cultivation;
the mind is not found there, and thought is not found there. (23)
p.
202) Nothing exists there, nor is any worshipper perceived therein.
The Goddess said:
Today, O Lord, I know that my life is well-lived. || 24 ||
O Śaṅkara, tell me of that which slightly agitates the mind—[that which is] devoid of consonants and vowels, and free from the form of letters. (25)
"O Lord, how is it known that what was declared by you, O Master,
is the tradition (sampradāya) arising from the supreme beyond the Guru, O Goddess? (26)
And I shall not speak of that which is not [the truth], apart from the nectar of the teacher’s mouth;
for the teacher, who knows the true state of beings, speaks according to and by means of whatever disposition [is appropriate]. (27)
But that is not so, for there is nothing else; indeed, O beautiful one, it must be believed.
And just as existence arises from non-existence, O beautiful one, so does existence manifest. (28)
"In this way, I shall explain to you that cessation by which you will attain liberation.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter of the *Niśvāsakārikā*.
The Goddess said:
This knowledge is manifold; no certain conclusion can be reached.
Therefore, let that single word be reflected upon by which I may attain the highest good.
The Lord has taught that knowledge, though manifoldly divided, is expounded in the world.
That which is to be known is distinct from that [knowledge]; in knowledge, the object of knowledge is established. || 2 ||
Śiva is both exclusively pure and impure along with the imperishable syllables;
the naturally pure form arises effortlessly indeed. (3)
For the attainment of milk is not desired by the mere word "cow"; rather, there are distinctions such as honey, milk, water, nectar, and so forth. (4)
Even when spoken, no fruit arises from the contact of the lips;
however, those who know the Dharma praise the Lord for the sake of liberation— this is what should be known.
From consciousness, however, there is the attainment of qualities, just as the elements [attain qualities] from contact;
just as iron-slags are [transmuted] by mercury alone through the process of "piercing by touch. (6)
Through contact with fire, the state of gold is brought about; knowledge is taught to be like touch, while the object of knowledge is held to be like fire. (7)
O Supreme Lord, the temporal bond (pāśakālikā) of bound souls (paśus), once seized, attains identity with that [bond] due to the influence of the qualities of its own cause. || 8 ||
Likewise, all yogins attain equality through consciousness;
that is the cause of their respective sovereignty and their commonality of dharma.
Everywhere they attain supreme reality through consciousness;
indeed, by means of consciousness, the threefold bondage is shattered. 10.

When the bonds have fallen apart, the living being attains the state of the power of will (*icchā-śakti*). Through the pervasive quality of the power of will, the living being shall no longer be a partaker of suffering. (11)
(206) He attains the state of being the cause of all things; of this there is no doubt.
The Goddess said:
How could there be a path for Śiva, who is perfectly complete? || 12 ||
But tell me truly, what is the nature of the path of Śiva?
Just as in the case of space, it has no top, no middle, and no bottom anywhere.
Thus, the all-pervading God does not exist within the paths of time;
having transcended the state of being a bound soul (paśu), He abides in the state of the Lord (pati). || 14 ||
Since He is all-pervading, what "going" could there be for Him? Nevertheless, it is figuratively said that He "goes," meaning He attains the state of being elevated and the state of being Śiva.
"Awakening is called 'going'; how can there be going for that which is all-pervading?
The Goddess said:
O Śaṅkara, that god is said by me to be all-pervading.
How can this contradiction within one's own position be rendered beyond doubt, if [the deity] is present everywhere—in leaves, flowers, fruits, and water? (17)
How can worship be performed when it involves the cutting of one's own limbs, which is suffering, and [involves harm] to all things, whether stationary or moving, such as seeds and the like? (18)
How can the burning of one's own limb be appropriate for burnt offerings (homa), if [the burning] of leaves, flowers, fruits, and so forth is not employed therein? (19)
In that case, it would lack pervasiveness; how then could it be all-pervading?
For those who recognize form and color, there is no manifestation within the unmanifest. (20)
If one accepts what is spoken [by another] or eats what is given out of desire, the body indeed becomes manifest in form; it is clearly of a conditioned nature. (21)
Those who possess a physical form perish in due course of time;
the God is all-pervading, yet worship is praised when performed upon the body.
O God, the ritual for the worship of the *liṅga* is not desired by me;
it is bewildering in its obstruction, like the all-pervading sky. (23)
That which was previously described as the unborn and imperishable space is obstructed by stone pillars, water, walls, and mountains. (24)
In that same way, [they conceive] Īśvara as unmanifest, not independent, insentient, dependent on another, a non-agent, ignorant, and characterized by productivity. || 25 ||
That which is pervaded, non-pervasive, subject to agitation, graspable, and endowed with qualities is said to be characterized by transformation,
excellence, and manifestation, while being unmanifest in its essential nature. (26)
Its lack of omniscience is declared to be its very source;
this is taught to be the nature of the Void, namely its lack of lordship. (27)
But the Lord, having understood this, spoke again: "O Goddess, you shall no longer fall into delusion;
for one who pervades the supreme reality cannot be obstructed. (28)
Just as a reflected form enters into the middle of a mirror of water,
neither emerging nor being divided, so does the Lord shine forth.
Pervasive and non-contradictory, it is not obstructed by anything; indeed,
that which stands both within and without is not dependent upon anything whatsoever.
There is for me no inference, nor comparison, nor anything else that belongs to me.
Pure by its very nature, stainless, and free from the application of the impurity of arising—nothing whatsoever can be said regarding its characteristics of quality. (31)
Just as the moon situated in the sky is seen in water,
so too the all-pervading God, due to his subtlety, is not perceived.
And that [Self] may be seen through yoga as if directly perceived, like the moon in water;
yet the moon waxes and wanes, being unstable, uneven, and moving. || 33 ||
The moon, once arisen, undergoes transformation;
yet he who is free from deceit and devoid of change abides both externally and internally.
The one who has attained union, having transferred his reflection into the mirror, remains situated in the void and not in that water;
yet the Supreme Lord is seen even within his own impure body. (35)
O Goddess of gods, through instruction, [the truth] becomes manifest like the moon in water;
just as the Supreme Lord, though existing within the body, is not seen, so too is He [not seen] in leaves, fruits, and the like. 36.
For by its very nature, the moon is seen there in the sky;
O Goddess of gods, through instruction, it is perceived as being present everywhere. (37)
Just as leaves, flowers, fruits, and the like are not seen because they are impurities, so too, O Goddess, you are deluded, remaining fixed upon that which is ungraspable. 38.
Just as the circles of rays are seen in a gem, in water, or in a mirror,
so too is the Supreme Lord seen within leaves and flowers. (39)

Because of its subtlety, it resides everywhere within leaves, flowers, fruits, and so forth, as well as within seeds and the like; having seen it thus situated there, one should not entertain conceptual constructions regarding it.
Although [the effect] exists everywhere within leaves, flowers, fruits, and so forth, as well as within seeds and the like, it is not perceived because of its subtlety. || 41 ||
When seeds are being burned, they are not consumed because of their subtlety;
likewise, the fire-element within gems and corals is seen even in the sky. || 42 ||
Indeed, no Vedic injunction is seen here regarding the ripening of water, weapons, leaves, fruits, and so forth, nor regarding the germination of seeds and the like. (43)
Because of the extreme subtlety of the God of gods, neither cutting nor burning is perceived.
213) His hands and feet are everywhere; his eyes, heads, and faces are on all sides. || 44 ||
Since reality is all-pervasive by its very nature and is omnipresent, it should not be conceptualized; it shines forth through non-investigation. 45.
But when direct perception is being experienced, no logical reason can serve as its cause;
it is the appearance of all things yet devoid of appearance, formless yet possessing all forms.
And since it does not abide in a single location, how could there be an invocation of it?
It is recited that [the Self] is all-pervasive within its own body during the dissolution of the phonemes.
Furthermore, because the term "yogapīṭha" was previously established, how could its cessation—which has been recited within one's own body—be forgotten? (48)
Since the term "presence" (sānnidhya) is recited as being within one's own body,
there is neither a cause for [its] presence nor any contradiction. (49)
In this way, these forms and others of Śiva are proclaimed in the inferior teaching as being caused by the collection of ritual procedures. (50)
O Goddess of gods, the invocation and the dismissal are of the nature of ritual action;
this is not a mere explanatory statement (arthavāda), but is proclaimed as an injunction (vidhi).
Having resorted to the doctrine of ritual injunction (vidhivāda), the gods, led by Brahmā,
attained incomparable sovereignty, gain, and eternal immortality.

O Great-Souled One, the Śaiva scripture, which bestows the state of both worldly enjoyment and liberation, possesses neither defect nor flaw; it is the means for the accomplishment of both goals. (53)
The Goddess said:
"O Śiva, the fault is as it would be for a man on a street."
The function would be localized; it could not be all-pervading for the omnipresent Lord. || 54 ||
The Lord Śiva,
the supreme cause, is the deity who consists of both the manifest and the unmanifest;
he is endowed with specific characteristics in the form of an image, and likewise in the yoga of recitation.
The mind, the intellect, and the ego—designated as the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa)—are said to be that very locus; thus, the mind, intellect, and so forth are merely conceptual constructs.
Devoid of the intellect of volition, free from egoism,
and liberated from the rules of praise and the like— this is remembered as being established in the Supreme.
But he, O Goddess, is omnipresent and described as both having and not having marks.
The Goddess said:
If the God is omnipresent, abiding in all states of existence; || 58 ||
Therefore, O Maheśvara, one should not entertain a doubt regarding that location;
Śaiva knowledge has been proclaimed for the sake of accomplishing both goals. (59)
The Great Lord is all-pervasive; what fault could there be in liberation?
The Blessed Lord is the master of all moving beings, for He is not worshipped merely within physical bodies.
The Lord Śiva should be worshipped either in a liṅga or elsewhere in an auspicious place;
this involves invocation, meditation, and the restraint of mental enjoyments.
One should contemplate union with Śiva through the mind and the intellect;
one should worship the manifest (sakala) God and recite the mantra of the manifest-and-unmanifest (sakalaniṣkala). (62)
One should meditate upon that which consists of light, subtle, and distinct from the kalās;
one should satisfy [the deity] in the sky, appearing as pure as crystal, the destroyer of old age and death. 63.

For the sake of attaining liberation through the mind, effect absorption into the partless [reality]. Through bathing, the practitioner becomes pure; through recitation, success is attained—of this there is no doubt.
Through worship, the Lord grants fruit when he is present; through fire-offerings (homa), he grants it even when not present;
and by meditating upon the all-pervading God, one attains the state of a master of yoga. 65.
Through the vow, there shall be purity of body; in initiation, liberation is desired.
[The rites of] invocation, installation, presence, and confinement [are performed]. (66)
The names of the rites established in the ritual manual have indeed been declared;
yet, no one at all is obtained [as a recipient], nor is anyone at all established [in the rite]. (67)
O Goddess of the gods, it does not cease, nor is its presence [limited];
pervasive in the form of mantra, they contemplate Supreme Śiva. (68)
"Then it is said: 'The vehicle,' and 'Forgive me' is the dismissal.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter in the *Niśvāsakārikā*.
The Goddess said:
For the mind is constantly wavering; it moves with force like a flowing current.
O Lord of Gods, even one established in meditative absorption—how can he remain unmoving? (1)
Īśvara (p.
219) [taught] the yoga of the renunciation of action, as well as the great yoga of the intellect.
Yoga is said to be of five kinds, characterized by the possibility of return.
O woman of excellent complexion, for those beings who are subject to rebirth,
their minds are always constantly attached to karma.
The Goddess said:
"O Blessed One, I desire to hear about the yoga of action, renunciation, and likewise the great yoga of the intellect; you should explain these to me. (4)
The Lord [perceives] that which consists of egoism, designated by the terms "yoga" and "action";
when that very [egoism] has been cast off, being thus one who has accomplished his purpose, it is called renunciation (sannyāsa). || 5 ||
Together with them, there is dispassion, union, and mastery over primordial nature (prakṛti). Having transcended the eight forms of nature, they abide as lords of the Puruṣas.
Four yogas have been taught so that the Great Yoga may come to be;
these yogas, which increase one's practice, exist one above the other for the practitioner.
In that very same way, they dissolve into their own karmas which consist of the qualities of yoga;
yet, once the purpose of their dualistic existence is fully accomplished, they undergo creation once again.
The qualities such as *aṇimā* consist of the perception of forms and so forth;
for those who achieve perfection in yoga through suppression [of the senses], liberation does not exist.
Having attained the qualities such as *aṇimā* and others, and being great lords with mastery over their limbs,
they do not attain union (*sāyujya*) so long as there is no oneness.
But for those who are intent on the syllable Oṃ and established in exhalation (recaka) and inhalation (pūraka),
there is no supreme state, because they destroy the self and the senses. (11)
The syllable *praṇava* is the wind below in the channel, while *udāna* is established above;
for yogins who have reached this state of doubt, there is a return once more. (12)
O Goddess, when the cage of knots has been ceased through the union of going and coming, the Vidyā, whose essence is Yoga, is attained by one who realizes the state of Vidyā. 13.
For one possessing knowledge, [this realization] arises in dependence upon other existences and eons;
however, because they must necessarily enter [into that state], those [others] are cited as the objects of pervasion.
Whatever things exist, they are not liberated due to the absence of a cause; they are not of that nature.
There is no yogi who practices yoga, nor is there any closing of the eyes. 15.
(222) Furthermore, gazing at the tip of the nose is not praised as yoga.
The Goddess said:
In that which has support, there is impermanence; even in that which is without support, there is emptiness.
There is a fault in both positions; what then do the yogins meditate upon? [They say:
"The Lord is like a child—knowing nothing, even though he is a fool, he was not laid down [to sleep]. (17)
Persons who do not know the supreme reality are like children;
when that [reality] is unknown, it is called "knowledge," but once it is known, it is held to be the "object of knowledge. (18)
Consciousness arises from the object of knowledge, and consciousness consists of that very [object].
(Devī, p. 223)
Just as the mind will remain immovable through union with that which is to be known. || 19 ||
Tell me this with certainty, for I have a great doubt in this matter;
I shall describe the Lord as the Mind, endowed with its fourfold divisions.
That which has not been told to anyone, I shall tell you today—
specifically regarding the *sāttvika*, the *rājasa*, and the *tāmasa* [natures].
I shall explain in brief, according to the sequence of the divisions of yoga,
that fourth [stage], the great yoga, which is incomparable and free from affliction.
I shall proclaim those movements of the mind that are stirred within the mind; by the mere knowledge of which one attains the state beyond the mind (unmanatva). || 23 ||
The instructed mind, the withdrawn mind, the distracted mind, and the mind in motion and return—these are said to be the fourfold mind; hear now this classification of it. (24)
There is no mind, nor anything to be thought, nor is a thinker perceived;
well-absorbed and liberated from sense objects, he has become one, like one in deep sleep.
Even while perceiving sense objects, he attains the state of being the knower;
yet he is not joined with them, for when he is thus known, he is called "disciplined" (saṃśiṣṭa).
From ignorance one goes to knowledge, and from knowledge one indeed goes to ignorance;
for him who wavers due to weakness, there is this coming and going.
Because one who is devoted to the objects of the senses is constantly deprived of knowledge throughout the three periods of time, he is said to be distracted. || 28 ||
Among those, the *svalīna* is the highest; he has transcended the qualities (*guṇa*) and is free from affliction.
He, however, should be known as the middling; he is remembered as being disciplined and characterized by purity (*sāttvika*). (29)
The lowest, characterized by meager results and belonging to the *rājasa* nature, is subject to coming and going;
that which is *tāmasa* is distracted, and this fourth type is considered the most base.
It is taught that for embodied beings, the mind is generally composed of the qualities (guṇas);
yet, due to its preeminence in the state beyond qualities (nirguṇatva), it will eventually become absorbed therein.
Having attained a state of oneness within tranquility, it is perceived by its own time alone; because it is superior to deep sleep, there is no further qualification required here.
It is impossible to describe it, nor can it be retained;
there is no other indicator for it until one knows it by oneself.
The happiness that is personally realized when both the mind and the vital breath are well-restrained— this,
indeed, those who know yoga declare to be the supreme state of yoga. (34)
When the mind, having attained its mark, becomes absorbed in the supreme reality, then all cognition without exception comes to destruction. || 35 ||
For one whose being is all-pervading, he abides both externally and internally;
even if his mind moves, where could it go after having moved? (36)
Knowledge is the awakening to the meaning of reality and the illumination of meditation on the self;
the object of knowledge is the equality of all things, and through meditation, the mind becomes free from objective referents.
Supportless, free from conceptual construction, devoid of all substrates, without qualities, and beyond any defining characteristic—this is proclaimed as Śivayoga. || 38 ||
He is considered to be one whose mind is well-composed within the cavity [of the heart], just as even the very swift wind does not go anywhere once it has left the sky. (39)
It should be known that even one whose mind is distracted remains motionless while standing in poison;
yet he experiences all sense objects, for he is neither licked nor smeared by them.
He whose state is all-pervading, established in the object of knowledge, and uninterrupted, does not move even when the body moves; he is immovable. (41)
For one whose mind has practiced until it is motionless and for whom this entire knowable world has ceased, what will that wise person do after having conquered the womb? (42)
Just as a calf turns away from its mother's udder when the milk is exhausted, so too does the mind of men quickly turn away when passion is exhausted. || 43 ||
The fluctuation of the mind is required for the sake of the moving and unmoving body;
yet that renouncer shall not be firmly bound by the body. (44)
Desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, dispassion, and knowledge—by means of these thirteen types, the instrument was rendered steady. (45)
Nothing other than that which is immovable by its own nature can be moved by anything else; for that which is immovable could never become so, whether it be unjoined or joined.
The Goddess said:
"The five vital breaths beginning with prāṇa, the mind, the five deities, the subtle elements, as well as the intellect and the ego—this is the city of eight (puryaṣṭaka). || 47 ||
But being agitated by these and joined with the mind,
O Goddess, the vital breaths always move about, deluded by pleasure and pain. (48)
The mind is agitated by this delusion consisting of pleasure and pain;
he for whom pleasure and pain are equal, his mind is perfectly steady. (49)
The Goddess said: "O Lord, the closing of the eyes and the gazing at the tip of the nose—
this is not truly yoga as you have described it."
"O Mahādeva, tell me how the yoga that consists of both— the supported and the unsupported— is to be understood."
The Lord is neither the instrument of yoga here, nor is He the support or the object of focus.
The gaze is fixed on the tip of the nose, not closing the eyes, while the mind is directed toward the heart.
Having perceived even a slight manifestation of that supreme body,
the vital air (vāyu) becomes as if completely filled through the subtle cavity.
"Just as it is not known where one has gone, so too is the union with the object of knowledge.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord, a body filled with air appears like a leather bag. (54)
But what is to be done with that which is artificial?
O Lord, one must understand in every way the path of that which is artificial, consisting as it does of external fabrications. (55)
The knowable has no product, nor does it have temporal paths or conceptual construction.
O Lord, tell me that which is the truth regarding this doubt of mine. (56)
Ishvara is the glorious [power] belonging to that reality which is beyond description and devoid of qualities.
Having performed the grasping of the qualities, one should speak of the Supreme Lord.
One may describe Śiva as merely a slight appearance,
as well as the path of the ritual procedure, the paths of the stages, and the utterances and instruments.
But it must be made to stand still, O beautiful lady, by abandoning [all objects] entirely;
in this way, that mind—difficult to conquer and fickle—will remain subdued. (59)
It would never move, and it would always remain in the state of the object of knowledge;
like an undefeated wrestler, it would bring many others under its sway.
The wise man remains as one who has conquered [the self], and so too is the mind of those who know what is to be known.
Indeed, there would be no goer, nor does any destination exist. (61)
Free from coming and going, it remains like the space within a jar; for the space enclosed within a jar is merely carried here and there [when the jar is moved].
Just as a jar passes through but not the space, so indeed is Śiva like the sky;
the body, which stands enveloped by the petals of the elements, is like the core of a plantain tree.

Therefore, for one whose mind has reached the state of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) regarding the realization of the formless Self (*nirākārātma-vijñāna*), that [mental activity] then becomes like an expenditure, as it abandons even the [notion of] reality. (64)
He who has no longing even for the slightest liberation attains that liberation;
it is renowned as liberation, being embodied yet formless. 65.
Liberation is inconceivable and devoid of qualities; liberation is not accompanied by dissolution.
Therefore, there can be no path to liberation at any time. (66)
The absence of views everywhere—that is liberation for those who proclaim liberation;
it belongs to those by whom dispassion has been repeatedly cultivated and the self pervaded. (67)
There is no one else here besides them who, having gone there, is without justification;
likewise, others too, whoever they may be, are extinguished through their state of dispassion.
In that same way, they too shall go to Nirvana first, just as water resting upon a rock is dried up by the rays of the sun. 69.
Thus, when the self is extinguished, it goes to a state beyond rebirth;
it has not entered the water, nor has it entered the earth, nor does it remain in that very place.
And that [vision] was not drunk by anyone; it departed without any logical basis.
Thus, the detachment from the nature of the graspable object, which was spoken by the Guru for one's benefit, [has been explained]. (71)
This state has reached the path that is free from decay; it is that one eternal reality.
For what hope can there be for those who preach liberation, wherein all things have gone to destruction?
Even this absolute detachment brings happiness to the mind;
yet, for the most part, no one will find contentment therein. (73)
He who is liberated is free from conceptual construction, while he who possesses conceptual construction is bound.
