Just as the name and form of rivers cease upon reaching the ocean, [so do they cease for the liberated]. 74.
There they do not perceive any mutual distinction, nor does any other distinction of the water arise there. (75)
In that regard, the rivers have reached their end, yet the great ocean remains;
likewise, the embodied being is like a river, while nirvāṇa is like the ocean. (76)
Free from possessiveness, those rivers dependent on the ocean remain;
indeed, they abide in stillness, for contentment arises within them.
He does not experience pleasure or pain; he grasps the auspicious qualities by relying on existence within non-existence, having rendered existence supportless. (78)
Having made the mind abide in the Self, one should not think of anything at all;
relying on existence within non-existence, even while dissolved in existence, one remains free from doubt.
He is to be understood as all-pervading; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
How could there be existence for that partless Great Self, which is itself non-existence? (80)
For him for whom all states of being dissolve in the waking state as if in deep sleep, there is no instability; that is his state of Nirvana. (81)
His consciousness is sufficient; those three steps have not been transgressed by you.
The first should be known as imperishable, O well-reflected one, for it is beyond syllables.
Then, through the practice of *kumbhaka*, one should know Śiva, who is beyond both the perishable and the imperishable;
having abandoned everything within the range of the internal organ, one remains established in *samādhi*.
Then, that which is eternally perceived by yogis and worshipped by them is seen according to the tradition as it exists, as pointed out by the instruction of the Guru. (84)
He is both external and internal, subtle, beginningless, auspicious, and immutable.
The Goddess said:
O Lord, [tell me of] the path of the ancestors and likewise the path of the gods. (85)
O Lord, I wish to hear the definitive teaching on the distinction between the two paths.
Those devoted to sacrifices and charitable works travel by the path of the ancestors to the celestial realm.
There they enjoy the fruits of whatever good deeds were performed here;
when those deeds are exhausted, they return and are born again upon the earth. (87)
When his store of merit is exhausted, he returns from that path, just as a leaf falls and turns back;
the Moon’s path is his entire route, and Mṛḍa is his charioteer.
This should be known as the path of the ancestors (pitṛyāna), the way of those who perform sacrifices;
it is the moon that wanes and waxes, unstable, uneven, and flickering. (89)
The destination of one who has set out upon the path of the ancestors is likewise such as this:
on the path of the gods, the Sun is his chariot, and Suṣumnā is his charioteer. (90)
Having pierced through that, the yogi proceeds by the southern path, never to return,
[to the realm] of the virtuous who have become the self of all beings and who perceive reality.
For those yogis who have desisted from all desires and practice the yoga of that path,
those yogis do not return again by way of the path of the gods.
Therefore, having renounced everything, proceed by the southern path;
O Goddess, thus they know the path of the ancestors (pitṛyāna) in brief.
There is no path leading to the gods; hear the reason why:
whatever path one travels by is merely a mental construction.
In this regard, what kind of path is there for the unindicatable Dhātā?
239) Just as neither the path nor the yoga exists within any tantra. || 95 ||
It has been thus enjoined in the scriptures for the purpose of instructing disciples;
this statement regarding its measurement is exactly as it is in the case of the Devayāna path.
What kind of path is it that leads to the realization of all-pervasiveness?
Wherever one goes, that [destination] does not exist, nor is there any path there at all.
There is no movement of yoga there; that state is beyond all characteristics. Once reached through yoga, one does not return, even from the most distant places. || 98 ||
On the path of the gods (devayāna) there is no [return]; therefore, he does not return. But as for any man who has gone by way of the path of the ancestors (pitṛyāna), [he returns]. || 99 ||
Even if one has traveled a very great distance, having relied upon that vehicle,
he goes by the path of the gods (devayāna), freed from all sins. (100)
And thus one should enjoy sovereignty free from the snares of hope;
likewise, the instruments, the designations, and the ego-sense as well. (101)
Since everything ceases [therein], how can anything be differentiated there?
Sovereignty, as described in the scriptures, is incomparable and belongs to one of little strength.
In the state of non-appearance, such sovereignty will never exist;
for even a lord is praised as one who has attained hopelessness and is free from desire.
By whom the entire world has been renounced, yet the self alone is to be enjoyed;
for the sake of the self, he engages in all activities, having become the very embodiment of hope. (104)
For one who has renounced even their own self, for what reason would they have hope?
One remains bound in saṃsāra only so long as one does not abandon hope. (105)
He by whom hope has been severed is liberated from all bonds—past, future, and likewise the present. (106)
Furthermore, the self’s possession of qualities such as being the limit of all stationary things or omniscience is artificial;
that which has arisen does not exist, and likewise, that which is unarisen certainly does not exist, especially in its specific form. || 107 ||
In this way, through a state of hopelessness, one will abandon great delusion.
Because it is unarisen, there is no "unborn"; that which is born does not exist, nor is there anything indestructible. (108)
And that fourfold knowledge is itself considered to be conditioned;
the great tree of worldly existence has desire as its root and is filled with sharp thorns. || 109 ||
It is drenched by the water of passion and grows through the grasping for its fruit;
the wise man will conquer that [tree] of sensual desire. (110)
He will uproot the entire cycle of existence, which is like a tree;
all the power of the previously mentioned factors is comparable to a flash of lightning. (111)
Whoever attends to a sacrifice is attended by death;
therefore, one should attend to the chidra, the pavitra, the kṣema, and the aṅgula. (112)
May there be well-being, peace, and auspiciousness for him whose heart is devoid of radiance;
from the netherworld (pātāla) to the ends of the seven worlds—all this is merely a source of terror.

Those practitioners of mantra who remember the *bhaganāśā* mantra with the *śūnya-mantra* have neither offered oblations nor given gifts, neither for the sake of the next world nor for this one. (114)
And herein no one is bound, nor is anyone liberated; neither that which is to be bound, nor the binding itself, nor likewise any other binder exists. (115)
The giver and the recipient, as well as that which is to be given;
the fire, the darbha grass, the mantras, the priest, and that which is to be offered—[all these must be present]. (116)
Where there is emptiness and the absence of appearances, how could these things exist:
the Agnihotra and other sacrifices, the Vedas, and likewise the sages? (117)
Asuras, ancestors, and gods—all are indeed non-ultimate realities.
All deities consist of mantra; the deity is traditionally understood as the collection of mantras. (118)
The rites for the gods and the ancestors, as well as all sacrifices, are established through mantras;
therein the mantras abide, and therein that which is to be known exists in its perfect, undivided state.
Therefore, one should know that everything proclaimed in the mantras is not ultimately real;
for all phenomena are contradicted by the determination of ultimate reality. (120)
This knowledge is not for householders; rather, it is for those who have reached the final stage of life.
Nor is there no ritual action; sacrifices exist, and when they do, they bestow their fruits.
The fruit [of this] is that their beloved self has been abandoned by them; therefore, Sundarī belongs to them.
One should not speak to anyone unless asked, nor when questioned improperly. (122)
But he who does not speak when questioned by improper means,
even though he knows the true nature of yoga, is one who has been defeated and shall not be accepted again.

One should speak to him by whom it was said, "I shall not return to the household life"; one should first inform that person whose resolve regarding dispassion is certain and who has declared what is to be known. 124.
This entire world is attached to children, wives, and family;
the renunciation of that [attachment] by one who has done so is the characteristic of dispassion. (125)

It should be spoken by one who has not yet reached the final goal to a householder desiring a social circle, who is full of longing, devoid of dispassion, evil-minded, and whose senses are unsubdued. (126)
"O Goddess, it has been made known to me that you are my devotee, O beautiful one;
therefore, with the exception of a renunciant (sannyāsī), you must not disclose this to anyone."
She said:
"O Mahādeva, tell me according to the established conclusion: what fault is revealed in householders who, being envious, do not perceive equanimity? (128)
The path proclaimed by the Śruti and Smṛti is joined with dharma, kāma, and artha;
whereas in the Siddhānta, there is only pure knowledge, devoid of dharma, kāma, and artha.
In that case, dharma and the other [aims] are lost, and only those [negative results] manifest; his purpose is not accomplished, and his undertaking is useless. (130)
If one who is possessed by ignorance offers impure substances upon the altar without first performing the purification of the impurities,
his medicinal herbs will not succeed for that embodied being.
O Goddess, in the same way, this fault becomes manifest for householders.
Tell me, "Is this not a fault?"—listen to the reason why. (132)
O fair-faced one, he who enjoys the excellent pleasures of this world and the next, yet only occasionally performs a sacrifice—by him the sacrifice has been defiled. (133)
For one desiring to eat what is unfit for consumption, this [rite] would be useless;
indeed, it is not appropriate for one who possesses worldly longing, even when the ritual sacrifice is the authoritative standard.
(247) It should be known that one attains perfection through renunciation, but one who possesses desire does not succeed;
for a householder, renunciation will never occur. || 135 ||
Having abandoned cravings for both this world and the next, one will become a renunciant;
yet even a householder cannot possibly abandon the concerns of this world.
The state of being a householder can never be successfully accomplished for one devoid of wealth;
therefore, the acquisition of wealth by every possible means is the primary cause. (137)
When one stands through dispassion, having abandoned craving without remainder, then one is no longer seized by the five defects that seize householders. 138.

The state of being a householder is a terrible fear; he who conquers it through greed will not abandon the vow that dispels the darkness of attachment and delusion regarding worldly existence. || 139 ||
p.
248) Just as the Śruti has declared that one should renounce everything, so it says: "All this, whatever moves within the world of moving beings, is to be pervaded by the Lord. (140)
One should enjoy that which has been renounced; do not seize the wealth of anyone else. For what external thing remains for a householder even while he stays in this world? (141)
O beautiful one, liberation is not seen even in the house of that person who, being attached [to worldly things], abandons compassion and seeks to destroy the multitude of living beings. (142)
Nor does even a householder fail to attain perfection through the yoga of renunciation, provided he avoids desire and hatred and is not possessed by deceit, envy, and the like. 143.
Those devoid of renunciation do not achieve success, for they mock both sides;
indeed, action is proclaimed to be of two kinds: engagement and withdrawal. (144)
For one who is devoid of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), nothing at all is accomplished;
such a person is silent toward the world in every respect, equanimous, peaceful, and composed. (145)
One should see everything within the fourfold collection of beings as being under one's own control.
The Goddess said: "Nothing whatsoever leads to benefit, nor does any other quality arise. (146)
"O Lord of Gods, silence is therefore meaningless;
for the Lord acts for the benefit of others out of a desire for their welfare. (147)
For by that through which the self is extinguished, dispassion is grasped;
for this reason, suffering ceases from the body. (148)
For by that through which the self is extinguished, detachment is grasped;
by this cause, suffering ceases from the body. (149)
"Whatever suffering one inflicts upon others through whatever speech one intends," the Goddess said.
Will there be success for this yoga of dispassion, or will there not? || 150 ||
"I desire to know this, O Blessed One; you should speak.
"Listen, O Goddess, to the supreme secret of that [mantra], which possesses incomparable accomplishment. (151)
It is neither form nor color, nor is there any cultivation of it;
it is both with parts and without parts, and is devoid of instruments and substrates. || 152 ||
It is devoid of vocalization, grammatical inflection, and the form of phonemes; it is the great yoga residing beyond the mind, which bestows all accomplishments. || 153 ||
O fair-faced one, the lineage consists merely of the grace of the Guru;
having obtained that, as soon as it is received, a man attains perfection. (154)
This knowledge is a composite whole and never exists in isolation;
devoid of vowels and consonants, it bestows all perfections and is auspicious.
Therefore, it is called "the knowable" because no delusion arises;
for this is the destroyer of delusion and the means of accomplishing all knowledge. (156)
This should be known as omniscience, which accomplishes all phonemes;
O Goddess, this is the great knowledge, the primordial wisdom that is empty and imperishable. (157)
This is declared to be that which is to be known as liberated from the *bindu* and *mātrā*, and devoid of vowels and consonants; it is the destroyer of old age and death. (158)
It removes all diseases and likewise brings an end to all sins;
it is inconceivable, subtle, like space, all-pervading, and supreme. (159)
Having slightly extended the mouth, one should apply the tongue to the space [within it];
in that place, one should perceive whatever slight touch may arise. || 160 ||
This supreme [practice] must be cultivated by yogīs for the sake of accomplishment;
O Goddess, one should explain this very same supreme method of yoga. 161.
"But one should act according to what has been requested; O Goddess, I speak the truth:
neither gods, nor asuras, nor yakṣas, nor nāgas, nor rākṣasas [can prevent it]. (162)
Neither Kinnaras nor Apsarases, nor Piśācas on the surface of the earth;
neither Vasus, nor Vidyās, nor the hosts of Vidyādharas [were there]. 163.
(253) Neither the world-protectors, nor the constellations, nor indeed the moon and the sun;
neither wind nor water, nor trees, nor mountains [are able to protect him]. || 164 ||
Neither Meru, the king of mountains, nor likewise the realm;
neither Brahmā nor Viṣṇu, O Goddess, nor even I together with you [are equal]. 165.
All this is infinite; he should not think of even the slightest thing.
Thus the yogi should meditate upon the pervasive, empty, and imperishable. (166)
Neither Yama nor Death has any power over him, even if he is bitten by great serpents such as Ananta, Gulika, and others. (167)
Poison does not affect him who contemplates emptiness;
moreover, both the other world and this one are established within it. (168)
(254) O Goddess, this meditation on emptiness has been duly explained by me to you;
it brings about the exhaustion of merit and demerit, and the destruction of karma, birth, and disease. (169)
O Great Goddess, one should not grant the existence of such knowledge to just anyone; having initiated them, it should be given only to one who has been thoroughly tested.
Moving here and there within the range of the body, [one thinks]:
"This is reality, this is reality; this is knowledge, and this is indeed omniscience. (171)
"Having thus understood this very movement within the channels (nāḍī), one is liberated.
Thus speak many who are proud of their mutual knowledge. (172)
Having ascertained this with certainty, one should not reveal that reality;
rather, one should say, "I am a celibate student," or again, "Oh, how peaceful! (173)
Having thus satisfied [the deity], one should remain silent and act accordingly.
Listen, O Goddess, to the supreme secret, the most excellent performance of mudrās. (174)
By the mere realization of this, one shall attain the state of non-existence;
with the left hand, one should perform the unsurpassed binding of the mudrā.
This great [teaching], which removes all pride, is for all wise ones;
it applies even if some wise person should come to the house of another wise person. (176)
O Goddess, demonstrate a gesture by which my exhaustion may be recognized;
for when one who possesses knowledge has thus been made known, he should indeed be questioned once more regarding that knowledge. 177.
O Goddess, one should explain the deity corresponding to whichever mudrā [is used] in due order; then, furthermore, one's gurus must be questioned by him in succession. 178.

Having understood the lineage of the gurus and the sequence of the scriptures, one who is likewise proficient should then worship that [teacher], O Goddess, like Śiva himself, being approved by Śiva. (179)
O woman of excellent complexion, tell me the characteristics of that mudrā, by the mere knowledge of which one shall not undergo rebirth again. (180)
Brahmā resides in the little finger, Keśava in the ring finger; Rudra resides in the middle finger, and the unborn Lord in the forefinger. || 181 ||
It has been briefly explained that Sadāśiva resides in the thumb;
one should join the index finger and the thumb, raise them upward, and then release them again. (182)
But when performed in person, O Goddess of Gods, it is proclaimed as being done once;
it is joined with the middle finger, the ring finger, and the little finger. (183)
O Goddess, one should always perform the auspicious symbolic gestures (*mudrā*) such as *prasṛta* and others. By knowing this, one is liberated from the bondage of the fetters (*pāśa*). (184)
"More than a hundred million lineages shall be delivered from hell.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter of the *Niśvāsakārikā*.
The Goddess said:
Having understood the supreme, divine knowledge, the highest essence of yoga, the Goddess, with her palms joined in reverence, spoke these words. (1)
The Goddess said: "O Śaṅkara, [tell me] the yoga of the knowledge of reality, as well as Śakti and Nāda,
and the knowledge of the eightfold Bindu of the Deity."

(258) By your grace, O Lord of Gods, I have understood the knowledge of the true existence of Yoga, wherein [it is not found] in that Sūtra which contains the supreme true existence of the Pati. || 3 ||
"All that was told in the one [chapter] has been understood through your grace;
O Blessed One, I wish to hear it again, so you should deign to speak. (4)
O Maheśāna, O Lord, beginning from the primordial nature (prakṛti), explain the question regarding the channel (nāḍī) together with the vital air (vāyu), which is most secret.
Īśvara said:
Listen, O Goddess, to the supreme secret, the most excellent essence of Yoga;
I shall declare that which is common to all compendiums and yields great fruit.
Likewise, they say that withdrawal, meditation, breath control,
concentration, reasoning, and absorption— this is called the six-limbed yoga. (7)
Mind, consciousness, and likewise thought—these have been described by me as fivefold;
these have been declared by me to you as the instruments of yoga.
In this way, yoga arises, its practice being well-performed through exertion.
The Goddess said:
"Through meditation, concentration, and reflection, and by means of the initial activities for commencing yoga... (9)
O Blessed One, if [enlightenment] were accomplished through time, what would have been achieved by you, since it is attained without afflictions and without self-inflicted pain? (10)
O Lord of Gods, tell me that knowledge which bestows immediate fruit and prosperity, such as it has been described in the Purāṇas, Sāṃkhya, and Yoga, O Master. (11)
p.
260) Even here, such [a teaching] has been proclaimed; what specific distinction is being illustrated?
O Supreme Lord, the Vedas and other scriptures are conjoined with the practice of yoga-meditation. (12)
Without possessing great knowledge, what have you done here, O Blessed One, that which has been told is unspeakable and indefinable? 13.
Therefore, O Lord, it is known by me that he has firmly grasped the life-force,
as well as primordial nature (prakṛti), the individual soul (puruṣa), necessity (niyati), and time (kāla).
Tell me of the Lord of Māyā and Vidyeśa, and of His true yoga—how the Lord exists without instruments, devoid of meditation and concentration. (15)
Therefore, O Blessed One, I wish to hear this; you should deign to speak, O Lord.
I shall tell you the supreme, essential reality of yoga.
Knowing which, a person becomes successful in their purpose at that very moment—this [knowledge] which bestows ultimate happiness and is adorned with the fruit of all things. (17)
This knowledge of the deities and the sages has been revealed;
by means of this, every person attains the immortal Brahman. || 18 ||
Then the world will be liberated and the earth will become empty;
all phenomena, including the performance of the Vedas, sacrifices, and austerities, will dissolve away. || 19 ||
The Agnihotra sacrifices perish, as do the various established boundaries;
and the gods, being deprived of their sacred study and austerity, fall from their divine status.
For this reason, O Goddess, I have concealed [the truth] and spoken [only this];
for the sake of the dharma of yoga, the treatises are extensive and profound. (21)
Since mutually contradictory views have been observed among them, no final certainty is found therein;
thus the world indeed wanders, mounted upon the wheel of the bodiless [soul].
All yogis exist in mutual opposition;
yet I have been questioned by you, who are difficult to please, and am impelled by your devotion. (23)
"I have been seized by a firm grasp; I must certainly tell you:
neither Brahmā, nor Viṣṇu, nor indeed any other of the best of gods [is capable]. (24)
O fair-faced one, no one other than you could possibly speak in response to such a question;
therefore, listen to the truth clearly and without elaboration.
In an instant, they bestow the attainment of the qualities of the marks, free from all exertion;
they grant success, liberation, contentment, and the increase of nourishment. (26)
Jñānadā, Prītidā, and likewise Āyurārogyadā;
Ghoṣiṇī, Piṅgalā, Vaidyutī, and Bindumālinī. (27)
Cāndrī, Manonugā, Sukṛtā, and likewise another, Saumyā, Nirañjanā, and Nirālambā are thus described. (28)
These channels (nāḍīs) have been described as adorned by the winds and other elements;
previously, however, the wise one was [united] with the supreme Śiva.
Having first performed everything without exception, one should subsequently commence meditation, becoming single-minded, with anger conquered and the senses subdued. (30)
In the twenty-fourth principle (tattva), she is known by the name Ghoṣiṇī;
in the twenty-fifth principle, she is named Piṅgalā. (31)
The Vaidyutī [power] always resides, relying upon the twenty-sixth;
Bindumālinī is to be known as being in my twenty-seventh principle.
In the twenty-eighth principle, the lunar measure (mātrā) abides;
in the twenty-ninth, the measure that follows the mind (manonugā) abides.
Then, regarding my thirty principles, they call that "well-performed" (sukṛta);
having resorted to twenty-one, the gentle measures (mātrās) are established.
The stainless *mātrā* is established resting upon the thirty-second;
in the thirty-third it is without support, and no characteristic mark (*lakṣaṇa*) of it exists.
The thirty-three-fold [measurement] consists of nine finger-breadths suspended from the person;
among these, the characteristics and so forth are to be discerned by the wise. (36)
The Goddess said:
"How can the attainment of these principles, which indeed rest upon the nine measures (mātrās), be perceived immediately?"
In the common treatises on yoga, deer fall into traps consisting of many forms of verbal snares; they perish through great exertion, as if caught in a deceptive snare. (38)
O God, O Maheśvara, tell me that which bestows the bliss of immediate realization, even without the restraint of breath (vāyurodha) and devoid of meditation and concentration (dhyāna-dhāraṇā).
O Goddess, listen attentively, for this is not to be heard by those of unrefined soul.
Having attained which, they immediately obtain the state of Śiva, free from all exertion. || 40 ||

Devoted to their respective stages of life (āśrama) wherever they may be, and dwelling wherever they may be, they dissolve [into the source] just as [the world dissolves] in a moment, like a flash of lightning. || 41 ||
Likewise, when the ears are perfected, the thumbs [are joined], and the nose with the fingers;
then his sound, pervading everywhere, unfolds upwards.
The fire within the bodies of embodied beings digests whatever is eaten;
because of that function of his, they say his sound is uncreated.
By hearing the twenty-four principles, one is liberated from sins;
therefore, in ancient times, the Self-born One himself created the seven notes beginning with *ṣaḍja*.
By these [means], all this—along with the gods, asuras, and humans—is constantly [perceived];
for the seven musical notes (svaras) arise from one who is perpetually practicing sound. (45)
Then, within just one month, his *nala* becomes condensed into a single mass;
thereafter, having pierced through passion (*rajas*) and darkness (*tamas*), the light shines forth at the end.
Just as he perceives externally, so too does he perceive at the end;
in three months he becomes independent, and Śiva-hood arises for him.
O Goddess, this first measure of yours, Ghoṣiṇī, has been described;
since knowledge is attained within this hundred thousand [recitations] through the mind, you should not treat it with contempt. (48)
He who understands in this way is not defiled by evil;
even when eating among outcaste dog-cookers, he remains like a lotus leaf in water.
Thus, O Goddess, the first [form], Trātughoṣiṇī, has been described to you. Hereafter, I shall proclaim that which is devoid of dissolution (laya) and illusion (māyā). (50)
Having arisen from one's own body, one should immediately hear the Piṅgalā [nāḍī] as soon as it is perceived;
standing outside in the sunlight, one should remain for a short while, fully relying on devotion. || 51 ||
One should perceive the smoke of one's own self as it issues forth, having pierced the palate; and in whatever manner one fixes the mind upon this mark, [so does concentration proceed]. (52)
In that same manner, his great wick of smoke increases;
thus, by the practice for one month, the movement [of the breath] in the head becomes unobstructed. (53)
At the end of the fourth state, one should perceive the dissolution of Piṅgalā alone;
having beheld the path of the gods, one should see the Self within the Self.
Having seen all the worlds and sub-worlds situated both externally and internally, as well as the luminaries following the path of smoke, he did not perceive that full state. (55)
Liberated from all evils, one shall attain the state free from dualities;
thus has the mark of Piṅgalā been observed by you with the mind.
There he beholds himself as Śiva, both supreme and non-supreme;
by this method, O God, he becomes completely enveloped in splendor.
Through the yoga of constant practice, one attains perfection in just six months;
everything conceived by the mind is accomplished effortlessly.
Upon the fall of the body, one quickly attains the supreme state of Śiva;
this is proclaimed as the hundred-thousand-fold [practice] regarding my twenty-five principles. (59)
Thus has been told the secret, which purifies the path to liberation;
the twenty-fifth *lakṣa*, O beautiful one, has been narrated to you. (60)
Now, O virtuous lady, hear concerning the twenty-sixth principle, the Vaidyutī [power], which is adorned by the path of *līlā*, consisting of the commencement of yoga and *prāṇāyāma*. (61)
At night, at the time of going to bed, having entered the interior without [a lamp],
and in the darkness without lamps, he indeed closes his eyes.
Then, seeing those rays born from his eyes— flickering like lightning and resembling the glittering bracelets on his arms— the beholder perishes.
Having performed this practice repeatedly, one should rest;
after remaining for some interval of time, one should practice those very same things once again. (64)
In whatever manner the practitioner performs the practice at night,
in that same way his splendor increases, like a drop of oil upon water. (65)
Just as one sees the sky obscured by others like sparks within gold,
so too the wise man undoubtedly perceives those very same houses.
Through the practice for five months, light shines forth at the end;
having seen the blazing [light] everywhere, the divine eye is activated.
Thereupon, it attains independence and enters the supreme Śiva.
Thus has been described to you the lakṣa situated within the Suṣumnā.
I have explained to you, according to the proper method, that which was hidden and kept secret by me;
consequently, there is no doubt that one attains autonomy through the essence of Śiva. (69)
I shall now describe to you the perception and the defining characteristic of that Bindumālinī who resides within my twenty-seven principles. (70)
Having become pure outside the village and having taken refuge in the shade of a tree,
he should slightly raise his face and gaze at the clear sky.
In that state, he perceives consciousness as having the brilliance of the sky;
[visions] resembling light and crystal fall and rise.
That form of the gods became visible through the *iḍā* [channel] by means of his luster;
for in whatever manner he fixed his aim upon that through yoga, [so it appeared]. (73)
In that very manner, all directions were as if filled by him on the outside;
yet, while he remained in mastery over many forms, he was situated both within and without.
Having perceived that by himself, the yogi is then no longer stained by merits or sins;
he becomes fortunate and pleasing to behold for all beings in the three worlds. (75)
It arises; of this there is no doubt, and from that it attains its name.
This measure (mātrā) of yours, O gentle one, has been described as Bindumālinī.
One is liberated from all diseases and, upon the fall of the body, shall go to Śiva; [this occurs] after twenty-seven hundred thousand repetitions of my mantra, performed without exertion. (77)
In my system of twenty-eight principles, there is a measure known as Cāndriṇī;
it is effortless, without the commencement of yoga, and devoid of the utterance of mantras. (78)
In whatever country he may reside and in whatever stage of life he may delight, he should practice the supreme *lakṣa* [of mantras], which is the cause for the past, middle, and future. (79)
One should observe the atoms (*paramāṇu*) as white, red, yellow, and black respectively, as well as brilliant and resembling crystal. (80)
Raising the face slightly toward the stainless expanse of the sky,
the lord of practitioners attains perfection through the practice of each one individually.

The Vāyavya mantras are black in color; the knower of yoga should always employ them at the beginning for the destruction of what remains, as well as for the purpose of eradication and driving away the insane.
And by others, [the rites] beginning with these—namely, striking, paralyzing, and so forth, as well as nourishing, increasing, pacifying, and the rest—are performed in their proper sequence. (83)
The illustrious master of yoga should perform these rites by practicing them one by one;
through this monthly application, he should carry out these actions.
Through the yoga of meditation for six months, that which proceeds within the three worlds becomes directly manifest to him; he attains success and shall become Śiva. (85)
The fifth performs all actions;
for this fifth, which is proclaimed, indeed possesses five forms. || 86 ||
Having meditated upon the self in this manner, the yogi should perform all actions;
yet, in the midst of them, the yogi perceives [the mind] as agitated by waves. (87)
Curved like waves and ripples, with a luster equal to a streak of lightning, resembling a serpent in its coils, and possessing a brilliance like that of a rainbow. || 88 ||
But as he focused his consciousness upon that target more and more,
so too did he perceive a wave-like fluctuation within it.
O Lord of Yogins, upon seeing this, the destruction of merit and sin occurs;
through the yoga of constant practice, one attains perfection—of this there is no doubt. (90)
Within twelve fortnights, freed from hunger and thirst, he is born with a divine body and divine vision; of this there is no doubt.
In one year, the lord of yogis, with self-restrained mind and well-concentrated,
attains the knowledge of hearing from afar and the power of perceiving with the mind.
The three worlds as they exist become directly manifest to him; likewise, he possesses the power of invisibility, attraction, and movement upon the ground. (93)
And one should perform [rites] with the Vāyavya [mantras], as well as those concerning the sky-dwellers and so forth;
with the Āgneya [mantras], one should effect drying up, striking, and killings. (94)
One should effect immobilization and even muteness by means of the Pārthiva [mantra];
having performed the rites beginning with nourishment (āpyāyana), one should effect it by means of the Vāruṇa [mantra]. || 95 ||
This fifth [method] should always be employed by the yogi in all undertakings;
these are proclaimed as the twenty-eight measures for the attainment of a *lakṣa*.
In the twenty-ninth principle, the measure that follows the mind should be observed with effort if one desires success for oneself. (97)
Having gone to a solitary, secluded place, one should close the divine eyes;
the self, possessing a golden luster, remains there, covering the eyes.
Having focused his consciousness upon that, he enters the resonance, which is white, red, yellow, and black, possessing a splendor like a rainbow. 99.
Having repeatedly observed the colors of those who strike one another,
one should again mark that [target] as being the size of a mustard seed. (100)
Within the shadow, O Goddess, there are seen various auspicious forms, all-pervading and consisting of all the gods, yet distinct from one another among the deities. (101)
The beautiful woman sees those forms as the shape of drops;
through the union of those two, the yogi perceives nothing else with his eyes by day or by night.
Within a month, one becomes free from excessive excrement and is exempt from hunger and thirst;
the body becomes fragrant and divine, and there arises a state of constant contentment.
Through a practice continued for two months, the divine eye arises;
merits and sins perish, just as darkness vanishes at the rising of the sun. (104)
Through the yoga of constant practice, there is no doubt that in twenty-nine months this will be equal [to the goal], O fair-faced one. (105)
The Nāḍī is indeed well-prepared, possessing various names and destroying great sins;
O Goddess, listen with one-pointed mind to its characteristics from me. 106.
It is without application or effort, devoid of measure and the bindu;
it is free from the throat, palate, and lips, and is divested of the utterance of mantras. || 107 ||
A man who is well-versed in that [teaching] is fit for immortality;
it is characterized by non-application, non-commencement, and effortless ease.
O Goddess, listen with effort to that by which all this space is entirely filled; one should fix the mind upon that space. 109.
Whether situated here or there, whether pure or even impure,
one should fix the mind and the ear in meditative concentration, free from external sounds. (110)
O Goddess, in a windless place or one with only a slight breeze, the curtain—like a bell when struck—should listen to [the recitation], which brings about the destruction of merit and sin. (111)
Having heard a sound similar to that of perfectly pure bell-metal (kāṃsa) which is devoid of bright luster, one becomes fit for immortality. || 112 ||
By that [consciousness], all this is filled by the omnipresent space;
through constant practice of that, O Queen of Consciousness, one beholds the earth. 113.
By this, for half a month, the lord of yogis is not afflicted by diseases;
he attains good fortune and, upon the fall of the body, shall go to Śiva.

That which consists of three syllables from the beginning, which has been proclaimed as being of three kinds—that indeed is to be known as belonging to Śiva; because of its universality, it is illuminating. (115)
O Goddess, the second *praṇava* is endowed with the form of a swan (*haṃsa*);
together with the *bindu*, it is proclaimed to have the form of Rudra. || 116 ||
Those beginning with "akāma" proceed, characterized by pervasiveness;
this subtle, self-willed activity is called the treasury of the syllable Om (Aṅkāra). || 117 ||
The letter *ha* joined with the letter *u*, endowed with the syllable *oṃ*, and accompanied by the *bindu*, O Goddess—this is proclaimed as the third. (118)
The origin of the syllable Oṃ is proclaimed to extend up to the path of Brahmā; Rudra, beginning with Śrīkaṇṭha and ending with Ananta, is said to be the syllable Oṃ.
Above that, it should be known, is the third, remembered as the Praṇava.
The accomplishment of the science of peace is the attainment that culminates in death at the time of death. (120)
But his unsurpassed movement has transcended the space of sound;
all this path is proclaimed to be divided into three.
The "entire" (sakala) consists of the five elements; the "entire-and-partless" (sakalaniṣkala) consists of three.
When, through the absence of utterance (uccāra), it has entered the state of partlessness (niṣkalatā), it becomes the Bindu. || 122 ||
By the will of Śiva, the practitioner is graced; he desires liberation.
This is renowned as the Saumya-nāḍī, which destroys even great sins. (123)
O Goddess, is that sound which is heard—characterized by the resonance of a bell and so forth—something that transcends the primary vowels? That sound is called the syllable Om of Rudra.
Divine, performing all rites, and bestowing fruits such as *aṇimā* and the rest—one should know it to consist of thirty-one [syllables]; Śiva’s *oṃkāra*, however, is beyond that. (125)
The thirty-two [channels] are said to be devoid of the qualities of the subtle elements (tanmātra).
The channel conjoined with the Pervasive One (Vyāpaka) is called Narañjanā. 126.
The auspicious syllable Oṃ is known as the supreme, divine, and stainless Oṃ;
through the yoga of constant practice, it bestows [its fruits] upon practitioners. 127.
Within half a month, one attains the eight qualities beginning with atomization (aṇimā), as well as the power of hearing from afar and the knowledge of what is spoken in all worlds. 128.
And he of great splendor perceives [himself] established everywhere; indeed, he is all-pervading, possesses the power to assume any form at will, and likewise possesses omniscience.
The fall of the body leads one swiftly to the supreme state of Śiva.
At the conclusion of the cessation of the sound of the bell, the syllable of Śiva (Śivoṃkāra) is proclaimed. (130)
That crest-lock (śikhā) is described by its characteristic as the "Stainless" (vimalā);
it is said to be the very principle of Time (kālatattva), and the channel (nāḍī) is called the "Untainted" (nirañjanā). 131.
O Varārohā, [I shall describe] that which is called Vimalā, conjoined with the supreme syllable;
I shall explain the supportless [state], which bestows the fruit of the nine principles.
One should recollect the principle of the *bindu*, which is beyond syllables and beyond utterance;
thereafter, however, one should not think of anything further than that supreme state. (133)
O fair-faced one, that reality is known as the thirty-third, which is stainless;
it is declared to be the thirty-second, established in the supreme state beyond support.

That which is beyond the thirty-three, which is to be designated as "devoid of name"—knowing that, O Goddess, one attains success; this is what is proclaimed as the goal of a hundred thousand [recitations]. (135)
Thus has the one reality been proclaimed by Śiva in many ways;
it bestows both spiritual perfection and liberation, and one should contemplate that which has been revealed.
Having thus understood this entire essence of knowledge, conduct yourself as you please;
this auspicious nectar of knowledge must not be given to anyone.
All this has been fully declared as the perfectly pure meditation on reality (tattva-dhyāna). O Goddess, this supreme [meditation] among all realities (tattvas) has thus been proclaimed. (138)
Of these, that which is beyond description, free from affliction, and the sustainer of all—indeed, it is itself devoid of any support. (139)
"O Goddess, such meditation as this has not been proclaimed for you.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter of the *Niśvāsakārikā*.
O Goddess, the Ācārya knows the Śiva-tantra, the knowledge of Śiva, and everything pertaining to Śiva in its entirety; he is free from worldly motives. || 1 ||
Detached from worldly treatises and possessing exclusive passion for the knowledge of Śiva, one should speak the answer to them by whatever means leads to the Lord. (2)
"Therefore, O Maheśvara, I desire to hear this through your grace.
Īśvara said:
"If someone were to ask, 'Which word is recited as being perishable? (3)
p.
287) Furthermore, one should say this to him: "Listen to that, O fair-faced one!
Is the *pudgala* composed of the three qualities (*triguṇa*), or is it a quality of space (*ākāśa*)? (4)

Then, distinct from the phonemes (varṇa) and ending with the subtle sound (nāda), the sphoṭa consisting of words and sentences—which expresses the Lord in the form of the Bindu—having been saluted, ceases its activity. || 5 ||
"The teacher declares that the *saṃhitā* of words comes first;
every sentence is based on words, and a word is traditionally held to be based on phonemes. (6)
All phonemes have speech as their support, and speech rests upon the vital breath (prāṇa). For the Lord Vāyu, the vital breath, is said to rest upon space (ākāśa).
Resting upon the subtle element of sound (śabdatanmātra), he is established within the sources of the elements;
the origin of the elements (bhūtādi) and Mahat likewise rest upon that which is beyond them.
O Goddess, because he is the source of the internal sacrifice and so forth, he is the essence of all; even beyond him is the Supreme God, the cause of all causes. (9)
O God, that which is beyond him is undoubtedly Śiva;
this entire universe has him as its support, and he is considered the supreme, the highest.
Neither speech functions nor does the mind truly reach that place where this supreme deity, the cause of all causes, resides. (11)
That by which the one to be propitiated is accomplished is, in brief, the word;
the deity is accomplished by means of the word, yet there is no deity apart from the word.
From the unmanifest arises sound; sound is its manifestor.
Then, that which is threefold and free from [grossness] is called subtle sound.
By means of that non-final sound, the intellect [perceives] that which is devoid of mind and speech;
by that divine sound, it is eternally seen as free from affliction.
But that which is merely sound, subtle, and situated within the body, is distinguished by all sounds; it is incomparable and free from affliction.
The divine Śiva is remembered as subtler than the subtlest;
for those who [attain Him] through the mere taste of hearing, He is the Lord of Pradhāna and Puruṣa.
It is not grasped here by sound, nor by hand, nor by the eye;
that which is without sound is the sound [of the fire] which resembles a bean in the sacrificial fire.
In the hearts of all embodied beings, the Supreme Śiva is pure, existing as resonance (ghoṣa),
roar (rāva), sound (svana), that which is called the "burst" (sphoṭa), and indeed as vibration (dhvani).
The humming sound and the sound of "huṃ," as well as the eighth, which is the sky-like sound itself—
that sound which arises from the joining of the ear and the thumb. (19)
That which is equal to the flame of a blazing fire is designated as *ghoṣa*;
however, that sound which is proclaimed and perceived as slightly soft is called *īṣanmanda*.
That which has the sound of broken bell-metal and is harsh is proclaimed as *ravet*.
Thereafter, the subtle sound of the flute is like windless rain. (21)
The fourth is the great sound, the supreme, most subtle, and that state which is free from affliction; it is the devourer of all sounds.
The word "Sva" accomplishes everything for the yogi; of this there is no doubt. The fifth great sound brings benefit to all yogis. (23)
For men, the *sphoṭa* alone is considered the medicine that brings delight to the mind;
one whose mind is absorbed within the sound should merge it into the supreme reality of sound. (24)
The *sphoṭa*, which bestows the accomplishment of all goals, attains supreme perfection—that sound which proceeds entirely free from the resonance of the vocal organs. (25)
Eternal, beginningless, and unmanifest, sound is characterized by resonance;
it is the sound like the gentle tone of a lute, resonating with the peaceful ringing of a bell. || 26 ||
The humming sound of bees intoxicated by the fragrance of flowers is known as *jhaṅkāra*; it is the very voice of the Supreme Goddess in her entirety. (27)
It appeared like a mass of lightning, dense and with a deep resonance;
it was a collection of all the unmanifested elements, as terrifying as the fall of a thunderbolt.
The sound remembered when the *dhvaṃ* sounds have ceased is the abode of the dissolution of all sounds;
that is Śiva, established in the principle of Śiva, the *dhvaṃ* sound remembered as the *praṇava*. (29)
O Goddess, eight sounds have been briefly described as supreme;
they should be practiced with effort if one desires one's own spiritual perfection.
"O Lord, I wish to hear in truth how the word 'goddess' (devī) makes its meaning known;
O Maheśvara, how do they exist as non-different and yet as different? (31)

The Lord [establishes] the relationship between word and meaning; that relationship is not employed as being of the nature of cause and effect, nor as being of the nature of the signified and the signifier. (32)
Otherwise, however, this effort would be a source of doubt for everyone;
for it is held that the nature [of a thing] is inseparable from itself, and not otherwise. (33)

And if the relationship of cause and effect between entities were derived from a [prior] cause, then that term would indeed express something other [than its own object], and it would apply to all things. (34)
Now, is sound the lamp and the preceding sound its wick?
Like consciousness, knowledge is that which is the excellence of sound. (35)
But the sound of Dharma shall bind [the senses], accomplishing peace, desire, and worldly prosperity. || 36 ||
After the word *paśu*, knowledge in the form of the *pati* is prescribed;
for by means of the word the object is established, and indeed the object is [revealed] through the word. (37)
Knowledge that has forgotten the meaning of words is ignorance, yet it is useless;
however, those who are bound by words and sounds are the masters among those who possess power here. (38)
The Self-existent Ones have declared that words are the means for the accomplishment of the comprehension of meaning;
whatever word brings about the accomplishment of a particular meaning within the fourfold collection of living beings.
That very word is to be understood as having a purposeful meaning by which an effect is accomplished;
for in this world, speech proceeds that is devoid of purpose. (40)
That which is known as an *apaśabda* (corrupt word) may be entirely Prakritic; however, words that convey meaning—even if spoken by sages or deities—are [valid]. (41)
The wise describe those [works] as containing ungrammatical forms (apaśabda) even when they conform to the scriptures; what is the use of such a language, however soft and elegant it may be? (42)
By hearing this discourse on ignorance and passion, which is the cause of the afflictions of saṃsāra, whatever merit arises brings about the complete destruction of sins and other evils. (43)
Even though that statement has perished, it should be understood as most excellent:
"The cycle of worldly existence consisting of sons, wife, and so forth belongs only to men of deluded mind. (44)

For the learned, immersion in the scriptures becomes an obstacle to the practice of yoga; when, in body after body, the state of agency and the state of being a knower proceed from the mouth [of the teacher]. (45)
At that time the living being is liberated; otherwise, never. Some men say this, but it is entirely false.
"The Blessed One, the Supreme Self, resides within the body—you who are in the midst of flesh, worms, phlegm, blood, and urine. (47)
O Sage among gods, how is it that which is so difficult to attain resides within the body,
while the entire world is seen even in every single house? (48)
The sole sun of the world is delighted by the *nāḍikā*;
thus, by means of the supreme subtle power (*sūkṣmaśakti*) abiding in the beyond, [he shines]. (49)
A web of delusion has been woven among the creatures in the world.
The Goddess said: "What are those eight supreme, subtle sounds, and what are the phonemes (varṇas)? (50)
"O Lord of Gods, please graciously tell me of the deities therein.
The Lord said: "I shall describe these deities among all the principles (tattvas)."
O lady of excellent hips, by the mere knowledge of which the practitioner attains accomplishment, there are no sins; those [letters] are the castes and they are the deities. (52)
O fair-faced one, those sounds and those principles are to be understood;
O beautiful one, they are joined by the gods, by the principles, and by my imperishable syllable (akṣara). 53.
Then, O Goddess, one attains perfection; upon the falling of the body, one is liberated.
And in sound, O fair-faced one, all the deities beginning with Brahmā reside.
O beautiful one, the gods beginning with Śrīkaṇṭha have gone to dissolution in that [state]. The gods are the supreme abode of sound, and from sound the phonemes (varṇas) arise. || 55 ||
From the phonemes and other elements, the manifestation of mantras arises; from that, everything proceeds.
From Sound (Śabda), this entire triple world, with its moving and non-moving beings, was born. 56.
Therefore, O Goddess, this ritual procedure involving the supreme Word must indeed be practiced by you.
Having become intent on meditation upon the Word, one who practices it with a well-concentrated mind [attains success]. (57)
Success has been described to you by means of that very success which is without sound;
first, one should touch the sound that is natural and bestows success. (58)
The third is that supreme sound which bestows human perfection;
the third is that supreme sound which invariably grants accomplishment. || 59 ||
The fourth is the principle of sound (śabdatattva), which is, in brief, the principle of limited agency (kalātattva).
By meditating upon that in the Lord of Gods, one becomes a partaker of the fruits of all [practices]. (60)
The fifth, which is known as Sound (Śabda), is the supreme Māyā, difficult to restrain;
the sixth, which is the principle of Sound (Śabdatattva), is remembered by the name Vidyā.
But that goddess Vāgīśvarī is not born there; he who is born there is not born [again]. That which is the seventh, supreme reality, the Lord (Īśvara), shall now be explained. (62)
In that regard, when one is absorbed in sound (śabda), one becomes equal to Īśvara;
[this is] the eighth, which is the supreme sound, incomparable and free from affliction.
Therein, when the yogi is absorbed, O Goddess, he reaches the ninth state, which is called Sādākhya, the supreme, and is known to consist of all sounds.
Emerging from that sound, well-rounded both below and above—
by means of that meditation, O Goddess of the Gods, one shall partake in the fruit of all [merits].
O Maheśvarī, all sounds are established within that Bindu-deva;
therefore, he has been called Bindu because he consists of the aggregate of all sounds.
O Goddess, ten [kalpas] beyond that are devoid of verbal cognition;
there alone, in that very succession, is established the state of representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*). (67)
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter of the Niśvāsakārikā. || 67 1/2 ||
The Goddess said:
"O Maheśvarī, all this that has been spoken by you was born from Sound (Śabda). By your grace, the collection of the principles of the phonemes (Varṇa-tattva) has been understood by me. (1)
O Maheśvara, for every single sound there is the manifestation of other gods;
likewise, O Lord of Gods, there is the yoga and meditation of the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas). || 2 ||
O Lord, please tell me today, out of your grace, about the eightfold powers beginning with *aṇiman*.
Listen, O Goddess, to the supreme secret which you have asked about.
Therefore, I shall fully proclaim this great boon, which brings benefit to practitioners; it has not been revealed by me to anyone else.
O Goddess, neither by the sages nor by the deities has this ever been asked in any way;
they were satisfied with the mere sound [of my voice], but I myself was not questioned, O beautiful one. (5)
I shall describe the creation in each and every word, as well as the occurrence of injunctions and so forth, for the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas), beginning with Aṇimā and ending with Bhava.
That which is called the sound of resonance (ghoṣa-śabda), devoid of the utterance of phonemes (varṇa), is attained through the [inner] instrument; I shall now describe its creation.
Therefore, that *prakṛti* which has arisen is called *māyā* by you;
the mantra that expresses it there is proclaimed to be the vowel *ū*. (8)
Ananta is proclaimed as the first among the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas) within that principle;
and for yogis, it is remembered as the Paiśāca birth among the wombs.
But that which is attained through the instrument [of yoga] is proclaimed as the power of atomization (aṇimā), as well as sovereignty and contentment. || 10 ||
The knowledge of *tāra* has been fully explained; the supreme *śi* sound is remembered [as the next].
In the first principle of sound (*śabdatattva*), this creation is proclaimed. (11)
The word *rāva* has been fully explained by you, and it was known to you previously;
for that which is born from a person is indeed what I have described to you.
In that regard, this mantra, the letter *ya*, is proclaimed as the designator (*vācaka*);
it is declared to be the subtle Lord of Knowledge (*vidyeśvara*), which is well-remembered by yogins. (13)
The Rākṣasa is said to be among the sources of birth, and sovereignty is remembered as its dissolution;
it is called the creation of water, and no son was proclaimed by the king.
This creation has been proclaimed in relation to the second reality, that of sound;
now I shall fully explain it regarding the third—listen to me with a one-pointed mind. (15)
The Maya previously described has arisen from its own name;
however, O lady of beautiful hips, Śivottama is the designator of the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas). 16.
The majesty of the yogins has been proclaimed; the yakṣas are declared to be their source. Their sovereignty, greatness, and likewise their contentment are all in vain.
(305) That knowledge regarding Tārā has been declared to you as the third;
I shall now fully explain the fourth—listen to me as I speak it. 18.
O lady of auspicious countenance, the subject of sound was previously explained by me at your request;
therefore, the time has now arrived for that which is difficult for all yogis to conquer.
The letter *la* is proclaimed as the designator (*vācaka*) of this reality of sound (*śabdatattva*);
and within it, O [Queen], Vidyeśa Ekanetra has been described to you.
For yogins, he is called Brahmā; in the womb, he is called Gandharva;
O Queen of Gods, attainment and sovereignty are declared by you as the fourth.
O lady of beautiful countenance, contentment has been described by me as rain;
joy is declared to be knowledge, and this was told to you in the fourth [chapter].
(306) I shall now fully explain the fifth; listen, O long-eyed one!
Sphoṭa is the supreme sound, the highest, and the source of the principle of Māyā. || 23 ||
The word "self" deludes these people through their debates, chatter, and cavils;
not knowing the supreme reality, they are bewildered by verbal disputes. (24)
The letter *ma* is proclaimed to be the designator of that reality of sound (*śabdatattva*).
O Goddess, Vidyeśa is declared to be your single vision;
therein, the Vaiṣṇava state is proclaimed as the fifth for yogins. (26)
The womb of Indra has been fully described; now hear of sovereignty (aiśvarya).
It is renowned as "the power of will" (prākāmya), and supreme contentment is called [the next]. (27)
(307) Knowledge has been proclaimed by Śiva, the Supreme Self, as "the Joyful" (Pramudita). This fifth [stage] has been fully explained to you in its proper sequence and order. || 28 ||
I shall now fully declare the sixth; listen as it is being told by me.
Sound was previously described by me, in which the manifestation of knowledge occurs. (29)
The syllable *kṣa* is proclaimed as the designator of that reality of sound (*śabdatattva*).
Furthermore, the triple form of the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśas*) has been described in successive order.
Kaumāra is proclaimed for yogins; the gentle [state] is celebrated as being in the womb; and Īśitva is fully described among the qualities, O beautiful goddess. (31)
Excellent joy is called satisfaction (tuṣṭi), and knowledge is proclaimed as delight (moda).
This, O Goddess, has been told to you as the unsurpassed sixth sound.
(308) I shall now fully explain the seventh [sound], which is extremely difficult to obtain. O Lord, its origin in this [system] is known as *jhaṅkāra*. (33)
The speaker of that reality is the supreme mantra consisting of the letter Ra;
from Vidyeśa, Śrīkaṇṭha is proclaimed as the [teacher] of the yogins, beginning with the syllable Auṃ.
And within the womb, O beautiful one, he is called the Lord of Progeny;
furthermore, his sovereignty therein is proclaimed as his state of Śiva-hood. (35)
From Sunetra, Tuṣṭi is said to have arisen; knowledge is called Ramyaka.
Thus has this seventh, supreme sound been fully described to you. (36)
I shall now fully explain the eighth; listen with a one-pointed mind.
Because that reality is Sadāśiva, it is declared to you as Dhvaṃkṛta.
The letter *ha* is proclaimed as the designator (*vācaka*) of that reality (*tattva*).
Among the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśas*), Śikhaṇḍīśa is said to be the yogi Śrīkaṇṭha. (38)
The eighth is proclaimed and celebrated as Yonibrahmā;
there, O Goddess of gods, resides sovereignty that accomplishes all desires. (39)
Contentment indeed is the mark of that reality; of this there is no doubt.
Knowledge therein has been fully described by me as being ever-rejoicing. (40)
I have declared to you this eighth [topic]: sound is the supreme cause.
Through knowledge, a living being is liberated from the entire bondage of the fettered (paśu). || 41 ||
The ninth is satisfaction (tuṣṭi), which is declared to be the deity Bindu;
O lady of excellent vows, Bindu consists of four kalās and is the Śāntyatīta [tattva].
(310) I shall tell you that great [teaching], more secret than the secret, so that Śakti and Catuṣkala may indeed become ninefold. 43.
O virtuous lady, I have described to you these sixty-four divisions;
I shall now explain their worship to you correctly—listen to me.
On the previously mentioned plot of ground, free from hair, insects,
and bones, one should draw there an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp.
One should worship the god Śiva, the supreme cause, in the pericarp;
Ananta has already been mentioned previously, as well as Padmaśakti.
One should likewise place the limbs, beginning with Dharma, in their proper sequence;
and the placement (nyāsa) and the mantra in the heart-lotus should be exactly as previously described.
On the eastern leaf, however, one should worship Prakṛti with the Āgneya mantra; on the southern [leaf], Akṛta with the Paiśāca mantra, and with the Nairṛta [mantra]. || 48 ||
One should place Aṇimā in the west, and Vāyavyā in the water;
then, being composed, one should place Tārājñāna in the north.
O Great Goddess, one should visualize Bindudeva in the northeast;
having placed Ghoṣa in the center, one should then perform this again.
O beautiful one, by means of the short, long, and protracted *ukāra* alone,
one should effect the three principles (*tritattva*) there in the path of resonance according to the proper sequence.

The principle of the Self (ātmatattva) is indeed short, while knowledge (vidyā) is proclaimed to be long; one should always perform the principle of Śiva (śivatattva) everywhere with the protracted vowel (pluta). || 52 ||
O Goddess of the gods, in this manner the arrangement of the three principles (tritattva) should be performed, in due order for all, within one's own word consisting of three syllables. (53)
O beautiful one, those letters beginning with the vowel *ī* and ending with *ā*, which are situated starting from the east, are declared to be deities.
He is indeed the proclaimer for all of them until everything is completed;
one should assign him to all the various terrestrial rites.
In this manner, one should offer fifty oblations, beginning from the east;
one hundred should be offered for the element of sound, and three hundred should be offered for the three principles (tattvas).
The final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) should be offered while listening to the sound in a well-prepared fire-chamber;
one who desires the goals of spiritual perfection and liberation should meditate upon the God consisting of sound.
O Goddess, it is well-encircled by the five Brahmās, as well as the limbs of Śiva, the world-protectors, the lords of the vidyās, and the weapon-mantra. (58)
However, one should sacrifice in two ways; this is yoga in brief: with material substances when possessing wealth, and through meditation alone when destitute of means. (59)
The teacher, having severed all doubts, should liberate [the disciple] even by means of the various [methods].
In the second [stage], the partless reality (niṣkala-tattva) is proclaimed; "Rāva" is said to be sound.
In the third [element], the reality of emptiness is proclaimed as the sound of one's own voice;
in this manner, through such a sequence, the reality within sound follows its respective order.

O Goddess, one should not otherwise form the conceptualization of "it exists" or "it does not exist"; O Mistress of the Gods, when the command is accomplished, one should not think of anything at all.
Just as the accomplishment of the lines was taught by Śiva in the *Nayasūtra*, there is no doubt that the accomplishment of sound is attained through practice month after month. (63)
O virtuous one, there is no yoga equal to this in all the tantras;
no accomplishment equal to this is found in the three worlds. (64)
O Goddess, there is no other means of realization equal to these;
something supreme must be known, for the knowledge of sound is the highest. || 65 ||
The non-conceptual fourth [state] is direct perception established everywhere;
it is the Bindu, the Kalā, the four-cornered Kalā, and the fourfold Śakti.
This is declared to be the supreme sacrifice; one should place the Nāda within the pericarp (karṇikā).
The letter *U* is the *utkṣaṇī*, while Śakti is the first digit (*kalā*).
The letter *e* is indeed proclaimed as the second, the subtle one;
the third is indeed *amṛtā*, which is proclaimed as the letter *i*. (68)
Amṛtāmṛtā is the fourth; the vowel *ī* has been described to you.
As for the divine digit (*kalā*) of the Bindu, which was previously mentioned by me, [it is as follows]. (69)
O fair-faced one, I have also spoken regarding the *nāda* in the *binduyāga*:
first, one should place a portion of the deity *bindu* in the east. (70)
The second is indeed to the south, the third to the west, and the fourth to the north; these are proclaimed as the digits (kalās) of the Bindu.
One should place Utkarṣaṇī in the southeast, Susūkṣmā in the southwest,
and the digit named Amṛtā in the northwest.
One should place the fourfold group of Śaktis— Amṛtā and Mṛtā—
in the northeast; one should then install them, joined with Nāda-Śakti, within the pericarp.
O virtuous one, the reality of the self has been told to you;
indeed, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra abide according to their respective colors.
Īśvara and the power of Nāda are established in the upper portion;
all are expanded through the Tattva, for all are indeed Tattvas—of this there is no doubt. (75)
Initiation may be of two kinds; it is not auspicious when performed through meditation or material substances alone.
When accompanied by a hundred oblations for each [of these], initiation leads to liberation.
The principles beginning with earth have been previously described by me;
they are to be understood in their proper sequence within the Śakti, the Nāda, and the Bindu.
O Goddess, this supreme sacrifice is indeed difficult for those of unrefined soul to attain;
even the gods, O beautiful lady of the gods, strive for this sacrifice. (78)
O Goddess, such a rite as this is not obtained by me unless I am pleased;
it must never be given to one who is not a disciple, nor ever to one who is not devoted.
When she has been consecrated for one who is dear to the guru, self-controlled, and knowledgeable in the procedures of all paths, this is the manner in which it should be given. (80)
It should be given to a disciple endowed with noble birth, virtuous conduct, and good qualities, and who speaks kindly;
otherwise, it must not be given—this is the command of the Supreme Lord.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter of the Niśvāsakārikā.
The Goddess said:
"By means of the eye, by speech, by touch, by the mind, or by water..."
Through the yoga of meditation, she performs the act of sustaining [the world] out of a desire to bestow grace. || 1 ||
O Lord, this very great secret has been told by you;
yet this lack of distinction among them was hidden within your heart.
Therefore, O Blessed One, I wish to hear this; you should deign to speak.
As the Lord, I shall explain each of these to you in detail.
This must be understood by the teacher himself in brief at the time of initiation:
just as in the world the sun awakens the lotuses.
Thus, having purified the lotuses, Śiva, being gracious, awakens them—though situated afar, yet standing near; residing in the body, yet free from the body. (5)
Stained and yet stainless, he alone indeed abides as many;
ever subtler than the subtle, the all-pervading Lord is further away than the farthest.
When darkness is near, the body is pervasive, yet it is neither the Lord nor the imperishable;
likewise, the principles (tattvas) and the deities remain according to their respective divisions.
Sovereignty, the contentment of knowledge, and the other [perfections] along with the deities,
as well as their respective locations within one's own body, in due order.
Having known all this in its particulars, there shall be the destruction of all bonds.
I shall now describe the lotus of the body and, in particular, the lotus of the void.
(320) It is endowed with eight petals representing the Vasus and eleven filaments representing Rudra;
the twelve Ādityas are to be known as the pericarp, and they are recorded as being in the lotus.
O Goddess, I am the one who has been meditated upon by him in whose city, consisting of all the gods, there exists the state of contemplation; as for those other people, they have been led astray.
The heart of all embodied beings resembles the flower of a plantain tree;
situated in its center is an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp.

The lotus of the heart is one *vitasti* in size, while that situated above the navel measures four finger-breadths; however, the [lotus] measuring eight finger-breadths is established [above that]. (13)
The lotus stalk has nine openings and is filled with desires on all sides;
it is equal in size to a thumb-joint, while the pericarp indeed possesses filaments.
On the pericarp there should be the sun, and in its center the moon;
in the center of the moon there should be fire, and in the center of the fire, Maheśvara. || 15 ||
Sadāśiva is [the authority] for Maheśa, and Śiva is even beyond him;
I shall declare for all of them the authoritative measure established by Śiva.
One should make the sun slightly smaller than that, and the moon likewise;
one should know the supreme orb of fire to be smaller than the moon. (17)
Stainless, purified of all smoke, divine, and resembling the rising sun;
he is the Lord (Īśāna) who is pure being alone, shining like a blazing mountain peak.
Above that [face] is the supreme, divine [face], as pure as clear crystal;
it is the Great-Souled Sadāśiva, and above even that is the Parāpara (the Higher-Lower).
White, perfectly pure, divine, ungraspable, and supremely auspicious—this is declared to be the stalk of the body; the wise know it to consist of the petals of Brahman. (20)
Viṣṇu resides in the pericarp; the knot is proclaimed to be Māyā.
On the southern petal of the unmanifest is Buddhi, and on the southwestern [petal] likewise.
To the west, ego (ahaṅkāra) and the subtle element of sound (śabdatanmātra) for Vāyu;
to the north, the subtle element [of touch] and likewise the sense of taste (rasana) for Īśāna. || 22 ||
The grasper of form is situated in the east; the nose is located on the fire-petal. On the tips of the petals are the great elements, while the filaments are the sense faculties.
The mind alone abides everywhere within the subtle elements and the senses;
that which is obstructive within the heart is of the nature of darkness (tamas) and takes the form of sleep.
Below that pericarp, however, his body is established;
at the end, the pericarp is conscious and conjoined with all objective states (bhāva). (25)
That Śiva is situated above the pericarp in all bodies;
the gods reside in the lotus stalk, while those below are situated upon the filaments. (26)
Various hosts [of deities] were on his leaf, and likewise Daityas were upon his body hairs;
as well as planets, lunar mansions, and stars, along with Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Pannagas.
The sisters and the mothers stood at the base of the navel;
he who, having pierced the lotus composed of all the gods with the needles of his knowledge— || 28 ||
He perceives his own stainless self directly from within the body;
for all this that is awake, the teacher is said to be the Lord. (29)
When he is satisfied, may all the lords of the worlds be satisfied;
for the preceptor who initiates is the best of gurus, one who has reached the further shore of the Śiva-tattva. (30)
Otherwise, he is not to be known as a guru, nor does initiation grant liberation.
The preceptor is remembered as the embodiment of the mantra, and Śiva is the supreme reality beyond the form of the mantra. || 31 ||
The mantras should be known as being of that nature, and Śiva should be known as being of that nature;
therefore, grace proceeds toward all beings.
This is the will of the Blessed One; however, one should contemplate it thus:
Śiva, residing within the body of the teacher, is the one who bestows grace upon living beings. (33)
It bestows various accomplishments and leads the bound soul (paśu) to liberation;
it is that which is peaceful, the supreme reality, the cause, and the lord of causes. (34)
Having become established in that, one should manifest the principles of Śiva, Vidyā, and Ātman,
as well as the supernatural powers such as *aṇimā* and the rest, and Śiva, the supreme cause. (35)
"Abiding therein, he reveals it as it truly is and as it exists.
The Goddess said: "But what is the true nature of the three principles (tritattva), and how is it known from the Imperishable (akṣara)? (36)
Tell me how there can be ignorance regarding all beings in the world, when each being exists exactly as it is, according to its own nature of virtues and defects. (37)
O Lord, since all fruits and merits are known to you, tell me how anything could remain unknown in this world when you possess omniscience. (38)
When the knowledge of reality, which is perfectly pure, is known to be situated in the middle, [then] the Lord [is realized]. (p. 326)
Then, for him, omniscience is fully realized through every means. || 39 ||
Anger, malice, envy, lust, delusion, greed for wealth, backbiting, falsehood, and deceit—even toward men who have passed old age—[are present]. (40)
Hypocrisy, cruelty, instability, and crookedness of thought are what must be overcome;
the world is shrouded by these very things, and for that reason, one does not find the Divine.
Having performed this rite of the word, the preceptor, well-established and acting with great care, should initiate all living beings by means of this meditation. 42.
This is known as the procedure for meditation; now the mental [meditation] is being described.
One should apply this very procedure when all those [senses] are fixed upon a single sense-organ. (43)
O fair-faced one, all the senses function by means of the measure of a single sense; indeed, all beings and the principles [of existence] are likewise [unified] in that one.
Activity in all undertakings is beginningless; of this there is no doubt.
O Goddess, it is grasped by the mind, and the bound soul (paśu) is joined with the mind. 45.
O beautiful one, the mind exists in all [beings] through the measure of the single sense-organ;
since it is grasped by the mind, for that very reason it is of the nature of the mind.
That entire state [of the self] is to be perceived within Maheśvara by means of the mind, that mind joined with the intellect, and through the application of all the instruments of perception. (47)
One should likewise place Ātmavidyā and Śiva, along with the conceptualization of emanation and withdrawal; having thus arranged the principles (tattvas), one should place Śiva above them.
Having thus meditated with the mind, out of a desire to favor those who perform their duties,
this single mental rite has been described in brief. (49)
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, the procedure for the mental favoring of the presentation of purificatory rites, in the Jñānakāṇḍa of the Niśvāsakārikā.
Īśvara said:
Becoming Īśvara, he creates; as Sadāśiva, he withdraws. Śiva presides over the act of maintenance, while Śānti is the supreme state. (1)
The supreme reality of the Self (ātmatattva) is said to be the lotus petal;
knowledge (vidyā) is its filaments, and the process of withdrawal (saṃhāra) is the pericarp below.
In the pericarp is the Śiva-tattva, which is the agent of the state of persistence;
they know this lotus of Kailāsa to be the beginning of these three principles (tattvas).
The two lips are the petals of the lotus, the teeth are known as the filaments, the tongue is said to be the pericarp, and the body is called the stalk. || 4 ||
The deity who is the teacher of the world resides in the space within the mouth;
the tongue, which is the pedestal of Kailāsa, is situated in the middle of the palate.
Because he practices conduct himself,
shows others how to practice it, and gathers together the scriptures, he is therefore called an "Ācārya" (Teacher).
Though his body is soundless, he is the maker of sound; he is the bringer of the end to all performed karma.
He is the master weaver of the city of the illusion of the three worlds; whoever beholds him is the doer of all.
Having thus established the abode of the deities within the Lord of Gods,
he effects the placement of the mouth at the end by means of the final [syllable], out of a desire to bestow grace. (8)
"O Goddess of beautiful countenance, I have thus explained the favor of speech.
Thus ends the favor of speech. || 9 ||
The Goddess said:
O Mahādeva, that which is called Sūtra is a designation for the path of light.
O Blessed One, I desire to hear it; you should speak it.
They say that the Lord is the *sūtra* because of his indication; the name *sūtra* refers to the Great State (*mahatpada*).
By him all this was proclaimed, as bees [are guided] by the string. (11)
One should know that the unbroken void is all-pervasive, the undecaying state;
resembling the circle of a wheel, one should manifest it within the *ghaṭikā*. (12)
"You ought to draw that which is situated in the center of the heart-lotus, peaceful in the midst of the moon, sun, and fire, supreme, subtle, and well-defined. (13)
The Goddess said:
Since all the Gaṇas are established in the Nyāsa precisely because of that reality,
please graciously explain this marriage of their mantras.
Īśvara said: All deities consist of mantra, and all mantras consist of Śiva.
One should worship in the sacrifice to Śiva with a mantra that consists of Śiva.
(332) Even if they recite the Saṃhitā, those who do not attain the true nature of Śiva and perform initiation without understanding it— both the disciple and the teacher go to a lower state. 16.
Therefore, one does not attend as a pupil upon two who share the same residence;
nor does this favor toward both husbands proceed in such a manner. || 17 ||
The one supreme Lord alone perceives; thus the relationship between disciple and teacher proceeds.
That physician who performs a medical procedure without having himself correctly understood it [is at fault]. (18)
The patient suffers pain, and even the physician may not obtain the result, even if he is skilled in knowledge and realization and has mastered every possible condition. (19)
He liberates [others] from sins, his own defilements having been shaken off by knowledge;
even if devoid of all auspicious marks, one who possesses knowledge is called a guru. || 20 ||

The teacher (deśika), who knows the rules for initiation and the ritual procedures, is the burner of the net of bonds; he is a devotee of Śiva, possessed of great devotion, and acts with a spirit of devotion. (21)
There is no difference between the two: the Teacher and Śiva. He is indeed the bindu of the letter A, and he is the unmanifest sound (nāda) of dissolution.
In him all sciences are contained, and he himself is the supreme Śiva;
he is perfectly replete with all knowledge and is skilled in the meaning of all sciences.
Ananteśa and the other Śivas do not at all make any distinction between the Teacher, the Mantra, and Śivajñānaśiva. (24)
