Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter in the Jñānakāṇḍa of the Niśvāsakārikā, in the section on the Lotus of the Mouth concerning the Grace of Speech.
The Goddess said:
"O God, I wish to hear in truth about the infinite seat;
O Maheśvara, what indeed would its end and its seat be like? (1)
Those who are liberated from the ocean of worldly existence go to Śiva at the dissolution of the body, [being under the guidance of] Īśvara.
The seat known as Ananta, which arises from the power of will (icchā-śakti) and serves as the support for the principles (tattvas) and the sky, is that very seat. (3)
By me, everything from the primordial ether down to the earth was known there in its entirety; such is the power of Śiva, the Supreme Self.
(335) Rich with the mud of the karma of illusion, in the great ocean of the year,
it has Sadāśiva as its support and is designated as the "eternal foundation."
And by means of Māyā, those thirty-two principles (tattvas) are established in the water;
the thirty-third is Avidyā... || 6 ||
O Lord, the thirty-fourth [lotus] is situated upon eight petals;
it is rich with the primordial root-mud and originates from the water of knowledge.
The worlds are situated upon the thorns of the arrangement of the stalks of the process;
ten crores of mantras are established in the lotus of Śiva.
For this is the great essence of mantras, the supreme refuge of all deities;
indeed, the entire path and the lotus are dependent upon that which is called Śiva.
(336) Beyond the seat (āsana), O fair-faced one, there is no further path;
because persons (puruṣas) are infinite, the principles (tattvas) and so forth are likewise infinite. || 10 ||
Because the *prakṛtis* are infinite, their powers (*śaktis*) are also infinite;
there is no finite enumeration of the bound souls (*paśus*) nor of the worlds (*bhuvanās*). (11)
The mantras possessing the power to bestow grace upon those beings are likewise infinite;
this cycle of worldly existence is beginningless, and indeed no end to it is found.
Because it sustains all and because it is infinite, it is called "infinite" (ananta).
There is no measure for the lotus, for Śiva himself is infinite.
Because he is without end, he is infinite; therefore he is called "the Infinite.
He who is presided over by that Infinite is himself made infinite. || 14 ||

Śiva, however, is to be known as infinite, immeasurable, and incomparable; he is celebrated in the *Svatantrecara* by means of the *kalās* as being beyond the reach of the knowledge of bound souls (*paśu*). (15)
That which is beyond that is indeed infinite; it belongs to the Great Soul of the Yoga-pīṭha.
It consists of agency and lordship, eternal contentment, and perfect tranquility.
Because its power is unimpeded by any principle (tattva), this dharma taught by Śaṅkara is such that it is always existent everywhere, and knowledge and omniscience are ever-present.
And because it is the substratum of all knowledge, this knowledge of the Lord is supreme;
he is detached from material states and is always free from desire.
There is lifelong celibacy and supreme detachment toward the Lord;
and there is that prosperity which is characterized by all the powers such as *aṇimā* and others, yet remains unaffected by worldly things. (19)
The sovereignty of that supreme Śiva has never been tasted by others in this world;
neither his realm, nor his path, nor his form, nor even his speech has been experienced by another. (20)
Neither sound nor even the pure space that abides everywhere—the stainless, immaculate sky, unobstructed on all sides. (21)
It is devoid of qualities, beyond speech and mind, and free from planets and stars;
in some places it has the appearance of molten gold, and in others it resembles snow.
In some places it resembled a rainbow, in some places it had a luster like that of stars;
in some places it was like the moon or its crescent, and in some places it had the brilliance of emerald.
The lotus is stainless, free from defects, radiant with great splendor, all-pervading, immeasurable, universal, and intensely brilliant. (24)
The sky is its stalk, the directions its petals, and the space-points its filaments;
it is the vow [of the lotus] sustained by infinite, all-pervading powers of nectar. (25)
It is expansive and uninterrupted, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns;
it is the pure light of the universe, a great splendor whose own nature is infinite brilliance.
The powers of Śiva are wondrous, subtle, both peaceful and unpeaceful, incomparable, established, endowed with qualities, and infinite. (27)
By these powers, he shines eternally adorned;
he is as radiant as a stainless thread embellished with pure ornaments.
But he [beheld] that divine lotus-petal, radiant with light, wonderful to behold, exceedingly pure, peaceful yet brilliant. (29)
(340) It is like a mass of a thousand lightning flashes, crowded with many rays;
it has the form of pure moonlight and its filaments are quivering. 30.
With a mass of shimmering rays, variegated and upward-facing, possessing many colors yet devoid of color, and with trembling, beautiful filaments. (31)
It was struck by the rays of the sun, possessing a luster like that of a vaidūrya gem,
resembling many beams of light, and having a radiance equal to ten million flashes of lightning.

In some places it has the appearance of molten gold; in some places it resembles the dissolution of the world; in some places it is like a rainbow, and in some places its radiance is equal to the sound of a thunderbolt.
Resembling crystal stone and possessing a luster like that of rubies,
in some places it was a dense mass of rays that overspread the expanse of the sky.
In some places [the forms] possessed the majesty of the dissolution, with the splendor of the rays at the end of an eon;
and in other places they were masses of color, their bodies entirely liberated.
Manifesting the splendor of his own power, pervading everywhere, resembling a water bubble and possessing a radiance like the autumnal moon. (36)
It possesses the fragrance of fully blossomed rays, is swarming with the bees that are the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas),
has the Suṣumṇā as its continuous stalk, and culminates in Śiva, the fire of time that brings an end to all.
Surrounded on all sides like a circle of lightning,
it was a mass of a thousand rays, difficult to behold from any direction.
The power of his action and knowledge is certainly peerless;
having himself realized the ultimate limit of all phenomena, he acts according to his own will and independent mastery.

The power of will (*icchā-śakti*) is the supreme attribute (*dharma*) of Śiva, the Supreme Self. Endowed with that, He is called the "Essence of Good Attribute" (*sudharmātmā*) by those who are truly virtuous.
This property is said here to have a real cause when it resides in a permanent substratum;
a property does not attain established existence in the absence of a substratum. (41)

Desire (icchā), Impulsion (preraṇī), the one who is both the Timeless and Time (kālanī-kalinī), as well as the one who brings about existence from non-existence (abhāvabhāvinī) and Knowledge (jñānī)—this is proclaimed as the Power of Action (kriyāśakti). || 42 ||
Mohanī, Rañjinī, Bodhā, Prabhāvā, Vibhunī, Rasā, Damanī, Dhāmanī, Bodhā, Mananī, Unmanī, and Śivā. (43)
Dhātrī, Jananī, Krodhā, Ālinī, Aparigrahā, Virajā, Vijayā, Saumyā, Māyā, Avidyā, and Rāgiṇī. || 44 ||
Unobstructed and unimpeded, ageless and unconquered,
unborn and contrary, she is the fashioner even of the subtlest parts. (45)
Bestower of strength, giver of power, subduer, and giver of dharma;
she is the embodiment of her own nature, the form of all colors, and the one who binds with a net of nooses.
Pāśinī, Mohinī, Trāṇī, Nigrahā, Anugrahā, Mahī, Harṣiṇī, Bhāvā, Saumyā, and indeed Saumyadharmiṇī. || 47 ||
Existents proceed as possessing intrinsic nature; she is intense and peaceful, the bestower of accomplishment;
she is immeasurable and measurable, the means of valid cognition, and the conceptualizer. (48)
She is the all-pervading one and the protector of all; she is fear and the remover of fear.
She is the creator and destroyer, consciousness, contentment, sleep, radiance, and hunger.
The burner, the sacred revelation, the intellect, wisdom, the future, the discerning,
the one who brings about existence, the gentle, the constant, and the one who carries away the eternal. (50)
She is to be known as Anantā, Amṛtā, Īśvarī, Avyayā, as well as Rati, Prīti, and Viṣādajananī. || 51 ||
It is the sustainer and the destroyer of living beings, the fashioner of their forms, the one that enters them, the restrainer, and likewise the shaper of their destinies.
Amṛtā, Anantaśakti, and likewise Parāśakti—all these powers are eternally stationed in the filaments (kesara). || 53 ||
The hosts of Śaktis, possessing the luster of pure gorocanā, should indeed be known to illuminate the ten directions as far as the pericarp and the pedestal. (54)
The bulb (kanda), shaped like a *paṭola* gourd and surrounded by powers (*śakti*s),
is the eternal Lord situated upon the pericarp and constantly surrounded by powers. || 55 ||
Just as the rays of the sun are established as indivisible, so too all the hosts of powers are proclaimed to be like rays. || 56 ||
The Supreme Goddess always acts through her power within the heart-lotus;
all those powers are proclaimed to be satisfied by that splendor.
Having thus understood it to be of the nature of power (śakti), one is then liberated and liberates others;
like Indra, they pervade the moving and the unmoving with blazing strength.
And that is immovable, indescribable, infinite, without a core, without beginning, middle, or end, one, and beyond comprehension. (59)

It is free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), beyond the temporal paths (*niradhvāna*), transcendent of the senses (*atīndriya*), and free from affliction (*anāmaya*); it is partless (*niṣkala*), stainless (*vimala*), its activity sublime and all-pervading, and supreme. (60)
Resembling gold and the sun, it illuminates all principles;
its function is luminosity, it should be known as pure, with the sky as its pericarp.
"Having thus pervaded the supreme deity, from Ananta up to the end of Śiva.
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter in the section on the Power of Ananta within the Jñānakāṇḍa of the Niśvāsakārikā. The Goddess said:
O Lord of Gods, tell me of the form [to be worshipped] upon such an auspicious seat surrounded by Śaktis, and of the presiding lord of the seat. || 1 ||
(347) I have previously described the form of Īśvara, which existed before the intellects of Brahmā and the other [gods] in ancient times.
The sages, as well as others such as Durvāsas and yet others. || 2 ||
The self (ātman) should be known as the form, inactive and not independent;
its union with the mantra is performed, O beautiful goddess. (3)
The mantra is said to be fivefold by which it becomes "sakala" (with parts);
joined with mantras, it is the "mantrātman" (the essence of mantra), and joined with phonemes, it is "sadātmaka" (of the nature of existence). || 4 ||
But when joined with the *kalās*, he is then said to be "consisting of *kalās*";
likewise, he consists of the distinctions of words (*pada*) and the distinctions of the principles (*tattva*). (5)
The "Paśu" was previously described by me; that is proclaimed to be the [individual] form (mūrti).
Since the instrument (karaṇa) consists of the existent (sat), he is therefore called Sadāśiva. (6)
Because he is eternally constant and inconceivable, he is called Sadāśiva;
having attained that ever-peaceful state, he follows after that state.
The Guru, who is complete, auspicious, and peaceful, is worshipped by the thirty gods;
he is the support of all worlds, established within the seat of the sky.
Situated in the midst of the filaments of the Śakti, adorned with the ornament of Śakti, perfectly filled with all powers, and the illuminator of all powers. || 9 ||
Just as the sun, having dispelled the darkness of night by means of its own radiant rays,
remains in the sky, so too does the form abide within the supreme Śiva.
It shines forth entirely with its own radiances, as if arisen divided by those very radiances;
it blazes immovably, being both eternal and non-eternal, and stainless. (11)
It is tranquil, stainless, pure, all-pervading, and utterly immaculate;
it surpasses the splendor of ten million suns and possesses a radiance that shines forth once and for all.
Because of its pervasiveness, no measure of it is taught;
because it is beginningless, it has no origin; and because it is eternal, it has no end. (13)
He is devoid of qualities, all-knowing, the agent, independent, facing all directions, perfectly complete, imperishable, peaceful, subtle, unborn, supreme, and bodiless. || 14 ||
The eternally awakened and pure self, the cause, possessing immeasurable form;
he is infinite, without end, eternally satisfied, and without support. || 15 ||
The immutable, the source, the lord, the protectorless one of immeasurable luster,
the beginningless, the unique, the one who is to be restrained, the conscious, the heart-stealer of all— Śiva. (16)
The doer of all, the knower of all, Śarva, the omnipotent, unborn and imperishable;
he is the one who causes all to act and the non-agent himself—by him all this is pervaded.
The ultimate of all, the supreme of all, devoid of all defects, transcending the state of all principles, unborn, sovereign, and imperishable. || 18 ||
It is perfectly eternal, perfectly complete, perfect nirvāṇa, and most beautiful; it is liberated from all obscurations, the singular wonder, and the primeval. || 19 ||
All-pervading, omniscient, and situated above all; omnipresent and yet transcending the omnipresent, he is the entire impurity of all forms. (20)

This very Rudra, the Great God, whose body consists of mantras among all forms, is like the imperishable one who possesses a universal form through the division of the supreme and the non-supreme. (21)
He is of infinite forms and infinite; he is the infinite and indeed the infinite itself.
He possesses infinite power, an infinite self, infinite senses, and infinite faces.
He transcends all abodes; that state is beyond the senses.
This entire world, consisting of those very elements, is brought forth by Your speech.

The reality of reality is indeed [realized] through reality; the reality of reality is the destroyer of delusion. It is considered inconceivable, the most subtle of all, and beyond the reach of vision. || 24 ||
Ananta is the union of all forms; he is proclaimed as the one who possesses all.
This Ananta has been described to you, whose end is not to be found.
But because he does not know the supreme, infinite ritual procedure regarding the Lord of Gods,
he performs the Śiva-sacrifice and does not liberate the bound soul (paśu). (26)
The grace [bestowed] by me through the eye and the application of the *bindu* has been explained;
the touch resulting from the union with the hand of Śiva is proclaimed to be everywhere present. (27)
Listen, O Goddess, as I tell you how one should act with water;
this procedure has been proclaimed as common to all the *saṃhitās*. (28)
The five Brahmās and the limbs of Śiva, conjoined with Śiva himself—these are the deities of the nyāsa there, which is proclaimed as the path. (29)
All [rites] should be performed everywhere, especially over water;
they are not [performed] by means of a sacrifice, nor by one who knows the ritual rules, nor by one skilled in the path.
The supreme rite should be performed by means of the three principles and the deity-principle:
grasping, joining, lifting up, and the application of that which is known by the knower of reality. (31)
He who knows the reality of all things— their conjunction, their dissolution, and even their final liberation— and who possesses all knowledge, is indeed fit for the sacrifice of Śiva.

He who understands primordial nature (prakṛti) together with its transformations (vikāra), being wise and knowing both the support and that which is supported, is indeed fit for the sacrifice of Śiva.
The high-minded Ācārya, together with the Sādhaka, is always to be worshipped;
he is the Guru of the lords of Sādhakas, while the others merely bear his name.
Thus, the preceptor who knows the rules and procedures, who has mastered the tantras,
and who initiates all living beings— he is indeed the leader to the supreme state.
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Arrangement of the Form," in the Jñānakāṇḍa of the Niśvāsakārikā.
The Goddess said: O Maheśvara, tell me of the worship of the Omniscient One and his ritual injunctions;
at what time, O Blessed One, should one offer the *arghya* to the Supreme Śiva? (1)
O Lord of the gods, please explain to me the mode of worship so that one may proceed to that [state] together with another and oneself as if in a single place.
O Goddess, listen to the supreme secret of worship that fulfills all desires; by performing this sacrifice, the sacrificer becomes the sovereign of all worlds. (3)
Likewise, O Goddess, on the left limb, Vāmā is proclaimed as the Śakti;
she is to be known through the eye of knowledge as the presiding authority over the Pitṛs. (4)
Furthermore, Jyeṣṭhā is the presiding deity of the gods on the right side;
one should always know that Raudrī is in the center, the yoga-deity of yogins.
The Vāmā energy resides in the iḍā on the left side of all embodied beings;
furthermore, the Jyeṣṭhā energy is in the suṣumnā, while the Raudrī energy is supported by the piṅgalā.
These powers have been described as resting upon the three phonemes (varṇa), joined with the three channels (nāḍī), and associated with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa. || 7 ||
The Lord Rudra resides in Piṅgalā, Brahmā in Suṣumnā, and Upendra indeed in Iḍā; they are established in all activities.
When the deity is situated in the left position, one should perform the ritual bath there;
however, the knower of mantras should perform the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) and recite [the mantra] for the sake of the cause in the right. (9)
One should always practice meditation established in the Middle Country;
having eradicated [obstacles] and caused them to spread, one shall become [liberated] in every state in an instant. 10.
Having formed a handful (añjali) filled with flowers and placed it at his mouth, he should offer that añjali full of water, whether mentally or with ordinary [water]. || 11 ||
One should recite the mantra according to the path established by one's own tradition as long as the sound persists;
until that sound dissolves at its end, this is here called the "time of merit."
One should contemplate that which is free from conceptual construction, having become stainless within the state beyond reality;
one should abide in that very state and thus becomes one who has accomplished all that was to be done.
Having thus caused [the breath] to pervade, one should enter again by means of inhalation (*pūraka*).
When the self is awakened, it becomes unawakened; it is not otherwise. (14)
One should bring about auspiciousness everywhere and likewise accomplish the higher goal; having performed all rites with Śiva, the remover of inauspiciousness, one should worship him. 15.
The Goddess said:
O Maheśvara, I desire to hear that which is the knowledge of the Siddhāntas, the object of knowledge, and its defining characteristics; by your grace, you should speak of it. (16)
The Lord, for the sake of that knowledge, has remembered the Vedas and thousands of philosophical systems;
for this reason, O Goddess, it is designated as "that which is to be known" (jñeya). || 17 ||
For the sake of establishing both the object of knowledge and the means of knowledge, the scripture establishes a proof in the form of a positive injunction;
therefore, that established proof is traditionally known as the *siddhānta*. (18)

It is said that the characteristic (lakṣaṇa) is [defined] by its name; the characteristic is remembered in relation to the object to be characterized (lakṣya). Through the thorough knowledge of the object to be characterized, the characteristic is thereby correctly recollected. || 19 ||
Devoid of meditative absorption and mental retention, and abandoned at the commencement of yoga, that consciousness which perceives it cannot indeed be known. (20)
The conceptualization previously mentioned exists by virtue of prior determination;
he who is not deluded regarding its existence is wise and possesses self-knowledge. || 21 ||
He who possesses exertion is established as omniscient;
yet the embodied being, deluded by Māyā, perceives through the sense of "existence. (22)
Just as there is nothing permanent, so have I explained it to you:
that is imperishable, that is the immortal, that is the truth, that is the eternal. (23)
Even one who exists in such a state is all-knowing through yoga;
yet the magician, bound by illusion, remains ensnared by the noose of hope.
"Released from the snares of hope, he attends upon the nectar.
Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Knowledge and the Knowable," within the Jñānakāṇḍa of the Niśvāsakārikā, concerning the Siddhānta of the Worship of the Omniscient One.
The Goddess said: Within this body composed of the five elements, which deities reside where?
And who reside in the feet, the knees, the shanks, and the pair of thighs? (1)
And on the *liṅga*, O Lord of the Gods, the two buttocks (*sphijau*) are situated at the hips;
likewise, [the goddesses] are located at the region of the navel, on both sides, and along the backbone. (2)

O Lord of Gods, in what [deities] are they said to reside within the intestines, the marrow, the blood, the phlegm, and the bile, as well as in the pores of the skin? And what are the hands and feet? || 3 ||
They are situated at the chin, the two eyes, the forehead, and the head.

O Lord of Gods, where do the channels of speech reside, and where is the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) situated? And which deities, O God, preside over the senses, and what fruit arises from their being known? || 5 ||
"O Lord of the gods of gods, you should deign to tell this to me out of your grace.
Īśvara said: (p. 361)
Listen, O Goddess, to the supreme secret concerning that which you have asked.
Therefore, O fair-faced one, I shall explain it for your pleasure;
beginning with the quality of goodness (sattva), I shall speak—listen! (7)
Sattva is said to be the Pradhāna, and he is called Brahmā; Rajas is Viṣṇu and Tamas is Rudra. Now hear of the eightfold intellect.
Knowledge of dharma, dispassion, and likewise supreme sovereignty;
as well as non-dharma and ignorance—these indeed are to be understood. (9)

Lack of dispassion and lack of mastery belong, respectively, to the lords of yogis; the qualities such as dharma belong to the deities beginning with Brahmā, while those beginning with power belong to the deities beginning with Śakra.
Rudra resides in the ego (ahaṅkāra); sound is established in the void (śūnya).
Wind is declared to be in touch (sparśa), and fire is proclaimed to be in form (rūpa). (11)
Varuṇa is established in that subtle element (tanmātra), while the Earth resides in smell;
Prajāpati is indeed in the Earth, and Soma is established in the liquid. || 12 ||
The sun, however, is established in fire; the wind is established in touch;
and the supreme, secret Śiva-tattva is firmly established in space. || 13 ||
O Great Goddess, all the directions are established in the sense-organ of hearing;
the Maruts are in the sense-organ of touch, and the Fire-eater (Agni) resides in the two eyes. 14.
O Goddess, Sarasvatī, the power of the earth, is always present in the organ of the tongue;
knowledge resides in the organ of smell, and Viṣṇu indeed dwells in the two feet.
What is designated as the power of action (kriyā-śakti) comprises both Mitra and Vāyu;
Jyeṣṭhā and Prajāpati are in the linga, while Vāmā and Raudrī are in the speech [organ]. (16)
Jalendu is to be known in the mind; Savitrī resides in the heart;
Gaurī Vāgīśvarī is in the ear; and Vimalāri is on the forehead. (17)
Ananta resides in the group of sinews; the subtle one is established in the semen;
the god Śivottamottama always abides in the collection of bones.
Ekanetra is situated in the flesh, Ekarudra likewise in another [the fat], Rudra is eternally established in the blood, and Trimūrti in phlegm and bile. (19)
Śrīkaṇṭha is ever present in the mass of body hair and in the urine;
and the supreme Rudra Śikhaṇḍin is situated everywhere within the nails.
Maheśa resides in the torso, while the Ṛṣis reside in the joints;
Caṇḍīśa is situated in the spinal column and in the sides. (21)
The Nāgas reside in the fingers, the Pitṛs are situated in the arms, and Agni himself resides in the navel of all embodied beings. 22.
The Vidyādharas and Yakṣas are situated in the pores of the skin;
the deities of the moon are in the two hands, and the Aśvins are likewise in the knees and shanks.
The two gods renowned as Mitra and Varuṇa are stationed on the pair of thighs;
[the others] are stationed in the eyes, the two nostrils, the neck, and the chin.
The seven houses, along with the serpents and their presiding deities, and the divine circle of constellations—whom do they not follow and abide by? || 25 ||
Thus, indeed, he who understands that the body is presided over by all the gods and is born from all [the elements], his knowledge is not defiled by sin. (26)
O Goddess, he who practices this supreme nyāsa day after day obtains prosperity, O Goddess, and becomes equal to the Lord.
There is neither sin nor merit, and no fear shall arise from fears;
one is liberated even from the terrible sins committed throughout seven lifetimes. (28)
This should be practiced with effort by a yogi desiring liberation;
this new method has been declared by me, by which you shall be established in the nectar of immortality. (29)
"He who is the supreme deity of all, established as the all-pervading one"—
thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Ritual Disposition of the Bodies of All Deities," in the Jñānakāṇḍa of the Niśvāsakārikā.
The Goddess said:
O Lord, you have stated in the teaching of Śiva that the Self is the form;
that which was previously called the bound soul (paśu) is likewise to be known as the God. (1)
You have previously described both *cetanā* (consciousness) and the *jīva* (individual soul);
that *paśu* (bound soul), moreover, is inactive, devoid of autonomy, and downward-facing.
How do the objects of knowledge, beginning with names and so forth, gradually attain the state of Śiva?
O Blessed One, I wish to understand this; you ought to explain it.
Īśvara said: Listen, O Goddess, to that supreme secret which you have inquired about;
I shall explain it fully for your pleasure, O lady of beautiful countenance.
(367) I shall explain this procedure, which is common to all the *saṃhitās*, in brief and according to the sequence for each one individually; of this there is no doubt.
The mental worship is to be known as sixfold, while power (śakti) is remembered as ninefold; it is called the "infinite worship" when it is endowed with emission (visarga).
Having thus worshipped Ananta, one should place liberation (mukti) right there,
conjoined with the syllables *hāṃ* and *hūṃ*, as the eighth of the eightfold division.
O Goddess of gods, the arrangement of the forms has been declared in this tantra,
as well as how the grasping [of the mantra] occurs according to its application at the time of initiation.
In that same manner, I shall explain to you how and by what means their grasping occurs;
this union with infinite forms has been illustrated by these seed-syllables (bījas).
Having thus performed the ritual placement with diligence, one should then proceed to the sakalīkaraṇa (the rite of complete integration).
Both that which transcends the mantra and the mantra itself have been previously described by me. (10)
Having known that entire deity, both with parts (sakala) and likewise without parts (niṣkala),
[one should worship him] in the head, the two faces, the heart, and the secret place, respectively.
O Goddess of the gods, one should assign Sadyojāta to the forms;
O Goddess, for the knower of the rule (samaya), this sakalīkaraṇa is beneficial.
I shall describe his worship; listen as I speak of it.
Upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), one should place a Śiva-liṅga, after performing rites such as sprinkling and pouring water over it.
O Goddess of the gods, one likewise offers the substance into the fire and to Śiva;
and by means of the five Brahmans, one performs the entire rite in its entirety.
One should place Īśāna in the center; one should assign Tatpuruṣa in the east, Aghora in the south, and likewise Vāmadeva in the north. (15)
One should always place Sadyojāta in the west on a well-prepared site;
whoever worships with this rite, being well-composed, [attains success]. || 16 ||
I have described the conjunction for attaining the Lord at the proper time;
through union with the five Brahmans and by means of the Kalās, he is well-enveloped.
O son, I have explained to you that which is conjoined with the ancillaries of knowledge (vidyāṅga);
the invocation and other rites of the deity have been told to you as before.
The instructor should describe it as being joined with the door and the enclosure;
having thus performed the ritual integration (sakalīkaraṇa), the worship is to be performed at the time of twilight.
"O beautiful goddess, that which must be performed by the son has been declared;
O Goddess, by this rite, the son shall be perfectly concentrated. (20)
He attains the state of proximity to the one called Sādākhya, without a doubt,
being endowed with those very limbs of Śiva mentioned previously.
Through the conjunction of the inhalation and retention of breath, those skilled in the yoga of meditation attain union with the Great Soul known as Sādākhya.

O beautiful goddess, one who is well-composed should worship [the deity] joined with the four veils by means of mantras through the application of the instruments; such a person is a bound soul (paśu). 23.
He would indeed become identical with the mantra, and that [being] is a bound soul (paśu); of this there is no doubt.
One who is without mantra is called a bound soul; consciousness alone should enter him.
(371) He who possesses consciousness is declared by the Tantras to be [a true practitioner], while he who knows nothing is declared a bound soul (paśu).
O Supreme Goddess, one who is always endowed with mantras is possessed of consciousness.
Then one becomes fit for the meditation on Śiva; there is no doubt about this.
The Goddess said: "O Lord, how is the body of a bound soul (paśu) known to consist of mantra? (26)
I desire to know this, O Blessed One; you should speak.
Listen to the prowess of that Lord whose body is bound by mantras. (27)
It shall lift up the Nāgas from Pātāla, cast down the Daityas and Rākṣasas, destroy all obstacles, and bestow peace and nourishment. || 28 ||
The leaders flee from one whose body is bound by mantras;
likewise, they rise up during invisibility and while moving on foot. (29)
In the case of the sword and the sandals, as well as in the recana and arcana rites,
and regarding the pill, the power of traveling through the sky, the staff, and the sacred ring (pavitraka).
The seat and the vehicle are accomplished by all mantras;
but when the conscious self is absent, O Goddess, nothing at all is accomplished.
O Goddess, one who is shrouded by ignorance is afflicted by the elemental spirits (bhūtas);
O virtuous lady, I have thus described to you the nature of the mantra-self and the conscious self.
And the secret has been told: the distinction between the two is that when the phoneme resounds through the union of *bindu* and *nāda*. (33)

That [state] is declared to be the nature of mantra, the auspicious supreme cause; it exists when Śiva is both differentiated (sakala), endowed with the portions of the five Brahmans, and undifferentiated (niṣkala). || 34 ||
In that [system], the Lord, the Supreme Ishvara whose essence is mantra, shines forth;
for Shiva, the ultimate cause, is established within the array of phonemes (varṇavyūha). || 35 ||
By him, O Goddess, the Supreme Lord, whose essence is mantra, was fully described;
he is known as the Praṇava, joined with fearlessness, and pervading the void. (36)
O fair-faced one, the Supreme Lord, whose nature is Dharma, is conjoined with the *pada-mantras*,
beginning with Ananteśa and ending with Śikhaṇḍin.

He alone, the Supreme Lord whose essence is mantra, is eternally established as the guardians of the world together with their weapons, and as the three worlds with all that is moving and unmoving. 38.
The god Śiva, the supreme cause, abides as the very essence of mantra.
Thus, O virtuous goddess, has that which consists of mantra been explained to you. (39)
This must be known by the teacher himself who follows the Śiva-tantras:
the point (bindu), the sound (nāda), the power (śakti), that which transcends them, and that which is beyond even that. || 40 ||
When, by virtue of its nature as consciousness, it transcends the mantra, that supreme one is the Supreme Lord who transcends sound, form, taste, and the rest. || 41 ||
Having realized this thread, O Goddess, the teacher becomes the destroyer of bonds;
that which transcends Nāda, the supreme peace, is designated as Śakti.
Beyond that, O Goddess, is the "beyond-mantra" (mantrātīta); it is so called because it transcends mantra.
One should first utter the phonemes and then cause them to dissolve into the sound.
Furthermore, sound dissolved in sound shall lead one beyond sound;
that which is beyond it, O Goddess, is called the Supreme, transcending even mantra. (44)
This determination of the *kārikā* has been told to you, O Goddess;
it was previously stated and explained to you, O lady of virtuous conduct, in the preceding sūtra. (45)
The Goddess said:
"O Maheśvara, you have explained in the Ādisūtra, O Lord, that after worshipping the Sakala [form], one should thereafter worship the Niṣkala."
The animal is said to be *sakala* (with parts), and it is proclaimed to be the *mūrti* (the embodied form).
How, then, can the Supreme Lord, who is *niṣkala* (without parts), be worshipped within it? || 47 ||
The partless [Śiva] transcends all parts; he is beyond the reach of mantra and phonemes.
How, then, can the supreme Śiva abide within a body possessed of parts? (48)
The Lord, having first placed Maheśvara within his heart, should utter the mantra;
when he is dissolved into the supreme sound of the *kūṭa*, he is indeed called the partless (*niṣkala*).
O Goddess, when through its utterance one attains the state free from conceptual construction;
O Maheśvarī, when it is realized within the body through the yoga of all [the elements], [then one is liberated]. 50.
Transcending the parts, he is indeed called "partless" (niṣkala);
when devoid of vocalization, he enters the state beyond conceptual construction (nirvikalpa). || 51 ||
That which is conceived by the mind and wherein there is conceptualization by the intellect—when it is free from both intellect and ego, that indeed is called the partless (niṣkala). || 52 ||
Whether one is a *samayin*, a *putraka*, a *sādhaka*, or even an *ācārya*, the ritual procedure must be performed by all; I have explained the specific distinctions. (53)
Thus ends the forty-second chapter of the Niśvāsakārikā.
The Goddess said:
"O Blessed One, I wish to hear the unsurpassed ritual for initiation."
Everything has been told in brief; tell it to me in detail.
Just as the connection with the seizing of the animal victim occurs at the time of initiation,
so too should you explain how the sacrifice is performed within this initiation.
Īśvara said: Hereafter, I shall proclaim the unsurpassed ritual procedure for initiation (dīkṣāvidhi).
Or rather, I shall explain the entirety of what is common to all the tantras.
O Goddess, these five Brahmās, who are the limbs of Śiva and are united with Śiva himself,
have been proclaimed as the mantra for you in this sacrifice for the sake of purification.
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī are proclaimed as the three Śaktis; they must be understood by the preeminent teacher through their separation, projection, and conjunction. (5)
The practitioner of mantras should unite [the soul] with Vāmā and separate it with Jyeṣṭhā;
the extraction is said to be performed with Raudrī, and one should again unite it elsewhere.
Having begun from the earth up to the stainless Tattva,
one who understands this ritual even once becomes purified through the homa of the Vyūha.
O Goddess, the supreme preceptor should offer each oblation one by one;
he should perform the rite in this very manner until everything is completed. (8)
One should offer the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti); this indeed is remembered as the prescribed rule.
One should perform the striking with the topknot (śikhā) using the mudrā joined with a flower.
The sacrificial animal (paśu) should be seized with the *saṃhāra-mudrā* by means of the sound *haṃ huṃ*.
Then, one should sever its bonds (*pāśas*) through the sequence of the *pūrṇāhuti* offering by means of Śiva.
The teacher should understand this very sequence;
however, upon the completion of all the paths, he should cause the cutting of the crest-lock (śikhā).

The mantra-practitioner should cut off the tuft; having cut it, he should again offer the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), having severed the various bonds (pāśas) in each respective principle (tattva) according to the proper sequence.
Those bonds which are subtle and gross, situated like a conch shell and its spines—
those thousands of millions of bonds were indeed described by Śiva. (13)
"Having reached the mouth of Śiva, the bonds are burned; there is no doubt about this.
The Goddess said: "O Mahādeva, O Lord, it has been stated that the bonds are indeed innumerable. (14)
And how can that which is utterly profound be consumed in the sacrifice to Śiva?
[He consumes] Īśvara, Prakṛti, Puruṣa, Niyati, and Kāla as well. (15)
Māyā, avidyā, Īśa, Sadāśiva, and likewise Śiva—these are remembered as the root bonds; O fair-faced one, these are the nine bonds.
By these staffs, O Goddess, these fifty crores of nooses have been burnt;
the fifty *praṇavas* were previously proclaimed by me. (17)
By those pure ones, these pure bonds numbering fifty crores are purified,
O Goddess, according to the path by means of the thirty-eight kalās.
By those purified [principles], these fifty crores of fetters (pāśas) become pure:
namely, Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, and likewise the power of Vidyā.
When the resonance (dhvāna) is purified by these, the fifty crores become pure;
that which is the digit named Amṛtā is likewise both immortal and mortal.
And just as it is proclaimed, O Goddess, that she is both extremely subtle and subtle;
by these [means], one should purify the path through the previously observed ritual action.
By these pure [mantras], these fifty million bonds (pāśas) become pure;
they are to be purified through the application of words and mantras in the sacrificial rite of Śiva. (22)
By these, when purified, these fifty million bonds (pāśas) are purified.
And thus, O Goddess, the path (adhvan) has been proclaimed as sevenfold.
Those who follow the Śiva Tantras should understand with diligent effort that the path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvan) has been described by me according to the number of oblations (āhuti). 24.
By those same digits (kalās), O Goddess, the entire path is to be known in its entirety;
when, through you, O Goddess, one becomes the most excellent of teachers, the path is realized.
One hundred oblations should be offered for each [tattva]; this is remembered as the procedure for the purification of the principles (tattva-śuddhi).
O Goddess, it is exactly the same for the nine principles; of this there is no doubt. (26)
p.
383) Likewise here, in the principle of *kalā*, there is indeed a second triad;
by means of one hundred and fifty oblations, the path of the phonemes (*varṇādhvan*) is proclaimed. || 27 ||

In the path of reality (tattvādhvan), the path of the creative powers (kalādhvan), and likewise in the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan), one should not perform here either the upward projection (ukṣepa) or the conjunction (yojana) by means of these [methods]. || 28 ||
Likewise, on the path of the feet here, one hundred oblations must be offered;
in this way, O Supreme Goddess, the path is purified sevenfold.
Having understood this, the supreme preceptor should then perform the initiation.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord, you have indicated the entire path, but not explained it in detail. (30)
Therefore, I wish to hear this; please explain it to me in detail.
Īśvara said:
In the initial sūtra, that which was spoken by way of the mere sūtra regarding the [three] time periods; || 31 ||
I shall explain that very thing in detail; understand it from me.
I will proclaim the path of the body (dehādhvan); listen as I speak of it. (32)
The Lord Ananta, the Supreme Ruler, stands upon the tip of the big toe;
he has four faces, possesses great splendor, and resembles the rising sun. (33)
One should visualize the infinite Lord of the World (Bhuvaneśāna) seated below the yogin, surrounded by the Vidyās and the lords of the Vidyās (Vidyeśvaras).
Oṃ, O Ananta, come, come; accept this oblation; Śiva gives it to you, svāhā! One should offer an oblation with the mantra "Oṃ, to Sadyojāta.
In this very sequence, one should offer the eleven-fold [oblation],
whether in the context of authority (adhikāra), enjoyment (bhoga), or dissolution (laya), according to the proper order.
Then, having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should withdraw [the ritual elements] in due order;
likewise for Kālāgnirudra and in the hells.
Oṃ, Kālāgnirudra, come; accept this oblation; Śiva gives it to you, svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to Avīci! Oṃ, obeisance to Raurava! Oṃ, obeisance to Mahāraurava! Oṃ, obeisance to Tāmisra! Oṃ, obeisance to Andhatāmisra! Oṃ, obeisance to Śīta! Oṃ, obeisance to Uṣṇa! Oṃ...
Homage to Sañjīva. Oṃ, homage to Sujīvana. Oṃ, homage to Padma. Oṃ, homage to Mahāpadma.
Oṃ, homage to Kāpa, the thread. Oṃ, homage to Sūcīmukha, the needle-mouthed one. Oṃ, homage to Kṣuradhārā, the razor-edged one.

Oṃ, homage to Parvata, the mountain. Oṃ, homage to Sitālavana, the cold forest. Oṃ, homage to Raudra, the fierce one. Oṃ, homage to Kumbhīpāka, the boiling cauldron. Oṃ, homage to Ambarīṣa, the frying pan. Oṃ, homage to Aṅgārarāśi, the heap of embers. Oṃ.
Homage to Bhuvana! Oṃ, homage to Tīkṣṇatuṇḍa! Oṃ, homage to Vajratuṇḍa!
Oṃ, homage to Śakuni! Oṃ, homage to Mīnodara! Oṃ, homage to Kharodara! Oṃ, homage to Sandaṃśa! Oṃ, homage to Kākatuṇḍa! Oṃ, homage to Vānarānana! Oṃ...
Salutation to Ugrīva. The Tejoraṣṭaka: Om, salutation to Lokākṣādhyakṣa; Om, salutation to Gaṇādhyakṣa; Om, salutation to Tridaśa; Om, salutation to Tripurāntaka; Om, salutation to Sarvarūpa;
Om, salutation to Śānta; Om, salutation to Unmeṣa; Om, salutation to Unmeṣa.
The eightfold fire-oblation (tejoṣṭaka) must be offered by the preceptors who are well-composed;
after this, the unsurpassed eighth yoga is fully described. (37)
Oṃ, salutation to Kṛta.
In this very sequence, one should again offer the eightfold yoga.
Above these, however, the twelve Suśivas are traditionally taught. (38)

Oṃ Vāma, homage! Oṃ Bhīma, homage! Oṃ Ugra, homage! Oṃ Bhava, homage! Oṃ Śarva, homage! Oṃ Vidyādhipa, homage! Oṃ Ekavīra, homage! Oṃ Pracaṇḍa, homage! Oṃ Īśvara, homage! Oṃ Jase, homage! Oṃ Ananta, homage! Oṃ Ekaśiva, homage! These indeed are the Suśivas.
These have been proclaimed as those to be purified in the Śiva-sacrifice. (p. 388) Hereafter, Vīrabhadra is the lord and sovereign of the maṇḍala.
Oṃ, salutation to the Lord of the Maṇḍala!
From this point forward are Mahādeva, Vāmadeva, and Bhavodbhava. (39)

Oṃ Vāmadeva, salutations! Oṃ Bhavodbhava, salutations! Oṃ Ekapiṅgekṣaṇa, salutations! Oṃ Īśāna, salutations! Oṃ Aṅguṣṭhamātra, salutations! These are remembered as the eight Mahādevas. Above these are two rows of gurus: Oṃ Śivānanta, salutations! Ananta, salutations! Oṃ Prabhu...

Homage! Oṃ Vāmana, homage! Oṃ Caṇḍa, homage! Oṃ Pratāpa, homage! Oṃ Vratārti, homage! Oṃ Śiva, homage! Oṃ Kapālin, homage! Oṃ Bhīma, homage! Oṃ Aṅkārāli, homage! Oṃ Piṅgala, homage! Oṃ Mahendra, homage!
Oṃ, homage to Dinakṛt! Oṃ, homage to Pratoda! Oṃ, homage to Dakṣa! Oṃ, homage to Kṣemīśa! Oṃ, homage to Kabaleśa!
Oṃ, homage to Kaṭaṅkaṭa! Oṃ, homage to Buhantāna! Oṃ, homage to Anādara!

Salutation! Oṃ, salutation to Śveta. Oṃ, salutation to the Yajurveda. Oṃ, salutation to the Sāmaveda. Oṃ, salutation to the Ṛgveda. Oṃ, salutation to the Atharvaveda. Oṃ, salutation to the Teacher. Oṃ, salutation to Śiva. Oṃ, salutation to Virūpākṣa. Oṃ, salutation to Nārāyaṇa. Oṃ, salutation to Vibucaṇḍodara. Oṃ.
Homage to Saṃvarta! Oṃ, homage to Yamamālī! Oṃ, homage to Gahaneśa! Oṃ, homage to Pīḍa!
This is intended as the first row. Oṃ, homage to Śveta! Oṃ, homage to Dāru! Oṃ, homage to Lokākṣi! (p. 390)

Oṃ, salutation to Sūtra. Oṃ, salutation to Suhotra. Oṃ, salutation to Ekapāda. Oṃ, salutation to Grantheśvara. Oṃ, salutation to Gautama. Oṃ, salutation to Jaimini. Oṃ, salutation to Dadhivāha. Oṃ, salutation to Ṛṣabha. Oṃ, salutation to Gokarṇa. Oṃ, salutation to Guheśvara. Oṃ, salutation to Guhavāsin. Oṃ, salutation to Śikhaṇḍin.

Homage! Oṃ jhaṭimāli, homage! Oṃ ugra, homage! Oṃ śikhi, homage! Oṃ śūlī, homage! Oṃ sugati, homage! Oṃ supāla, homage! Oṃ aṭṭahāsa, homage! Oṃ dāruka, homage! Oṃ ṣāḍhī, homage! Oṃ tridaṇḍī, homage! Oṃ bhāva, homage! Oṃ bhāvya, homage! Oṃ...
Salutation to Lakulīśa. The second row is intended [as follows]: Om, salutation to Devāvaraṇa; Om, salutation to Dīrghabāhu; Om, salutation to Ṛbhu. (p. 391)

Oṃ amṛte namaḥ | Oṃ bhṛte namaḥ | Oṃ sthāṇave namaḥ | Oṃ sadyojātāya namaḥ | Oṃ bhuvane namaḥ | Oṃ caṇḍe namaḥ | Oṃ ṣaṇmukhāya namaḥ | Oṃ caturānanāya namaḥ | Oṃ cakrapāṇaye namaḥ | Oṃ kūrmākṣāya namaḥ | Oṃ ardhanārīśvarāya namaḥ | Oṃ meṣāya ||
Homage to Saṃvartaka! Oṃ, homage to Bhasmeśa! Oṃ, homage to Kāmanāśana! Oṃ, homage to Kapālīśa! Oṃ, homage to Bhūrbhuvaḥ! Oṃ, homage to Vaṣaṭkāra!
This third row has been described; it is to be purified in the sacrifice of Śiva.
Now, regarding the creation of the principles (tattvas) above that, it must be understood by the teacher.
Starting from the earth element and extending up to the Pradhāna, whatever principles (tattvas) exist within this interval are to be purified by the wise. 41.
(392) Thus, O beautiful one, the principle of Prakṛti has been explained to you.
All those situated below it are to be purified in the sacrifice of Śiva. 42.
He remained stationed, completely surrounding it with the very atoms of barley;
and above primordial nature (prakṛti), he understood the creation of beings.
The wise should purify the atoms, the syllables, and the phonemes. || 43 1/2 ||
Oṃ Ambhaṇamaḥ. Oṃ Salilaṇamaḥ. Oṃ Oghaṇamaḥ. Oṃ Vṛṣṭiṇamaḥ. Oṃ Tāraṇamaḥ. Oṃ Supāraṇamaḥ. Oṃ Sunetraṇamaḥ. Oṃ Sumāriṇamaḥ. Oṃ Uttamābhāṇamaḥ.
These are the desired ones to be purified. Oṃ Tārāṇamaḥ. Oṃ Sutārāṇamaḥ. Oṃ Tārāyate.
Homage!
393) Oṃ pramoda, homage! Oṃ pramudita, homage! Oṃ modamāna, homage! Oṃ radyaka.
Homage! Oṃ, homage to Sadāpramuditā! Oṃ, homage to Siddhi! Oṃ, homage to Tārā! Oṃ, homage to Suvārā! Oṃ, homage to Sunetrā! Oṃ, homage to Sumānī! Oṃ, homage to Uttamābhā!
These are the Tuṣṭis to be purified. Oṃ, homage to Tārā! Oṃ, homage to Sutārā! Oṃ, homage to Supārā! Oṃ...
Salutation to Sunetra. Oṃ, salutation to Sumāri. Salutation to Umuttamābhā.
These [deities] of contentment are to be purified by the preceptors who are well-composed. || 44 ||
Oṃ, salutation to aṇimā. Oṃ, salutation to laghimā. Oṃ, salutation to prāpti. Oṃ, salutation to prākāmya. Oṃ, salutation to vaśitva. Oṃ, salutation to īśitva. (p. 394)
Oṃ, salutation to the power of fulfilling all desires.
The supernatural powers (aiśvaryas), such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest, must be purified by those seeking liberation.
Beyond this, O Goddess, that which is situated is known as the eightfold knowledge of the channels (nāḍī-vidyāṣṭaka). || 45 ||
Oṃ Omiḍā, salutations! Oṃ Caṇḍī, salutations! Oṃ Gaurī, salutations! Oṃ Śāntikā, salutations! Oṃ Mālā, salutations! Oṃ Malī, salutations! Oṃ Svāhā, salutations! Oṃ Svadhā, salutations!
From Rāga to Vidyeśa, these [deities] should always be purified by the wise.
Beyond this is the group of eight forms (vigrahāṣṭaka), which abides in both restraint and grace.

Oṃ, homage to the effect! Oṃ, homage to the cause! Oṃ, homage to happiness! Oṃ, homage to suffering! Oṃ, homage to knowledge! Oṃ, homage to that which is to be accomplished! Oṃ, homage to the cause! (p. 395)

Thus they are established in restraint and grace. The principle of the Puruṣa (puruṣatattva) is that which is to be purified. Hereafter I shall speak; listen attentively, O beloved, to which principle within Prakṛti the purification is intended. || 47 ||
Therefore, I shall fully explain that; listen to me as I speak it.
When one has reached the world of mortals, it purifies even the animal womb. (48)
First, the stationary beings are to be purified; then the reptiles are to be purified;
next, the bird-wombs are to be purified, and immediately after that, the wild animals.
And the sacrificial animal (paśu) is to be purified, O Mistress of the Gods, in due order and according to sequence.
Cows and the like are declared to be sacrificial animals (paśus), while lions and the like are remembered as wild beasts (mṛgas). || 50 ||

The birds, such as the *bhāsa* and others, are declared [to be the first group]; the reptiles, such as the snakes and others, are the second; and the immovable beings, such as the *saptacchada* trees and others, O Mistress of the Gods, are proclaimed [as the third]. (51)
One should approach these humans according to the rules of purification;
first, those of the lowest castes (antyaja) are to be purified, and after that, those born of Śūdra wombs.
Then, having led him into the womb of a prostitute, one should lead him again into the womb of a low-born woman;
and from the low-born state, having joined him with those of the Brāhmaṇa class, one should grant him authority in due order.
One should always renounce the authority over low-caste people, as well as the authority to impose bonds, imprisonment, execution, and the various methods of inflicting injury.
O beautiful goddess, service to the Śaivas and mastery [of mantras] are the prerogatives always proclaimed for the state of a Śūdra (śūdratva). || 55 ||
Trade and the duty of agriculture are proclaimed as the occupation of the Vaiśya;
O woman of excellent complexion, the portion of the Kṣatriya's duties is likewise established therein. (56)
War, gambling, physical exercise, conflict, and its fruit—these, indeed, have been described in due order as the prerogatives of Kṣatriyas. (57)
O Goddess, beginning from the rite of conception (garbhādhāna) and ending with the funeral rites (antyeṣṭi), the qualification for these has been declared for you, O Brahmin. (58)
O Goddess of the gods, at the beginning, through the rite of consecration (saṃskāra), forty-eight [verses] are to be known; these must be purified by the preceptor.
Having become a twice-born student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī), he should perform his duties in due order;
having performed the rite of union with a wife, he should offer sacrifices accompanied by sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
While it is being thus purified, one should apply those fifty [syllables];
as previously stated by the Sūtra, one should quickly perform all of that. (61)
O Goddess of the gods, by means of non-conceptualization, the wise and eminent teacher must always purify the eternal [Prakṛti] above the person (puruṣa) through the teachers. 62.
The teacher, the great-souled one, must purify two types of seats;
in brief, both the bond of pleasure and the bond of suffering are to be purified. (63)
Having practiced passion and beauty in conjunction with time,
I shall hereafter fully proclaim the stainless path of knowledge.
Oṃ Vāmadeva, homage! Oṃ Bhuva, homage! Oṃ Śarva, homage! Oṃ Bhavodbhava, homage! Oṃ Vajradeha, homage! Oṃ Prabhu, homage! (p. 399)
Oṃ, obeisance to Dhātṛ. Oṃ, obeisance to Kramaśa. Oṃ, obeisance to Sugeśa. Obeisance to Vikrameśa.
These ten are declared to be the Śaṅkaras, who are always established through the principle of leading [the soul].
At the time of initiation, all of these must be purified by the wise.

Above that, having taken [the elements] from Śiva, they are established in the principle of Time (kāla-tattva). It should be understood that those [entities] within Time itself are to be purified by the wise.

Oṃ, salutation to the Pure One. Oṃ, salutation to the Awakened One. Oṃ, salutation to the Fully Awakened One. Oṃ, salutation to the Tranquil One. Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme Imperishable. Oṃ, salutation to the Immutable One. Oṃ, salutation to the Auspicious One. Oṃ, salutation to the Eternal One. Oṃ, salutation to the Perishable One.
(400) These ten are declared to be those who are to be purified by the wise.
Beyond this, Hari, Hara, and the others are to be purified within the principle of *rāga*. || 67 ||
From this point forward, there shall be disciples such as Kalyāṇa and others, possessed of great austerity:
Oṃ Kalyāṇa, obeisance! Oṃ Piṅgala, obeisance! Oṃ Bhuva, obeisance! Oṃ Vīra, obeisance! Oṃ Pravara, obeisance! Oṃ Medhā, obeisance! Oṃ Amastita, obeisance! Oṃ Chedaka, obeisance!
These ten are to be known as the gurus; one should purify them within the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva).
I shall now describe Kālaraudra and those Rudras who are established therein;
Vāma, Jyeṣṭha, and Rudra are likewise proclaimed in that very place. (69)
Oṃ Vāma, homage! Oṃ Jyeṣṭha, homage! Oṃ Rudra, homage! Thus are the three mantras of Mahādeva.
And likewise, Gopati, residing at the heart-knot above,
is surrounded by countless tens of millions of Rudras.
Oṃ, salutation to Gopati. Beyond this, the universe is established.
Oṃ, salutation to Trikala. Oṃ, salutation to Kṣemeśa. Oṃ, salutation to Brahmaṇa. Oṃ, salutation to Adhipati. Oṃ, salutation to Śiva.
These five are declared to be those that must be purified in the sacrifice to Śiva;
beyond these, O Ananteśa, the fetters (pāśas) themselves are established.
And those aforementioned evils, in the sequence beginning with thirst (*udamāha*), are as follows: *Oṃ mada namaḥ* | *Oṃ moha namaḥ* | *Oṃ śoṣa namaḥ* | *Oṃ vaicitya namaḥ*.
In this very sequence, they are to be purified in the Śiva-sacrifice.

Above this is the Family of Sages (*ṛṣikula*). Oṃ, homage to the Family of Sages (*ṛṣikulanamaḥ*). Above this is the Goddess Vāgīśvarī. Oṃ, homage to Vāgīśvarī (*vāgīśvarī namaḥ*). Above this is the Oṃkāra; above that is the Sādhya-Oṃkāra. Oṃ, homage to the Sādhya-Oṃkāra (*sādhyoṅkāra namaḥ*). Above this are the Sustainers (*dhātāraḥ*). Oṃ, homage to the Sustainers (*dhātāra namaḥ*). Oṃ, homage to the Lord of Mind (*maneśa namaḥ*). Oṃ, homage to the One Whose Food is Meditation (*dhyānāhāra namaḥ*). Oṃ.
Salutation to Bhasmeśa.
403) All these [elements] within the belly of Māyā are to be purified; thus the wise know. Hereafter follow the authoritative sources. Oṃ.
Salutation to Pañcārtha; salutation to Śivaguhyā; salutation to Rudrāṅkuśā; salutation to Hṛdayā; salutation to Lakṣaṇā; salutation to Vyūhā; salutation to Mādaśī.
These eight authorities (pramāṇas) are to be purified by the high-souled preceptor.
Above those, the preceptor should indeed offer oblations to Māyā;
above that shall be Vidyā, the destroyer of the existence of all vidyās.
He is proclaimed to be divided into eightfold forms by his very nature;
yet, he is likewise said to be devoid of these ninefold divisions once again.
Oṃ, homage to Vāmā. Oṃ, homage to Jyeṣṭhā. Oṃ, homage to Raudrī. Oṃ, homage to Kālī.
Oṃ, homage to Kalavikaraṇī. Oṃ, homage to Balavikaraṇī. Oṃ, homage to Balapramathinī. Oṃ.
Salutation to Sarvabhūtadamanī. Within the principle of Vidyā (Vidyātattva), these are to be purified.
Above this, O Goddess, one should worship Īśvara, the Lord of Yoga, or alternatively, Ananteśa and the others, with a concentrated mind. (76)

Oṃ, obeisance to Ananta. Oṃ, obeisance to Sūkṣma. Oṃ, obeisance to Śivottama. Oṃ, obeisance to Ekanetra. Oṃ, obeisance to Ekarudra. Oṃ, obeisance to Trimūrti. Oṃ, obeisance to Śrīkaṇṭha. Oṃ, obeisance to Śikhaṇḍin.
These are to be purified within the principle of Īśvara. Beyond this is the group of four forms.
Oṃ, homage to Dharma. Oṃ, homage to Jñāna. Oṃ, homage to Vairāgya. Oṃ, homage to Aiśvarya.
These are the four forms. Oṃ, homage to Vāmā. Oṃ, homage to Jyeṣṭhā. Oṃ, homage to Raudrī.

The three powers. Above this are two powers: *Oṃ jñānaśaktir namaḥ* (Salutation to the power of knowledge); *Oṃ kriyāśaktir namaḥ* (Salutation to the power of action). Above this—Tejīśa and Dhruveśa are proclaimed as being within the sphere of valid cognition (*pramāṇatva*).
Oṃ, obeisance to Tejīśa. Oṃ, obeisance to Dhruveśa.
[This is] for those established on the path of the vital breaths (prāṇa), endowed with initiation and knowledge. || 77 ||
Nirvana is said to be the supreme state for you, O lady of virtuous vows.
Above [that], the *praṇava*: *oṃ praṇavāya namaḥ*. Above that, the three worlds of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra: *oṃ brahmaṇe namaḥ*; *oṃ viṣṇave namaḥ*; *oṃ rudrāya*.
Salutation! Oṃ, salutation to Pratodana. Oṃ, salutation to Manava. Beyond this, having transcended, is the Single Syllable (Ekākṣara).
Oṃ, salutation to Ekākṣara. Oṃ, salutation to Piṅga. Oṃ, salutation to Haṃsa. This is the triad of Saumya-Rudras. Above this is Dhruva.
Above this is the station of the eleven Rudras. Oṃ, salutation to Brahmā.
Oṃ Omarka, homage! Oṃ Daṇḍin, homage! Oṃ Muṇḍin, homage! Oṃ Saurabheya, homage! Oṃ Mṛtyuhara, homage! Oṃ Praṇīta, homage! (p. 407)
Oṃ, salutation to Sukha. Oṃ, salutation to Vijṛmbhita. The eleven Rudras are to be purified;
at the time of initiation, they should be known as being established in the throat. (78)
I shall now declare the third, Dhruva: *Oṃ Dhruva, namaḥ*.
Dhruva’s retinue consists of seven thousand crores;
however, for the Lord Nirañjana, no such number exists. (79)
Oṃ, salutation to Nirañjana. Above this, Śakti is to be purified: Oṃ, salutation to Śakti.
Above that are those eight Lords of the Worlds (Bhuvaneśvaras): Oṃ, salutation to Prīti; Oṃ, salutation to Pramādita; Oṃ, salutation to Pralamba.

Oṃ, salutation to Viṣṇu. Oṃ, salutation to Gahana. Oṃ, salutation to Vitata. These eight are the lords of the worlds (bhuvaneśas). Beyond this is the state of Bhava. That which is the small, pure fivefold action of Śiva. Oṃ, the Source.

Namaḥ | Oṃ Raudra, namaḥ | Oṃ Vimala, namaḥ | Oṃ Śiva, namaḥ | Beyond that is another, named Udghana, which is impenetrable by all yogins; Aghana, namaḥ. Above that, Rudra is proclaimed as the syllable Oṃ. || 80 ||
In front, at the palate, the Lord Rudra is proclaimed as the syllable Oṃ.
Thus, Īśvara alone is the reality. Om Rudroṃkāra, salutations.
Sadāśiva, through his eightfold division, is established between the eyebrows.
The seat is enriched with a hundred thousand petals, like the risen full moon;
upon that seat, the four powers of yoga are eternally established.
Oṃ, salutation to Nivṛtti. Oṃ, salutation to Pratiṣṭhā. Oṃ, salutation to Vidyā. Oṃ, salutation to Śānti.
Above this, there should be the Nāda, possessing a splendor like that of a lotus filament;
it is to be known as Puruṣa, established pervading everything. (83)
Pervaded by great beings whose splendor is equal to ten million suns,
he rules this cosmic egg, impelled by the power of Śiva.
Therefore, the Suṣumnā should be known as that which leads to the completion of the entire path;
it remains like a lotus fiber, dissolved within the aperture of the Brahman-sound (nādabrahma). (85)
The moon, which delights with its cool rays, should be constantly meditated upon by yogis;
above that, O Great Goddess, is a great mass consisting of light and sound.
The outflow of nectar from the moon, a treasury of the supreme ambrosia of splendor, briefly illuminates by the radiance of the rays of its own power. (87)
O beautiful one, all things shine within that great flood of his splendor;
that power of the God of gods must be meditated upon by the preceptor.
Without interior or exterior, without support, and devoid of all temporal paths;
it is the culmination of the creative process, the great gnosis, incomparable and free from affliction.
Having thus purified the path, one should unite it with the supreme state;
having established the locus of the *vidyā*-tattva, one should unite it with the supreme state. (90)
Having meditated upon the process within one's own body, and especially within the body of a bound soul (paśu),
one should know that the worlds are situated at every single *yava* and between-every-*yava*.
Primordial Nature (prakṛti) was previously described as being established below the navel;
the Person (puruṣa) is situated in the middle of the heart, and Necessity (niyati) is outside the feet.
At the time of initiation, the preeminent teacher, being composed, should know the Kālakaṇṭha [mantra] below according to the sequence of Kalās and Vidyās. || 93 ||
Māyā is situated above that, established at the location of the knot;
however, Vidyā should be known by the teacher as being in the region of the throat. 94.
O beautiful one, Īśvara has been described by you as being in the middle of the palate;
Sadāśiva, however, is at the end of the head—this is the explanation of the reality, O vanquisher of enemies. (95)
O Goddess of the gods, one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) in sequence with the mantra Śāntyatīta;
or it may be given with the Navātman mantra, or indeed with the Praṇava.
The final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) for Śiva must be offered with the supreme syllable (paramākṣara).
At the conclusion of all the paths (adhvan), one should perform the cutting of the topknot (śikhāccheda).
O Goddess of the gods, one should consecrate the scissors with the *śikhā* mantra;
then, O wise one, taking it with that very same mudrā, one should cut.
O Suvrata, the four fingers are indeed to be cut off;
having prepared them with clarified butter, the wise one should offer them as an oblation.
Having offered that oblation, the preeminent guide should cause [the disciple] to perform the bath of ashes.
Then, having sipped water, the teacher shall purify his own body. (100)

Having performed everything without exception, the wise one should cause [the victim] to fall by means of the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), having unified his own infinite self with the state of being the sacrificial animal (paśu). 101.
Then the mantra-practitioner should apply himself according to the ritual previously observed; perform the practice in such a manner as the path of the kalās has been described. 102.
But when [the time] is appropriate, O Goddess, I have previously declared the characteristics;
as for those duties of a practitioner that exist within the Śivadharmas. (103)
The Goddess said: "O Lord, you previously described to me that form is of three kinds.
By what means is it grasped? This I wish to know. (104)
Īśvara is declared to be the fifteenth self; by means of that which is called Haṃsa, one should effect the piercing.
One should take it together with a long-drawn *bindu*. || 105 ||
Having struck with the crest [mudrā], one should perform the withdrawal of what is to be grasped by means of the saṃhāra-mudrā,
with each hand turned downward and well-encircled.
The preceptor should take [the substance] with the "Hand of Śiva" joined with the mantra;
O Goddess of Gods, he should employ the upturned left hand.
O Goddess, this release of the bound soul (paśu) from capture has been explained to you;
it must be performed by the preeminent teacher through the ritual action prescribed by the rules. 108.
The Goddess said: O Maheśvara, [tell me] of the yoga and the sacrifice consisting of thirty-eight kalās.
How does initiation reside within them, and how should it be applied by the teachers?
"Or by what means is its apprehension? This I wish to know.
O beloved, listen attentively as I shall explain the sacrifice of the *kalās* to you, O Sovereign. (110)
I have not revealed this to anyone; I shall tell it to you, O lady of excellent conduct.
O Goddess of the gods, whatever specific yoga among the arts I speak of, [hear it]. 111.
And likewise, O lady of beautiful countenance, I shall describe the union with the *kalā* (digit);
there are five *kalās* of Maheśa and four of his faces.
The five-faced [mandala] has been fully described; O Suvṛta, this is called the inner enclosure (garbhāvaraṇa), which has been explained to you, O Suvṛta. (113)
By means of the conjunctions starting from the southeast and proceeding in order up to the north, one should place the Puruṣa in four ways: in the southeast, the northwest, and the southwest.
Having placed [the deities] in the four directions and in the intermediate directions starting from the east,
one should then place those eight digits (kalās) of Aghora, O Lord of Knowledge (Vidyeśa).
Now listen as I describe that which is the Vāmadeva-kalā;
the placement of the kalās must be performed starting from the east.
Two [kalās] in the east, two in the south, and likewise in the west;
then, O Goddess of the Gods, one should again place one kalā in the north.
In the four directions, Unmanī is declared to be the most excellent of the aforementioned Kalās;
for she is indeed the supreme Śiva, and one should contemplate her within the body. (118)
One should place the eight *kalās* of Sadyojāta fourfold within the causal [state];
O Goddess of the gods, one should then assign the nine powers (*śaktis*) to the syllable *praṇava* in the eight directions.
One should place the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) and detachment (vairāgya) in their proper order;
by that very means, O lady of excellent complexion, one should fashion the infinite lotus.
The wise preceptor must perform the union with the form by means of that very [mantra],
and the intelligent one should perform the principle of the Self (ātmatattva) with the Brahman-syllable (oṃ).
O lady of excellent complexion, one should arrange the seat of Unmanī for him;
O Goddess of gods, one should place the sleeping chamber within the principle (tattva) of Vidyā.
O fair-faced one, these are indeed the fourfold portions of Īśāna;
his seat should be prepared by the teachers as Rudra-Ūṅkāra. (123)
One should perform [the rite] with that which is called the Śiva-tattva, ending with the syllable Oṃ;
and that which is the fifth kalā of Īśāna, the Great Goddess.
One should have an image made with five heads, Īśāna at the top, and four faces; it has five faces as its seat, for by that there is no doubt regarding the end of suffering.
O Goddess, having performed the placement of the forms (mūrtinyāsa) again in due order with all the constituent parts (kalās),
and having rendered oneself complete (sakalīkṛtya), one should cause the supreme syllable to descend.
In this way, O Goddess, he becomes partless; of this there is no doubt.
One should then conceive of his praṇava in five ways according to the proper sequence.
The preceptor should place [the mantras], ending with the kalās of Sadyojāta and Vāmadeva, everywhere according to the sequence of the heart, the head, the crest, the armor, and the weapon. (128)
Those who are established in the reality of the Self should perform [the rites] with the syllable Om;
likewise, they should offer perfume, flowers, a lamp, food, and the presentation of the bali-offering.
Having worshipped Rudra with the syllable Oṃ in that which is called Vidyā—the form, color, and digits of Śiva—according to this procedure, one should then perform the initiation.
One should conceive of Vāgīśvarī as being of the nature of the Sadyojāta digit. || 131 ||
One should join [the elements] with that very [mantra] there, and offer those oblations with that same [mantra].
One should offer as many oblations as there are paths known as the worlds.
One should employ [the disciple] in seizing, striking, and lifting up; and likewise, having directed him toward the performance of specific tasks at every stage. (133)
One should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) at the end; this indeed is remembered as the prescribed rule.
[This should be done] for the Lord of Gods with either the Navātman mantra or the Śāntyatīta mantra. || 134 ||
The full oblations (pūrṇāhuti) should be offered in sequence with the supreme syllable (paramākṣara).
First, one should establish the Kalā, and then one should install Vāgīśvarī.
Alternatively, the path of the digits (kalādhvā) may be purified by the well-composed teachers, either by means of single units or by means of groups of digits. || 136 ||
Those arts which have been described as belonging to the *āsana* (posture) should not be practiced with the physical posture;
rather, O lady of excellent complexion, for those three [arts], one should remain there mindful solely of the *praṇava*. 137.
O Goddess, when the principles beginning with earth are to be purified in their proper sequence by means of the *kalās*, I shall explain that to you; listen with a one-pointed mind. (138)
One should offer a hundred oblations for each principle (tattva), beginning with earth and proceeding in sequence;
O Goddess of Gods, one should offer a hundred oblations for each at the end of Prakṛti.
Having thus renounced what has been described, O Goddess, one should offer into the fire one principle for each of the parts (kalās) that have been proclaimed. 140.
Furthermore, I shall speak of a specific distinction regarding Vāmadeva; listen to that.
Beginning with the Puruṣa, they are briefly described as being full of greed.
In each reality (tattva), however, one should offer two pairs of digits (kalās). O Goddess of the Gods, one should offer a hundred oblations with a single digit. (142)
O beautiful goddess, this has been fully explained as the portion of Vāma;
the wise one should offer Māyā and Avidyā with the portions of Aghora.
However, with each individual oblation, one should offer the twenty-five principles:
Īśvara, Devīśa, as well as the principle Sadāśiva. (144)
The oblation should be offered by a person with a well-composed mind at the very moment [of the breath];
one should offer fifty oblations for each individual [breath]. || 145 ||
With twenty or twenty oblations, according to the portion of Īśāna,
the principle of Śiva (Śivatattva) must be offered by the high-souled preceptor.
Now,
O Goddess of gods, when a hundred [offerings] are complete, the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) is prescribed as being twice that amount on the left side. (147)
Furthermore, the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) for Aghora is prescribed with one beat;
however, the full oblations for Śiva consist of four beats.
It should likewise be given by the lord of preceptors to the person;
O woman of excellent complexion, one should offer oblations with the five parts of the Īśāna-kalā.
The final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) should be offered by the high-souled preceptor;
as for the ritual procedure for the joining (yojana), that which was previously described by me [should be performed]. || 150 ||
O Goddess, this has been understood by you; what more shall I tell you?
O Goddess, this path of the parts (kalādhvan) has been fully explained in its entirety.
O Goddess of the gods, the path of worlds (bhuvanādhvan) and the path of aspects (kalādhvan) have been briefly described; they are to be understood by the teacher (deśika) in two ways. (152)
O Goddess of the gods, this has been told; it must be understood by the preceptor.
Thus, upon the completion of the initiation, the teacher, being well-composed, [should proceed]. (153)
Having dismissed [the deity], O Goddess of gods, one should worship Caṇḍeśvara there;
on the following day, O Goddess of gods, one should worship the Lord Caṇḍeśvara.
O fair-faced one, the mantras endowed with five limbs were previously taught by me in the first sūtra at the excellent city of Ardhacandra. 155.
Having performed worship with just one offering, the wise practitioner,
having performed the libation in the mandala, should offer oblations one hundred and eight times in sequence.
Thus, O Goddess, [it is said] regarding Caṇḍeśa in the great [section];
on page 425,
line 145, no insertion of a verse is observed other than the subject matter previously mentioned.
One should employ [it]. || 157 ||
Furthermore, one should worship in the second enclosure with the limbs of the Vidyā;
O fair-faced lady, all the outer enclosures are to be known [in this manner].
This lotus-wheel of yours, O Goddess, has thus been described to you.
The first is that of Śivagarbha, the second is that of the Cakravartins;
O Great Goddess, in the third [square], one should place the enclosures of Vāyu.
The fourth belongs to the Gaṇeśas, immediately following that in the southeast;
the sixth belongs to the Lokapālas, and the seventh is remembered as belonging to Mahendra. (161)
O Supreme Goddess, one should place the ten and the nine principles in their proper order; one should assign them outside the lines of the limbs of the Vidyā.
One should arrange them in sequence according to the order starting from the east;
those which consist of eight and one single padas each are declared to be the hymn (stotra).
O Dear One, all [the oblations] should indeed be offered in sequence, beginning from the conception;
or else, having performed the ritual procedure for the seat and so forth, one may begin from that point. 164.
O beloved, one should offer one hundred oblations each into eight external directions and eight into the womb-place; thus one is purified—of this there is no doubt. || 165 ||
The woman of excellent complexion should be given as the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) by Śiva;
furthermore, the eighty-one squares have already been described previously. (166)
I shall describe the auspicious sacrifice; listen, O Goddess, in due order.
It should be performed on the previously mentioned ground, free from husks, hair, and bones. (167)
On a level plot of ground, free from depressions and elevations,
in a region sloping toward the northeast, one should lay out the auspicious site with a cord.
The measurement of the field is proclaimed to be twenty-four cubits; having laid out the lines according to rule, one should divide it into nine parts. || 169 ||
Furthermore, one should mark out the middle section here itself by means of nine parts;
among those divided into nine parts, one should omit half a part.
The lotus is thirty-two finger-breadths [in size], according to the rule of thirty-two finger-breadths; it is endowed with the fourfold method and adorned with eight gates. (171)
I have previously explained the measurement for the door; one should construct it using that very measurement.
Just as it is for the center, so too should everything always be done by the preceptors.
O Lord of Gods, they say that the space between the surrounding petals of the line-lotus (*rekhāpadma*) should be sixteen finger-breadths; thus has the line-lotus been described.
There should be no doubt regarding the placement of the enclosures;
O Goddess of the Gods, listen as I explain the limbs of Śiva—understand them from me. (174)

Oṃ, homage to the all-pervading one! Oṃ, homage to the one whose form is space! Oṃ, homage to the infinite one! Oṃ, homage to the Lord of the self (Ātman)! Oṃ, homage to the one who does not depend on the self!
The limbs of Śiva are proclaimed as follows: Om, salutation to Dhruva; Om, salutation to Śāśvata;
Om, salutation to him who is established on the seat of Yoga (Yogapīṭha); Om, salutation to the Eternal Yogin; Om, salutation to him whose food is meditation (Dhyānāhāra).
The limbs of Vidyā are proclaimed as follows.
O Goddess of the gods, the *padabrahman* has previously been described as being within the limbs;
it must be known by the preceptor at the time of initiation, without a doubt. (175)

Oṃ, salutation! Oṃ, salutation to the one who pervades the sky. Oṃ, salutation to the one whose form is the sky. Oṃ, salutation to the all-pervading one. Oṃ, salutation to Śiva. Oṃ, salutation to the infinite one. Oṃ, salutation to the Lord (Ānātha).
Oṃ, salutation to the one who is not dependent on anything else (Anāśrita). Oṃ, salutation to the eternal one.
p.
430) First, one should deposit [these mantras] within the womb of Śiva; this has been declared [as follows]:
Oṃ, salutation to the Eternal One (Śāśvata). Oṃ, salutation to him who is established upon the seat of yoga (Yogapīṭha). Oṃ, to the Ever-Yogin (Nityayogin). Oṃ...

Homage to the one whose food is meditation. Oṃ, obeisance! Oṃ, obeisance to Śiva. Oṃ, obeisance to the source of all. Oṃ, obeisance to Śiva. Oṃ, obeisance to the one whose head is Īśāna. Oṃ, obeisance to the one whose face is Tatpuruṣa.
This is indeed proclaimed as the second enclosure, that of the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśa). || 176 ||

Oṃ, salutation to the heart of Aghora. Oṃ, salutation to Vāmadeva, the secret one. Oṃ, salutation to the form of Sadyojāta. Oṃ, oṃ, salutation, salutation. Oṃ, salutation to the one more secret than the secret. Oṃ, salutation to the protector. Oṃ, salutation to the one who is the end of the endless.
"Oṃ nidhanāya namaḥ.
O Goddess, this is proclaimed as the third enclosure (āvāraṇa) for the deities and others.

Oṃ, homage to the Lord of all vidyās! Oṃ, homage to the one whose form is light! Oṃ, homage to the boon-granting Supreme Lord! Oṃ, homage to consciousness! Oṃ, homage to non-consciousness! Oṃ, homage to the sky-like, the sky-like! Oṃ, homage to the pervasive, the pervasive! Oṃ, homage to the formed, the formed! Oṃ, homage to the primordial, the primordial! Oṃ...
"Oṃ tejas-tejas, obeisance! In the fourth group, however, the enclosure of the Gaṇeśas is proclaimed:
"Oṃ jyotis-jyotis, obeisance! Oṃ amūrta, obeisance! Oṃ agni, obeisance!"
Oṃ madhu namaḥ | Oṃ bhasma namaḥ | Oṃ anādi namaḥ | Oṃ nnānā namaḥ | Oṃ dhudhūdhudhū namaḥ | Oṃ bhūrnamaḥ | This indeed is the Āgneya enclosure (āvaraṇa).

The [mantras] beginning with *yoga* have been illustrated: Oṃ bhuvar namaḥ | Oṃ svar namaḥ | Oṃ anidhana namaḥ | Oṃ nidhanodbhava namaḥ | Oṃ śiva namaḥ | Oṃ sarva namaḥ | Oṃ paramātman namaḥ | Oṃ maheśvara namaḥ |
The sixth enclosure is indeed proclaimed to belong to the world-protectors.

Oṃ, homage to Mahādeva! Oṃ, homage to Sadbhāveśvara! Oṃ, homage to Mahātejas! Oṃ, homage to Yogādhipati! Oṃ, release, release, release, homage! Oṃ, first one, first one, homage! Oṃ, Śarva, Śarva, homage! Oṃ, Bhava, Bhava, homage!
Oṃ bhavodbhava, homage!
The seventh enclosure, that of Mahendra, is proclaimed as belonging to Tārā and the others. (178)
Oṃ, salutations to the bestower of happiness upon all beings! Oṃ, salutations to the one who brings presence everywhere!

Oṃ, salutations to the one beyond Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra! Oṃ, salutations to the one worshipped and unworshipped! Oṃ, salutations to the one consecrated and unconsecrated! Oṃ, salutations to the one who was present from the beginning and remains present from the beginning! Oṃ, salutations to the witness, the witness!
Namaḥ | Oṃ turu turu namaḥ | Oṃ pataṅga pataṅga namaḥ | Oṃ piṅga piṅga namaḥ | The eighth is declared to be the enclosure of the weapons of the world-protectors (lokapāla). || 178½ ||
Oṃ śabdaśabda, homage! Oṃ sūkṣma sūkṣma, homage! Oṃ śiva, homage! Oṃ śarva, homage! Oṃ sarva, homage! Oṃ oṃ namo namaḥ! Oṃ oṃ śivāya namo namaḥ!
Oṃ, obeisance! This is indeed proclaimed as the ninth enclosure (āvaraṇa) of those beginning with Ambhā. 179.
In the tenth [section], one should place the nine principles (tattvas) in their proper order:
