*oṃ ūn namaḥ*, *oṃ yan namaḥ*, *oṃ ln namaḥ*, *oṃ an namaḥ*, *oṃ kṣan namaḥ*, *oṃ ran namaḥ*, *oṃ han namaḥ*, and *oṃ prasannamūrtaye namaḥ*. One should place the ninth [syllable] in the center.
One should place the limbs of knowledge (vidyāṅga) according to the lines; these are proclaimed as belonging to Aiśvarya. || 180 ||

Oṃ, to the Self of All, the Supreme, the Supreme Lord, the Sovereign of Yoga, the Source of Yoga, the Giver of Hands, the Immediate Giver of Hands, the Arisen from Existence, O Vāmadeva, [this is] the mantra for the pacification of all undertakings. (p. 435)
O Sadāśiva, be gracious; salutations, salutations! [This is] the heart of the body of the Self of All.

Oṃ, salutations to Suśiva. Oṃ, Suśiva is the head of the God. Oṃ, salutations to Jvālinī, the Heart of Śiva. Jvālinī is the crest-lock (śikhā); she is the great splendor whose essence is Śiva, the omniscient, imperishable Lord.
One should recite the most formidable, auspicious, and tawny-hued armor-mantra.

Come, O Piṅgala, and roar loudly at the command of Śiva! Bind, bind the heart! Blaze up, blaze up! Reel about, O you who have drawn the subtle [thread]! O Vajradhara, Vajrapāśa, Vajraśakti, and Candrā, having entered my body and my heart—
p. 436) *Sarvaduṣṭastambhaya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*. That armor named Piṅgala is the binding of the syllable Oṃ; *huṃ phaṭ* is the armor, and the heart-mantra is: *oṃ prasphura prasphura ghora ghoratara*.

*tanurūpa caṭa caṭa pracaṭa pracaṭa kaha kaha vaṃ vaṃ ghātaya ghātaya huṃ phaṭ*—this is the Aghorāstra. *oṃ oṃ aghoraśivāya huṃ phaṭ*—this is the Heart-mantra of Aghorāstra. *oṃ vyomavyāpine vyomarūpāya sarvavyāpine śivāya anantāya anāthāya anāśritāya*.
Obeisance again and again to Śiva, the eternal and constant one, established upon the seat of yoga, the perpetual yogi whose sustenance is meditation;
obeisance to Śiva, the source of all; to Him whose head is Īśāna, whose face is Tatpuruṣa, whose heart is Aghora, whose secret part is Vāmadeva, and whose form is Sadyojāta; obeisance, obeisance!
To the one more secret than the secret, the protector, the imperishable, the presiding authority over all yoga, the sovereign lord of all ignorance,
whose form is light, who is devoted to the Supreme Lord, who pervades that which is both insentient and sentient, O Pervader, O Pervader, O Formless One, O Formless One.

The foremost of the foremost, the brilliance of brilliance, the light of light, formless, without fire, without smoke, without ash, beginningless, manifold, manifold—dhū dhū dhū dhū. Oṃ bhūḥ. Oṃ bhuvaḥ. Oṃ suvaḥ. O you who are without end yet the end, the source of the end, the auspicious one, the supreme soul of all, Maheśvara, Mahādeva, Lord of true existence!
O Lord of Great Splendor, Master of Yoga, release, release! O Primordial One, Primordial One! O Śarva, Śarva! O Bhava, Bhava! O Source of Existence!
O Bestower of Happiness upon all beings! O Maker of Presence for all! O Supreme One beyond Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra! (p. 438)
Unworshipped, O worshipper; unworshipped, O worshipper; unrefined, O refined one; previously situated, O previously situated one;
witness, O witness; *turu turu*, O sun; *pataṅga pataṅga*, O golden-hued one; *piṅga piṅga*, O knower; knowledge, O knowledge; sound, O sound; subtle, O subtle;
Śiva, O giver of all! *Oṃ namo namaḥ*. *Oṃ namaḥ*. *Oṃ śivāya namo namaḥ*. Supreme!

The Great Lord Śivabhaṭṭāraka: Oṃ, I take refuge in Sadyojāta; salutations indeed to Sadyojāta. In existence and beyond existence, protect me; salutations to Bhavodbhava. Salutations to Sadyojāta, salutations to Vāmadeva, salutations to Jyeṣṭha, salutations to Rudra, salutations to Kāla, salutations to Kalavikaraṇa.
Salutation to the one who causes the transformation of power; salutation to the one who crushes power; salutation to the subduer of all beings; salutation to the one who transcends the mind.

Oṃ! To those who are non-terrible, and to those who are terrible, and to those more terrible than the most terrible—to all of them, everywhere, to all those forms of Rudra, let there be salutation to you. Aghora. Oṃ! We know that Tatpuruṣa; we meditate upon Mahādeva; may that Rudra inspire us. Tatpuruṣa.

Oṃ. He who is the Lord of all beings, the Sovereign of all beings, the Overlord of Brahman, the Overlord of the sacred word—may that Brahman, Śiva, be mine; Sadāśiva! Īśāna! Oṃ. To that Great Lord we pay homage; we meditate upon Him whose speech is purified; may that Śiva inspire us.
All this has Śiva as its essence; from Śiva alone does it proceed.
For the sake of Śiva, for him who contains Śiva within, may the all-pervading Śiva impel [this].
440) Oṃ Āṃ Īṃ Ūṃ, salutation to the one who pervades the sky, Oṃ Oṃ, salutation to the profoundly peaceful one, Oṃ, to the Self of the Praṇava.
Salutation! Oṃ hūṃ, salutation to Śiva; oṃ hun, salutation; oṃ phaṇ, salutation; oṃ ju, salutation.
Worship is prescribed for the letters, for Śiva, the Supreme Self. 182.
Oṃ, I take refuge in Sadyojāta; obeisance! Oṃ, obeisance indeed to Sadyojāta!
Oṃ, obeisance to Bhava! Oṃ, obeisance to Abhava! Oṃ, obeisance to Anādibhava! Oṃ, favor me, obeisance! Oṃ, obeisance to Bhava! Oṃ, obeisance to Udbhava!
Salutation, *oṃ*, salutation again and again to Vāmadeva. *Oṃ*, salutation again and again to Jyeṣṭha.
*Oṃ*, salutation again and again to Rudra. *Oṃ*, salutation again and again to Kāla. *Oṃ*, salutation to Kala.

Oṃ, salutations again and again to the One Without Limbs (Vikaraṇa). Oṃ, salutations to Power (Bala). Oṃ, salutations again and again to the One Without Limbs. Oṃ, salutations to Power. Oṃ, salutations again and again to the Agitator (Pramathana). Oṃ, salutations again and again to the Subduer of All Beings (Sarvabhūtadamana).
Oṃ, salutations to Thought (Manana). Oṃ, salutations again and again to the Transcendent Mind (Unmana). Oṃ, salutations to those who are not terrible (Aghora). Oṃ, and so forth.

Homage to the terrible ones! Oṃ, homage to the terrible! Oṃ, homage to those more terrible than the terrible! Oṃ, homage from all sides! Oṃ, homage to all the Śarvas! Oṃ, let there be homage to you, O Rudra, homage! Oṃ, homage to the forms! Oṃ, we know that Puruṣa, homage! Oṃ, we meditate upon Mahādeva, homage! Oṃ, may that Rudra [grant us]... homage!
Salutation! Oṃ, may [the Lord] impel me; salutation! Oṃ, the Lord of all sciences;
salutation! Oṃ, the Lord of all beings; salutation! Oṃ, the sovereign of Brahman, the overlord of Brahman, the Brahman; salutation! Oṃ, may Śiva be mine; salutation! Oṃ, Sadāśiva; salutation!
One should join each word one by one and offer each word individually.
One should arrange the nine principles upon each individual footstool;
by means of each individual footstool, one attains initiation leading to liberation.
O Goddess, one should offer a hundred oblations for each leaf of every single word;
having performed the libation for the mandala, one should offer eleven-fold oblations.
The full oblations (pūrṇāhuti) should be offered in due order and succession;
having offered one at the "beyond-the-foot" (atipada) stage, one should purify the sacrificial path.
Furthermore, O Goddess, listen once more as I tell you in brief:
by the presence of the invocation, each individual word is purified. (187)
O Goddess, one should fashion exactly nine footprints upon each pedestal;
by ten oblations for each, there is no doubt that the purification of the pedestal is accomplished. (188)
Thus the initiation is completed by means of the wheel of words (*padacakra*) well-constructed;
one should perform this procedure, which is common to all *saṃhitās*. (189)
O Goddess, this unsurpassed *padayāga* has been fully explained;
it is common to all *saṃhitās* and is celebrated in all *tantras*. (190)
Having worshipped the Sovereign Lord of the Kings of Knowledge (Vidyārājādhirāja), one shall attain liberation.
Furthermore, I shall proclaim another most secret essence of mantras.
By the mere knowledge of which one shall attain supreme accomplishment—
that three-eyed, ten-armed deity has been previously described by me. (192)
Therefore, I shall explain that; listen with a one-pointed mind.
[He is] seated in the lotus posture, illuminating all directions.
One should contemplate the five-faced god situated upon the pericarp;
established there, he resides in the center of the *śakti*, resembling the rising sun. (194)
In some places it resembles Indra (sapphire), in others it is like emerald;
in some places it is a mass of liquid mercury, and in its radiance it is equal to ten million suns.
To the God who stands illuminating [all], resembling the thumb of the vital breath (prāṇa)—there are Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and likewise Śānti. (196)
The three mandalas:
the ten-armed deity Śiva, who is the essence of nectar, is for the sake of pacification.
They illuminate the seat of that god on all sides. || 197 ||
Having the form of the flame of a crest-lamp, she emerges after piercing the palate;
at its end, O Goddess, that which is beyond is proclaimed as Śakti.
That [process] should be understood as ending with the *prakriyā*; having pierced through that, one should unite [the soul] with the Supreme.
Having severed [the bonds] and established the bound soul (*paśu*) within oneself, it should then be united in the Excellent Abode (*suvṛta*).
Having known that reality, one should apply it for only the duration of a blink of an eyebrow;
this, O Goddess, O Supreme Sovereign, is declared to be the Self.
Thus, whoever perceives the Self is liberated, without a doubt;
and having seen the Lotus in the supreme Śiva, one shall liberate others as well, without a doubt. (201)
But without seeing it, one does not attain success, nor does the leader reach the supreme state;
therefore, it must always be meditated upon by yogis with the utmost effort.
Having placed the Self within the pericarp of the heart, the knower of yoga meditates;
thus, yogis perceive the entire region situated in its own place.
O Goddess, one sees a hundred yojanas; of this there is no doubt.
O Maheśvarī, I shall describe it according to its arrangement leaf by leaf. 204.
The eastern petal and likewise the one in the intermediate direction between Agni and Īśāna—by means of the union of these half-and-half petals, he perceives the eastern region. || 205 ||
By means of half of the [petal] of Īśāna and that of Vāyu, O well-formed one, and by means of the northern petal, one beholds the northern path. (206)
O beautiful one, the single western petal is adorned by the half of the northwest;
thereafter, the lord of yogis should look toward the region of the southwest.
O Goddess of the gods, by means of the southern half of the southwest [quarter],
and indeed by the southern half of the southeast, one beholds the entire southern region.
The four [deities] are indeed well-enclosed by the petals on the side;
they are declared in the second [chapter] as the Tāpanī, and one should know them according to their respective regions.
Thus, among all the principles (tattvas), this should be understood by those who know the truth:
having made the self hollow and having placed the regions in the middle. (210)
Having made oneself of infinite form, one sees [it] and not otherwise;
all rivers, oceans, and streams are contained within it. (211)
The yogi established in yoga perceives this; there is no doubt in this matter.
That true nature which was previously known to you has now been fully explained.
One should direct that gaze toward everything; there is no doubt in this.
Having made Mount Meru its pericarp, one then beholds the three worlds. (213)
One should relate the entire account; there is no need for deliberation here.
O Goddess, this supreme essence of yoga has been declared by me. 214.
One who is disciplined in yoga perceives [this] within three months; of this there is no doubt.
One who is disciplined in yoga for six months perceives everything; it is not otherwise.
With his self disciplined for a year, he beholds the divine and the non-divine;
he attains equality with the gods and traverses the worlds in due order. (216)
The practitioner who, being well-composed, meditates thus and performs the recitation, shall achieve success;
there is no doubt in this matter, for that lord of practitioners will be free from obstacles.
O Supreme Goddess, the yogi who is joined with this method quickly attains perfection; there is no need for deliberation on this matter. (218)
On the eastern petal is Vijaya; in the southeast is Śatrunāśana;
on the southern petal is Śāntida; and in the southwest is Māraṇa. (219)

One should seek prosperity in the western direction (Vāruṇī), or for the sake of destruction in the northern direction (Vāyavī); those desiring wealth should go to the north, and one desiring knowledge should go to the northeast (Īśānī). || 220 ||

O Goddess of the gods, those who desire victory over death should constantly meditate [on the breath] as rising upward, resembling cow's milk; thus they are not afflicted by the sufferings of death. (221)
O Goddess, she leads the best of men downward, and the lowest of men upward;
knowing this, O lady of excellent hips, she leads them—of this there is no doubt. (222)
The Goddess said:
O Mistress of the Gods, you have described its crest as being upwards and incomparable;
O Blessed One, I desire to hear about it—please deign to speak. (223)
How is it that by that form his crest-lock bestows the fruit [of merit], yet, O Lord, how does it lead downward the one who performs evil deeds? (224)
O Lord, how do yogins perceive [this] directly within the body?
Please, out of your grace, explain the procedure for the application of mudrās and yoga. (225)
O Goddess, listen, Lord; I shall proclaim the unsurpassed classification of the crest-lock (śikhā).
By the mere knowledge of which, practitioners achieve success on this earth. || 226 ||
In the Gāruḍa and Bhūta-tantras, as well as in those of the sisters,
there is the supreme, divine Śaiva knowledge, and the delightful ritual of the topknot (śikhā-karma).
Resembling white cow’s milk and similar to a conch shell, a kunda flower, or the moon—the crest-lock (śikhā) should always be meditated upon by yogins for the sake of conquering death. 228.
By the falling of torrents of rain, they fill [the world] on all sides;
they act as teachers for the entire world and destroy poisons and planetary afflictions. 229.
It brings constant satisfaction and consists of the meditation on the mantra;
and one does not see the streams flowing with distinct divisions. (230)
In an instant, one should effect nourishment; there is no need for deliberation here.
When the yogi has performed the meditation on the red-colored crest, he becomes [successful]. (231)
I shall likewise explain that to you; listen with a one-pointed mind.
[I shall teach] subjugation, possession, killing, and likewise withering.
Because it effects the removal of poison, brings about nirvāṇa, and renders one seedless; because it is without the kindling of fire, as well as causing fainting and purification. (233)
This has been proclaimed by me while wearing red-colored garments; now listen, O virtuous lady, as I shall speak while wearing yellow-colored garments. (234)
Through meditation, one attains accomplishment that bestows wealth, grain, and fruit;
he can paralyze the entire earth and the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile. (235)
O virtuous one, listen as I shall explain the rites for the black-colored crest-mantra:
the performance of eradication, inciting enmity, and likewise liberation. (236)
There is no doubt that it causes the transmission of poison and induces muteness;
there is no doubt that it paralyzes all principles (tattvas) and the sense objects. || 237 ||
O Dear One, everything is accomplished for him who knows the application of the *śikhā*;
however, no rite devoid of the *śikhā* is ever successful for practitioners. (238)
The Vāyavyā is black in color, while the Āgneyī is red, O virtuous one;
the Mahendrī should be known as yellow, and the Vāruṇī is said to be white.
Black, red, white, yellow, and crystal-like in appearance—
these are always to be well-guarded by those who know the ritual of the crest-tuft for the performance of all rites. (240)
O Goddess of virtuous conduct, this Śikhā-yoga has been told to you;
it is the common accomplishment of all tantras, without a doubt. (241)
O Goddess, he who desires accomplishment while devoid of the *śikhā* strikes at the sky with his fist and drinks from a mirage. || 242 ||
O Goddess, he who knows this fivefold nature attains success.
I shall now describe the restraint of initiation; listen with a one-pointed mind. (243)
O Goddess, one should perform this [rite] against one who is foolish, deceitful, cruel, and who walks the path of injustice; but never against anyone else. 244.
Having drawn [the soul] from the supreme reality by means of his own reality, the teacher leads it—
by means of five oblations with each of the five [mantras]— to wherever he desires. (245)
Then, having established it and covered the ground over it, the excellent preceptor remains there; for that teacher who attempts to leap over it is of a wicked nature.
In whatever place one applies [the practice], one experiences suffering there.
O Goddess, listen as I shall explain how the obstruction of success occurs. 247.
Having placed a balance on the wind-wheel for the sake of accomplishing its success,
it is then completely covered by Māhendra, who assumes the form of the earth.
Thus stabilized, O Goddess, he remains; there is no doubt in this.
Listen to how this becomes directly manifest even to yogins. || 249 ||
At whatever time a particular yoga is to be practiced by yogins, that I shall fully declare; listen, O Goddess, in brief. (250)
When one-third of a ghaṭikā has passed, O woman of excellent complexion,
she should practice for as long as it takes to sit three times.
With a well-pleased mind, one should cause that [mind] focused on the *lakṣa* to be absorbed by the city;
then, O fair-faced one, one beholds her trembling within it. (252)
One sees that very same similar target; there is no doubt in this matter.
In the first stage, yogis always see it as copper-colored and blue.
Red, yellow, and white— each with an equal brilliance corresponding to its color—
one should close one's eyes for one hundred thousand [repetitions] while that hundred thousand is being observed.
"O Goddess, behold that supreme, great form shaped like a chariot wheel.
Having seen it, the yogi shall directly enter Śiva, even while remaining in a different location. (255)
Without doubt, O Goddess of gods, he shall attain the state called Sādākhya;
he alone certainly perceives and knows the Self as the target. 256.
But through practice, one attains equality equal to that of the Lord of Gods.
Thus, I shall describe to you the sign of attainment for the supreme yogi. (257)
But when dead, the fire-god draws a lotus and honey-mixture;
he trembles and gives a painful command, O beloved of the yogin. (258)
It shines like a drop of indolaka; O Goddess, at whatever time the crest-lock (śikhā) of the yogin comes under control, he lives through great affliction. (259)
O Goddess of the Gods, one should predict success in whichever direction the crest-flame moves; it is perceived without doubt, there is no uncertainty in this matter. (260)
When one perceives within the heart that unsurpassed union with the crest (śikhā),
conjoined with the swan of vital breath (vāyu) and endowed with the sixth vowel, || 261 ||
By means of the final seed-syllable of the Nāda, one perceives that which is endowed with Bindu and Nāda; of this there is no doubt.
Then, O fair-faced one, when the yogin perceives the heart as the target within the interior of the radiant wing, [he attains success]. (263)

Then indeed, the yogis should place the *lakṣa* upon the region of the ear, having abandoned the color of the wind (the letter *ya*), and endowed with the *ū*, the *bindu*, and the crest (*śikhā*). 264.
When the yogi, well-composed, reaches the location of the head,
he is liberated from all sounds and joined with the syllable *ra*. (265)
When the state of the head, which resides in the crown of the skull, is fully attained, then that which is released from the *bindu* is proclaimed as the *śikhā*.
The supreme Śakti transcends the crest (śikhā), and the supreme Śiva transcends Śakti;
these are declared to be the Vāyavya and the Āgneya [padas] respectively. (267)
The Māhendra and the Vāruṇa [mudrās] are likewise, without a doubt;
the fifth is proclaimed as the support for all yoga. || 268 ||
The supreme Śiva, whose nature is consciousness, is the realization of the true form of consciousness;
for that singular knowledge indeed emerges spontaneously, even from among gods and asuras. (269)
The second [aspect], its true nature, is difficult to discern even for the gods.
O virtuous one, this knowledge has been proclaimed in every way throughout all the tantras. (270)
Having known [this] by means of the half-portion of all [the breaths], one is liberated from bondage;
for it is from this that the division of day and night proceeds, O Goddess. (271)
Therefore, O beautiful Goddess, this was previously explained to you regarding the lineage:
the Guru knows him who stands in the center, situated within the lotus. (272)
Beyond this, O Goddess, is that which is supreme and beyond the lineage of gurus;
having set aside these three, that is proclaimed as the highest. (273)
In the Cāradeva [mandala], which is not auspicious, it is known to be thirty-six finger-breadths;
therein, the emission of the void (śūnyoccāra) is proclaimed according to the division of parts.
The practice is remembered as being exactly as it was declared in the *Navasūtra*.
By that, O Goddess of Gods, success is achieved; no doubt should be entertained in this matter. (275)
O Goddess, listen as I shall speak of another most secret [practice] according to the truth;
O Goddess, one may behold this supreme application at that very moment. (276)
O Goddess, having rendered the left and right hands divine,
the king of yogins should behold the four digits blazing like a lamp.
When the beginning is joined with the end, it is auspicious for both;
however, that which is touched in the middle region is seen by both. (278)
When one does not perceive the "third eye" (Aṃbaka) during the uprooting of light, listen to the fruit of the yoga of meditation for all yogas indeed. || 279 ||
One gains intelligence, beauty, and likewise health; one grasps whatever is said even once.
One sees everything, whether divine or non-divine, and not otherwise. (280)
Within three months, they shall become knowers of all branches of speech;
likewise, they shall possess the power of rising [into the air] and invisibility through the application of ointments and collyrium.
The accomplishment of pills and other such preparations shall occur within six months;
O Goddess, this supreme nectar of practice has been fully explained.
O Goddess of gods, O auspicious one, truth is seen directly as equal [to experience];
yet those who know other tantras are merely investigators of what is logical and illogical. || 283 ||
In this way, having obtained knowledge, those ascetics disparage themselves;
O Goddess, they do not understand this knowledge, the supreme true essence of knowledge. (284)
Cultivate this conviction, for it belongs to both yourself and others; of this there is no doubt.
O Goddess, this Haṃsa-yoga has been explained to you in detail according to the prescribed ritual. (285)
Therefore, O Goddess of noble conduct, for one who understands the knowledge and realization of the process,
there is the vision of the three deities therein.
By that [method], it shall be seen directly according to the prescribed rite, and not otherwise.
O beautiful goddess, I shall explain the sacrifice once again.
The seat [is offered] with the five Brahmakalās, with the one joined by the nine Śaktis, with the Praṇava alone, and likewise with the limbs of the Vidyā. || 288 ||
The Supreme Lord is to be worshipped by means of Varuṇa alone;
He should be worshipped within the lotus of the heart and upon the sacrificial ground by one who desires spiritual perfection.
O Goddess of the Gods, if the yogin practices for six months, he attains accomplishment; on the very first day, there shall be a manifest sign of realization.
O Goddess, from that very churning, success (siddhi) always arises;
from sacrifice, success is born, and through knowledge, one attains absolute liberation (kaivalya). || 291 ||
Through meditation and the practice of recitation, he bestows perfection; of this there is no doubt.
One should place Īśāna above, and Tatpuruṣa is traditionally taught for the east.
Aghora is indeed in the south, and Vāmadeva likewise in the north;
while Sadyojāta, O Goddess of Gods, is situated in the west. (293)
One should place the heart in the southeast and the head in the northeast;
O Goddess, one should likewise place the crest-lock in the southwest and the armor in the northwest. (294)
The wise one should place [the vessel] in a region where blood flows;
thus, being well-composed, she should sacrifice with a single *āvaruṇa* [offering]. (295)
Having performed the libation for the maṇḍala, one should offer oblations consisting of eleven [deities];
O Goddess of the gods, one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) in sequence with the mantra of Śiva.
Sacrifice is declared to be performed upon a sacrificial mound and within a mandala;
now listen, O Goddess, as I describe to you the sacrifice performed within the heart-lotus. || 297 ||
One should contemplate reality from the letter *e*; the letter *ai* is to be pointed out as such.
Furthermore, *ṛ* and *ṝ* are to be understood as the four bases of dharma. (298)
O Goddess of the gods, one should not install the Śaktis with the syllable Oṃ;
rather, by means of that [syllable], one should first fashion the form of the deity in its entirety, without exception. (299)
Having invoked the supreme Śiva with the tenth *praṇava*,
the wise one should effect the three principles (*tritatva*) by means of the application of the *praṇava* through the method of ritual placement (*nyāsa*). (300)
The letter Ā should be placed in the east, the letter Ī in the south,
the letter Ū in the west, and the seed-syllable of space (HŪṂ) in the north.
O Goddess of the gods, one should place the seed-syllable *maṃ* in the northeast;
the seed-syllable *vyāṃ* in the region of the wind (northwest), and the seed-syllable *bīṃ* in the southwest.
O Goddess of the gods, one should place the seed-syllable in the southeast;
it is proclaimed that this very placement is to be performed at the time of meditation. (303)
Listen again, O Goddess of gods; I shall tell you everything:
the stationary and the moving, as well as those born from eggs and those born from sweat. (304)
Seeing those of evil mind who are harmful toward him— whether they be gods, dānavas, animals, or fanged beings of cruel deeds— the wise man should reflect upon them. (305)
O Goddess, I have declared this to you through my vision; one should contemplate all those [beings] of a wicked-natured yogin according to my initiation as it was in the past. (306)
Having resolved upon both reality and unreality, one should contemplate the imperishable Śiva;
O auspicious lady, by merely being thus contemplated, they attain pacification. (307)
Thus, among all those sinful mosquitoes, those evil-minded beings did not harm the yogin; having seen Śiva, they attained equanimity. (308)
Reflecting thus constantly, wander at ease, having become one with the auspicious Samarasa, devoted to the yoga of meditation. (309)
Wherever the mind may go for the yogi who is meditating,
that very thing is the Supreme Brahman, established in its entirety within all things. (310)
Regarding auspicious and inauspicious actions, and regarding desirable and undesirable rebirths,
as well as among all stationary beings, the wise one remains established everywhere.
That which the mind goes toward—both the inconceivable and the conceivable—that alone is to be known as the Supreme Brahman by those who desire their own welfare. || 312 ||
Having become equal in flavor toward all things through their true nature, and thus having become equal in flavor, one enters the imperishable Śiva. || 313 ||
Thus, O Goddess, O beautiful one, the state of equal flavor (samarasa) has been proclaimed to you;
it is common to all that is conjoined, and it is spoken of as being cherished by the Conqueror (Jina).
Thus, having become of equal flavor, the well-concentrated yogins attain perfection;
there is no doubt in this matter, they are liberated; there is no uncertainty in this matter. || 315 ||
Listen, O Goddess, I shall declare the supreme secret in brief, by the mere knowledge of which one is liberated from the bondage of birth. (316)
O Goddess, I shall now explain that supreme and auspicious binding of the mudrā:
having placed the two hands palms-upward, one should form the braid-binding (veṇībandha). || 317 ||

the heart is distinguished [by them], the vidyā by the clenched fist, and likewise the armor. (320)

Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter of the Niśvāsakārikā.

Having obtained sites belonging to the celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial realms, and having thoroughly examined them,

Or on the Himalaya and Vindhya mountains, or likewise on Pāriyātra and Ambuda; on Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, or on the delightful mountain of Puṇyaśiloccaya.
In the Ganges and other excellent rivers, as well as in Antarvedī;

It is of four kinds—white, red, yellow, and black—and sweet and so forth.

The earth of a Vaiśya is said to be yellow, and that of a Śūdra is black;

For the Vaiśya, however, the earth is said to possess six tastes; for the Śūdra, it is remembered as being pungent.
Today, the earth has the scent of fragrance for the twice-born Brāhmaṇa, while for the Kṣatriya, it has the scent of blood.

The practitioner, having gathered the necessary provisions, should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) there,
using perfumes and flowers, as well as the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and unbroken grains (akṣata).
Having worshipped with the *garbha* mantras, one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) right there;
having offered oblations to this God of gods and to the mantras in their proper sequence. (16)
O fair-faced one, one hundred oblations should be offered to the deity;
having offered a tenth part of the total number of mantras, one should then present the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Having reached the path by means of that, one should worship all of them there;

Having thus worshipped the principles (tattvas), perform the ritual immolation (ālambhana) of the sacrificial animal; having immolated it with all the mantras, one should then deposit the principles in their proper sequence.

Having performed the *karaṇī* and *kartarī* [mudrās] and having prepared the various kinds of ritual materials (*saṃbhāra*), one should visualize all of them as being completely integrated and united with the deity. (21)
Having thus performed the rite according to the rules in the fire-places in due order,
one should bring the Jātavedas [fire] into either a copper vessel or an earthenware bowl.
O Goddess of the gods, perform the sprinkling with the Gāyatrī mantra according to its true essence;
having worshipped it with the five Brahmans, one should then cast it into the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
There, the expert in purification should place a seat;
he should purify the pit with the Astra-mantra, having drawn lines upon it, sprinkled it, and cleared it out.
Having done this, O Goddess of the Gods, one should prepare a seat;
there, one should establish Vāgīśī, the great sovereign who is in her season.
Then, O Goddess, O auspicious one, having recited each mantra three times,
the fire of Śiva becomes ignited by means of the eleventh mantra. (26)
O Dear One, for the purpose of purification,
one who knows the mantras for the oblations should subsequently offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) into the Śiva-fire that has been generated.
O Goddess, one should cook the sacrificial oblation according to the ritual procedure prescribed by the rules;
having deposited all the tantras, one should then place the three principles (tritattva) therein.
One should wrap the ear with a thread and cause it to be smeared with milk;
[one should also offer] balls made of linseed, śyāmāka, barley, and wheat.
It should be prepared with honey and medicinal herbs, and likewise with *kaṅgu* grain;
the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) must always be made until the vessel is full.
Furthermore, whatever ritual action is proclaimed, such as moving and rotating,
is performed with the five Brahmans and also with the eleventh. (31)
In this manner, the preceptor should again perform the rite as prescribed;
having offered the oblation with all the mantras, he should do so once for each, using the residual drops.
O Goddess of the gods, one should cause the weapon-substance to be placed in the fire with the *svāhā*-offering;
having thus offered according to the rite, one should again divide it into three parts.
Having offered it to the deity, the woman of excellent complexion should set aside two or three portions;
she should then assign the third portion to the practitioners according to the prescribed rite.
The five products of the cow (pañcagavya) should be prepared according to the ritual procedure prescribed by the rules:
cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with kuśa grass. (35)
Having brought these together, O beautiful one, the *pañcagavya* should be prepared:
cow dung with the *Sadyojāta* mantra, and cow urine with the *Guhyaka* (Vāmadeva) mantra. (36)
One should take the clarified butter with the Aghora mantra, and one should take the curd with the Vaktreṇa mantra;
one should take the milk with the Īśāna mantra, and the water from Kuśa grass with the Gāyatrī mantra.
Having consecrated it, O lady of excellent hips, one should recite all the mantras once;
whatever food or drink is to be given, it should be offered with the Vaktra-mantra.
Even the tooth-stick used here should be excellent, provided with milk and leaves, auspicious, free from notches, devoid of sharp edges, and measuring twelve finger-breadths in length. (39)
One should give that which has been consecrated with the Vaktra-mantra to his preceptor;
having performed the placing of the clarified butter on the fire, take it down and perform the purification (utpavana).

Then, having performed the *nīrājana* rite, one should perform the sprinkling of the faces (*vaktrābhidhāraṇa*). The wise one should perform the sprinkling of the faces with the *sadyojāta* mantra using the left [hand]. (41)
One should perform the expiation with the Astra-mantra; this is remembered as the extraction [of the fire] by means of its true essence.
When this has been done, O Goddess of the Gods, the fire of Śiva will be generated.
Thereafter, those who are well-composed should perform the ritual procedure for the lotus;

One should invoke the Lord of Gods according to the ritual procedure previously observed;
the wise man should always install Brahmā in the eastern quarter.
They say that Rudra is in the south and Viṣṇu in the west;
one should always install Śivā, the Supreme Goddess, in the north for the sake of Śiva. (45)

One should worship the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśas), the World-Protectors (lokapālas), and the weapons in their proper order, seated upon their seats, using the *pāvamāna* hymn according to the sequence. (46)
O Goddess, hear now in due order the ritual procedure that must first be performed:
one should fashion jars made of gold and silver, filled with jewels.

they should be smeared with sandalwood paste and decorated with seasonal roots and blades of kusha grass.
Having prepared the seat, one should place the jar called Śiva;
the principle of the Self (ātmatattva) in the lower part and the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva) in the middle.
One should place the third principle, Śivatattva, above;
there, the one of great intelligence, having gazed with his vision upon all things. (50)
All that becomes like a crest of flame; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
When the *vardhanī* vessel is filled with water, [one should offer] with all the mantras once each. (51)

One should rotate [the vessel] within the square and then place it back in that very same spot;
having scattered the syllables, the wise one should worship with that [offering].
Having sprinkled them again with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and with scented water, one should then rotate the jar; this indeed is the prescribed ritual.

One should draw the divine maṇḍala with perfectly straight and beautiful lines;

O Goddess, one who has reached the further shore of the Śiva-tattva should feed [the guests] upon seeing them;

likewise, one should prepare the *karaṇī*, the *kartarī*, the *saṃhitā*, as well as the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles. (85)

Neither the gods, including Indra, nor the sages, nor other yogis dwelling upon the earth were able to leap over her.

Mantras are accomplished when their beginning is suppressed by their end; not otherwise.
The principle of Śiva (śivatattva) is supremely pure, abiding both externally and internally. (14)
At the beginning and at the end, below and above, the central principle has emerged;
by that, those mantras and powers are impelled—of this there is no doubt.
Whatever is desired by the mind is accomplished; there is no doubt in this matter.
Having placed the syllable *oṃ* at the beginning, one should employ the word of salutation (*namaskāra*). (16)
O beautiful one, this conjunction of mantras has been explained to you:
namely, the utterances of Svāhā, Vaṣaṭ, and Suvauṣaṭ.
O Goddess, the syllable *phaṭ* accompanied by the syllable *huṃ*—this should be understood with effort as the union of power (*śakti*). || 18 ||
The rites of worship and recitation are joined with *namaḥ*;
491) those of fire-offerings (*homa*) and summonings (*ākarṣaṇa*) are joined with *svāhā*.
One should employ the *vauṣaṭ* syllable for rites of pacification (*śāntika*);
and for the sake of nourishment (*puṣṭi*), one should always perform [the rite] conjoined with the syllables *sa* and *o*.
The second [syllable] is joined with that [vowel], conjoined with the letters 'a' and 'u',
through the application of the mantra of the letter 'ṣa' together with the letter 'ha'.
For the sake of nourishing all mantras, whether for oneself or for another,
one should perform the rite of immortalization (amṛtīkaraṇa) accompanied by the syllable *vaṣaṭ*.
One should employ the mantra "namo namaḥ" for the purpose of fueling all the collections of mantras without exception when they are devoid of the syllable Om (praṇava). || 23 ||

O beautiful one, by beginning with the syllable *huṃ* and ending with *svāhā*, one should summon [the deity] through recitation and so forth; one who is always pure through the vows and recitation [attains this]. (24)
By employing the *huṃ* syllable at the beginning and joining it with the *phaṭ* syllable, one causes even spirits dwelling in divine realms to be expelled. (25)
That same [mantra], joined with *mā* and ending with *phaṭ phaṭ*, is the second;
one should perform this rite for killing, while all the remaining [mantras] are joined with *namaḥ*.
Thus it has been declared that they grant success in all undertakings for you;
this purity applies both at the time of the fire-oblation (homa) and always during the practice of recitation (japa).

Having understood this through which [the goal] must be accomplished by the teachers at the time of initiation, [the disciple] should always be intent on eating only one meal, or even devoted to fasting. (28)
One should always eat only at night, or constantly subsist on alms-food,
or even perform the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances during the time of recitation. (29)
In this very sequence one should accomplish the deity of the mantra; otherwise, the practitioners do not achieve success at all, but rather wither away like trees. (30)
I shall explain to you how a practitioner should accomplish all rites through the fire-oblation; listen to me with a one-pointed mind. (31)

Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa according to the procedure previously observed, the knower of mantras—who understands the three locations, times, and principles, and who is devoted to Śiva and Śakti—[should proceed]. || 32 ||
Then the practitioner, being self-restrained, should perform the fire oblation while remaining disciplined in his recitation;
he should maintain the connection between each syllable and the *akṣata* offerings, neither too fast nor too slow.
Clearly joined by conjunctions, depending on short and long [vowels],
protracted (pluta), joined with *visarga*, and joined with its own [consonant]— this has been declared by me. (34)
Having understood this, the wise man should perform recitation and fire-offerings;
and having prepared a beautiful seat, he should also perform the consecration with *śrīparṇī* wood. (35)
Likewise, O Goddess, there may be a seat of kusha grass or a seat of cow dung; with these excellent seats, which are spacious and well-prepared, [one should sit]. (36)
Standing, the mantra-practitioner should always perform the fire-oblation (homa) and never be restless;
having risen from his seat, the preceptor (deśika) should perform the oblation upon the ground.
Great and intense pain arises; of this there is no doubt.
When the practitioner is afflicted by such pain, he never attains the hundred-thousand-fold [recitation]. (38)
When the Adhipa is Kaṭigranthi, there is indeed consumption (aśoṣa), disease, and a great stiffness of the chest;
likewise, there is a most terrible paralysis of the chest and disease in the sides. (39)
Such miseries as these arise; of this there is no doubt.
Now, regarding the application of medicine when disease occurs, the physician should act as follows: || 40 ||
Likewise, I shall speak at the end; listen briefly, O virtuous one!
The commencement of yoga should never be undertaken without [proper] instruction.
Neither when afflicted by hunger nor by thirst, and certainly not in the midst of a crowd, should one practice while staying in that divine shelter protected from the wind. 42.
But another who acts otherwise never attains the target;
O beautiful one, that has been described to you as the yoga of conceptual construction (vikalpa).
O Goddess of the Gods, listen as I explain in brief how the initiation rite (dīkṣā) must be performed by the preceptor (deśika) through fire-offerings (homa). (44)
For even among the great, the remainder is born afflicted by hunger;
when tormented by thirst, a fault arises that causes a most terrible agitation of the walls.
From the agitation of bile (pitta), disease will undoubtedly arise for the guide;
there will be trembling, and bile, pustules, and so forth, born from fire. (46)
O Goddess, from the agitation of bile (pitta) arises a most terrible illusory disease;
it occurs for one afflicted by hunger and thirst, O virtuous lady, along with the desire for meat. 47.
One who is fit for the application of perfected mantras becomes the most excellent of teachers;
yet, he may become distressed by hunger even while engaged with the nine mantra-syllables. (48)
Therefore, the best of teachers should eat in a well-prepared place;
having partaken of a sacrificial meal (haviṣya), it should be saturated with ghee and milk. (49)
Having consumed milk-rice (pāyasa), he should then commence the initiation;
it should be concluded with the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), but one should not perform the ritual dismissal (utsarga).
If the fire's heat does not burn [the practitioner], he should cause it to fall by means of the *prasṛta* [mudrā];
when the mantra-practitioner is being burned, he should perform an expiation (*prāyaścitta*). || 51 ||
But for one whose face is burning with the mantras, they turn away and do not accomplish the rites; therefore, one should avoid such a person.
O beautiful one, when the eyes are being burned, the gods become angry; O goddess, because of that, harm arises—therefore, one should avoid it.
When the *romas* are being burned, the sages always become enraged;
when these are being burned, [one should act] with diligence for the sake of expiation. (54)
O Goddess of gods, having bowed with a composed mind and uttered this single verse, and having meditated upon the reality, one shall be purified of all doubts regarding expiations. (55)
The preceptors should offer the ladle full as the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti);
the preceptor, having placed both big toes together, [should do so] with the hand extended.
The wise one should cause [the oblation] to fall with both hands turned upward;
O Goddess, in this way the vessel is not burned, and likewise the oblation does not fall [uncontrollably]. || 57 ||

But when the vessel is burnt, one should perform an expiatory rite (prāyaścitta) by means of oblations (homa) according to the previously mentioned procedure; it becomes pure, of this there is no doubt. || 58 ||
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter in the Niśvāsakārikā.
The Goddess said: O God of gods, in former times the earth was placed by you as a deposit in heaven with a portion [of yourself];
O God, that deposit was maintained according to the rules of the sacred convention.
O Goddess of the gods, how are the principles (tattvas) to be known within one's own body by the high-souled teacher? O Blessed One, you should explain this to me.
O Goddess, listen, for I shall tell you the supreme secret, the unsurpassed knowledge of all, by the mere realization of which one is liberated; of this there is no doubt. (3)
First, O Goddess of the gods, one should contemplate the Mātṛkā;
one should join the seed-syllable on the right and place the womb-syllable on the left.
(500) Endowed with the *praṇava* at the beginning and ending with the word of salutation (*namaskāra*),
the mantra should indeed be performed by the preceptor for each and every class of letters.
Following that, the ninth [syllable] is the prior arrangement of the *mātṛkā*;
having again uttered the ninth, one should cause it to transcend sound.
Having thus performed the placement, O Goddess of gods, one should again distinguish them; the letter 'A' is to be known as that which one should place below the navel.
