thereafter, O Goddess, one should place Niyati upon the petals.
Thus, Māyā, Vidyā, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva—the Śivatattva, O Queen of the Gods, stands above them all. (9)
Having thus deposited the principles (tattvas) according to the sequence beginning with the Sakala,
one should likewise diligently deposit the Bindu, the Nāda, and the Śakti. (10)
O Goddess, listen now to the deity-assignment (devatānyāsa) originating from the heart;
thereafter, one should first contemplate the arrangement of the solar orb (sūryamaṇḍala).
The second is the placement (nyāsa) of Aindra, and the third is the placement of Vahni;
likewise, there are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Īśvara.
Sadāśiva, Śiva, and [the other] in their respective order;
likewise Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and Śānti. (13)
One should then install Nāda-śakti and Śiva in their proper order;
[there are] the kalā named Sūkṣmā and the second, Su-sūkṣmā.
Amṛtā, Mṛtā, and the third, Bījāmṛta; beyond that, O Goddess of Gods, one should always install these five [syllables] according to the manner of the Śaktis. (15)
O Great Goddess, the placement of the wheels (cakranyāsa) has thus been described previously;
it has been understood by you, O Goddess—what else shall I tell you? (16)
And that which was told by me here through fear of the eye—that has been understood by you, O Goddess; is there any truth beyond this? (17)
I shall now declare the ritual placement upon the hands (karanyāsa); listen with a one-pointed mind.
First, one should perform the placement of the nine-fold self (navātman), each part being distinct; of this there is no doubt. (18)
Then, having again uttered the mantra, one should place [the thumb] with the tip of the right thumb;
the whole [mantra] should be placed on the right thumb, and the remainder should be performed as before.
O Goddess, when the *kara-nyāsa* has been performed, one should contemplate Śiva right there. Having first deposited the three principles (*tritatva*), one should subsequently deposit Śiva. (20)
When this has been done, O Goddess, the Hand of Śiva is then remembered;
by that, all this work—the worship as well as the sprinkling—is accomplished.
One should perform both the grasping and the joining with the hand of Śiva;
first, the placement of the hands is prescribed, but not the [placement] of the self. || 22 ||
O Goddess, having indeed placed the second syllable of Mātṛkā, the third is Navātmā, and the fourth is distinct from that. || 23 ||
The fifth is proclaimed according to the sequence beginning with Sakala;
O Goddess, the thirteenth is supreme and established as the remedy for all diseases.
Having first performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) in this manner, the knower of yoga should meditate upon the reality (*tattva*).
If there is the presence of the thirteenfold self for the knower of reality, [then success follows]. (25)
O fair-faced one, he indeed bestows grace even upon one who is powerless;
he performs initiation by his word and by his glance, of this there is no doubt. (26)
O Goddess, this great nyāsa should be practiced with diligence;
by its mere sight or even by its recitation, a living being becomes purified—of this there is no doubt. (27)
O Goddess of gods, when the ritual placement (nyāsa) has been performed, there is no doubt regarding the mind, nor is there any doubt regarding touch; one becomes capable in all rites.
O Goddess, this meritorious and great Nyāsa has been proclaimed by me;
even he who understands it alone is liberated, of this there is no doubt. (29)
Having thus first performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), the teacher, with all doubts severed, is not stained by merit or sin; he is the liberator even of his own teacher. (30)
Thus, O Goddess of gods, this ritual placement (nyāsa) should not be given to just anyone;
it must be given to a wise preceptor who has been duly consecrated.
Otherwise, by speaking [falsely], one becomes a partaker of the state of wicked mortals;
therefore, the general characteristics of all the *saṃhitās* must be understood by the preceptor.
O Great Goddess, when this has been performed in that place, whoever they may be who have committed evil deeds, they are liberated by the sight of that Ācārya; of this there is no doubt. (33)
By this [mantra], one has indeed accomplished [the goal]; behold or listen even to you: merely by the sight of his form and by the hearing of the mantras. (34)
(506) Certainly by the mere sight [of you], and certainly by the leading [of you] forward;
indeed, O lady of beautiful hips, by the word "Agni" and by the word "noose. 35.
O Goddess, even the lowest of men is liberated from sins by hearing the sound [of the Guru], and [is further purified] by beholding the body of the high-souled teacher, O Goddess. (36)
One shall go as far as the world of Brahmā; there is no doubt about this.
Listen, O Goddess, for I am telling you: it occurs simply by hearing the mantras. (37)
Upon hearing the mantra, O Goddess, the sinful soul attains union with Rudra;
by beholding the smoke, one attains union with Viṣṇu. || 38 ||
O lady of beautiful hips, O goddess, listen as I speak with the word "Agni":
it refers to that manifestation which arises within the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva) for one who performs evil deeds. (39)
There is no doubt regarding [the merit gained] through the mind, nor is there any uncertainty regarding [the merit gained] from physical touch.
This great fruit of the greatness of Śiva has been told to you, O Goddess. (40)
Knowing this, O Goddess of gods, perform initiation according to your will;
by this, mortals who were bound like animals become liberated from their fetters.
Being stainless and free from the fever of affliction, they attain union with Śiva;
therefore, O fair-faced one, I shall now describe the division of mantras.

Oṃ aṃ ūn namaḥ | Oṃ yaṃ namaḥ | Oṃ laṃ namaḥ | Oṃ maṃ namaḥ | Oṃ kṣaṃ namaḥ | Oṃ raṃ namaḥ | Oṃ haṃ namaḥ | Oṃ hṛṃ namaḥ | Oṃ āṃ namaḥ | [The one] consisting of the nine [vowels]. Oṃ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ namaḥ | Oṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ [ñaṃ namaḥ] |
To the Tantra, obeisance! Oṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ, obeisance!

Oṃ taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ namaḥ | Oṃ paṃ phaṃ baṃ bhaṃ maṃ namaḥ | One should place [these] upon the fingers of the hands. Oṃ ya ra la va namaḥ | [These are placed] in the middle of the hands. Oṃ śa ṣa sa ha.
Homage! Oṃ from the wrist. Oṃ kṣaṃ namaḥ. This is the placement of the left hand during the *sampuṭīkaraṇa* (the joining of palms).
Oṃ a ā i ī u ū ṛ ṝ ḷ ḹ e ai o au aṃ aḥ. Homage! One should place one syllable upon each joint. Oṃ aṃ namaḥ; this is from the center of the hand.
O Goddess of the gods, one should place the supreme syllable at the wrist;
beginning with the thumb, one should place the five Brahmans.
One should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the limbs of Śiva, beginning with the middle finger, in their proper order;
[each limb] is joined with the syllable *rudra* and the syllable *oṃ*, and accompanied by the syllable *phaṭ*. (44)
One should perform the purification of the hands as well as the anointing of the body;
having purified the ground of the temple, one should carry out all of this with this [mudrā]. || 45 ||
O Goddess, this has been declared for the sake of some purification; indeed, everything whatsoever that is required for purification must be performed by means of this.

Oṃ, salutation to Earth. Oṃ, salutation to Water. Oṃ, salutation to Fire. Oṃ, salutation to Wind. Oṃ, salutation to Ether. Oṃ, salutation to Ego-consciousness. Oṃ, salutation to Intellect. Oṃ, salutation to Primordial Matter. Oṃ, salutation to the Puruṣa. Oṃ, salutation to Necessity. Oṃ, salutation to Time.
Oṃ rāgāya namaḥ | Oṃ vidyāyai namaḥ | Oṃ kālāya namaḥ | [p. 510] Oṃ vidyāyai namaḥ | Oṃ īśvarāya namaḥ | Oṃ sadāśivāya namaḥ | Oṃ śivāya namaḥ |

One should perform the placement (vinyāsa) beginning from the feet: *oṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *oṃ gīrnamaḥ*, *oṃ hunnamaḥ*, *oṃ śiva namaḥ*, *oṃ laṃ namaḥ*, *oṃ raṃ namaḥ*, *oṃ juṃ namaḥ*. One should place [these] upon the heart, the throat, and the space between the eyebrows.
O virtuous lady, the placement of the *śakti-kalā* has been described to you;
one should place the fifth *śakti*, and then place the *śiva-śakti-kalā*.
But the remaining [rites], O fair-faced one, should be performed as a mental placement (nyāsa). When the high-souled preceptor bestows the hand of Śiva, [the disciple should perform this]. (48)
One should perform the sacrifice and the ritual placement (nyāsa) in their entirety with the left hand.
O virtuous lady, listen as I explain the procedure for the Mātṛkā-homa at the time of the fire-oblation. (49)
Having performed the fire-consecration rite first, O woman of excellent complexion, the guide should then perform the binding with either one or four coverings.
The most excellent preceptor should offer oblations there one by one in the forward order, and then again in the reverse order, as the rite proceeds smoothly.
One who desires success in the direct order should perform the practice even in the reverse order; indeed, the instructor must offer the oblation both in the direct and reverse orders.
Thus, O Goddess, this most rare ritual placement (nyāsa) has been told to you;
and the arrangement of the mantras as well has been explained to you, O beautiful one. (53)
The Goddess said:
O Lord, with what as its primary basis is sacrifice declared to be performed?
I wish to understand this, O Blessed One; you should deign to speak.
O Goddess, listen; I shall explain that which you have asked.
O Goddess of beautiful countenance, I will fully declare it to you. 55.
O best of goddesses, those who are composed in mind should first perform the sacrifice to Gaṇa;
he is endowed with five limbs and has one hand.
With his mind fixed on the meditation of Śiva, he should perform the placement of the five-fold Śiva-mantra;
he should place an eight-petaled lotus, complete with filaments and a pericarp.
One should place the god Gaṇeśa, worshipped by the world, upon the pericarp.
Having placed the Heart-mantra in the southeast, one should place the Head-mantra in the northeast. (58)
O Goddess, one should place the *śikhā* [mantra] in the southwest and the *tvac* [mantra] in the northwest;
one should place the *astra* [mantra] in the four directions—this indeed is the prescribed rite. (59)

Oṃ hṛn namaḥ | Oṃ hin namaḥ | Oṃ hun namaḥ | Oṃ haiṃ namaḥ | Oṃ hannamaḥ | Oṃ jahi namaḥ | Oṃ hanala namaḥ | Oṃ jahi namaḥ | Oṃ annamaḥ. These are for the heart, head, crest, armor, and weapons, respectively.
Oṃ hrauṃ namaḥ | Oṃ Gaṇapati! Thus one should always worship in the pericarp of the Blessed One's lotus; the invocation should be performed with the heart-mantra, and the dismissal likewise.
Sprinkling and pouring over with water should indeed be performed with the five [mantras], there is no doubt;
one should purify the ground with the Astra-mantra—this is the prescribed rule. (61)
One should perform the rite of cremation (agnisaṃskāra) with all of these;
having performed the libation (tarpaṇa) within the mandala, one should offer the sacrificial oblation (bali) in the ten directions.
One should cause an offering to be given everywhere to the ninefold deity;
by that, all the hosts of spirits without exception attain satisfaction.
O Goddess of good vows, who would not be pleased during the festival of the lords?
Therefore, all beings are always satisfied by Śiva through his offerings.
And the offering (bali) should be of two kinds, to be given by the high-souled preceptor:
milk-rice, rice mixed with sesame, turmeric-colored food, and rice with jaggery.
One should likewise prepare yellow and black offerings mixed with meat;
O Goddess, this sixfold bali has been proclaimed by me to you. (66)
It should be given by the preeminent teacher who desires his own welfare;
thus has the sacrifice of Gaṇapati been fully described by me to you. (67)
O Goddess of the gods, one should perform sacrifices so that they always proceed without obstacles.
First is the sacrifice to Gaṇeśa (gaṇayāga), and second is the acquisition of the ground (bhūparigraha).
The third is known as Adhivāsa, while the fourth is remembered as Maṇḍala; the fifth is declared to be for the sake of the great-souled Caṇḍeśa. 69.
The worship of the Guru is remembered as the sixth; thus they have been proclaimed to you. He who, being well-composed, worships these six kinds [of teachers] is an Ācārya. (70)
He is released from all fetters and goes to the auspicious state that is free from affliction. || 70½ ||
Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter of the Niśvāsakārikā.
The Goddess said: "Regarding that deposition (nyāsa) of the earth and the other elements in their proper sequence which has been described by you..."
The arrangement for the utterance of the mantras and their respective locations in successive order. || 1 ||
O Goddess, those [beings] have been known by me according to their respective positions;
yet I wish to hear more, for I have a doubt, O Maheśvarī. (2)
Without form there is no ritual deposit (nyāsa), nor does accomplishment proceed;
those devoid of form do not achieve success, whether they be gods, lords of the Daityas, or Rākṣasas. || 3 ||
Deprived of their proper form, these exceedingly cruel leaders create obstacles; they are overcome by spirits, and serpents enter their dwellings. (4)
The rites of eradication and possession, killing and striking, as well as pacification, nourishment, and the making of nectar (immortalization). || 5 ||
Subjugation and the accomplishment of commands do not succeed for one who is devoid of beauty;
therefore, O Mahādeva, tell me the form of the mantras.
O Lord of Gods, tell us specifically the nature and form of the principles (tattvas), the deities, and the constituent parts (kalās) that arise from the placement of the fruits (phalanyāsa).
O Blessed One, you ought to explain this task in its entirety;
[you are] the Lord.
Excellent, excellent, O one of great wisdom, that I have been exhorted by you! (8)
I have not been questioned by anyone—not by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, the gods, or the asuras.
This question is of great merit, bestowing the ground of all fruits without exception.
Indeed, among these, the production of even one [image] and its installation are extremely difficult to attain;
therefore, becoming intent on breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should [perform it] endowed with the proper form and characteristics.
O Goddess, being composed, one should place the collection of seed-syllables on the right side—
[the syllable] which resembles the seven-rayed sun and is as pure as clear crystal.
It had the luster of a glowing iron ball, yet it was free from attachment;
it was pure and stainless like the rays of the moon, with a radiance equal to ten million flashes of lightning.
O Goddess, one should contemplate the seed-syllable which destroys all sins, illuminating everything on all sides with thousands of garlands of rays. (13)
O Goddess, by mere meditation, sins such as the killing of a Brahmin are purified;
indeed, yoga arises within the span of a month.
Such is the arrangement of the seed-syllables; now hear concerning the wombs (yoni), which shine forth on all sides like the fierce-rayed sun. 15.
One should contemplate the yoni-cakra as flowing with divine nectar that destroys old age and disease, resembling the moon and its crescent rays.
In the center, the ninefold deity, resembling molten gold, should be constantly meditated upon by yogis as illuminating all directions. || 17 ||
Or else, in the seed-source (bījayoni), one should contemplate the rays of the God and Goddess—
the rays that possess the brilliance of the sunbeams at the end of an eon— as having become unified. (18)
But within the seed-syllable, O Goddess, the Lord himself resides, illuminating;
O lady of excellent hips, one should know that Navātman is Sadāśiva. || 19 ||
The rays of these three— the seed, the womb, and the self— should be contemplated by the wise as having coalesced into a single drop (bindu) located at the position of the head.
Above that is the divine crest, a sound most difficult to attain;
beyond that stands the Śakti, illuminating all around.
Īśvara is to be known as the Bindu, and Sadāśiva is to be known as the Nāda;
but you alone, O Goddess of the lords of gods, are proclaimed to be Śakti.
"O Goddess, listen here to what is proclaimed as Mātṛkā—both 'this' (paratva) and 'that' (aparatva). I shall now tell you of the principles (tattvas) in their combined state. (23)
The syllable *ukāra* should be known as primordial nature (*prakṛti*), endowed with three forms;
it should always be meditated upon by yogis as black, red, and white. (24)
The place previously described by me must be known by the teacher;
one should contemplate the syllable *ya*, which is the principle of *puruṣa* and has the form of Śiva. || 25 ||
Or even one who has just died, if [the practitioner] remains focused on meditation while [the deceased] is still encircled by the lotus, he shall attain the perfection of yoga. || 26 ||
The letter *va* is to be known as Niyati; one should contemplate its color as either white or black, impelled by a red thread. (27)
Meditating upon such [a form] at the time of the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), O fair-faced one, one attains success; there is no doubt about this. O Goddess, I speak the truth. (28)
One desiring purity should meditate upon the syllable *la*, which has a smoky-colored lower surface, possesses the form of desire, and illuminates its own place. (29)

Having meditated upon [the deity] who has the appearance of a dark blue cloud, who is most terrifying through the reality of illusion (māyātattva), and who illuminates his own abode, there is accomplishment without a doubt. (30)
At the time of performing the ritual placement (nyāsa), one should indeed contemplate the Vidyā as richly endowed with the color red;
for the practitioner who is well-composed will succeed without hesitation. || 31 ||
Those great forms previously mentioned are accomplished by that [syllable] without doubt;
indeed, the letter *ra* is declared to be the Lord (*īśvara*) and is of variegated form (*citrarūpa*). || 32 ||
Illuminating the great reality (mahātattva), it is situated in the place of the crown of the head;
indeed, one succeeds without even deliberation—thus one should contemplate this ritual placement (nyāsa). (33)
Above the syllable *haṃ*, Sadāśiva, the God of gods,
is to be meditated upon by yogis constantly as possessing the brilliance of rays at the end of an eon.
By this, all these three worlds, including the moving and the unmoving, are pervaded;
through this, the yogi attains perfection, and omniscience proceeds from it. || 35 ||
Bindu and Nāda have been fully explained, as well as Śakti, in brief;
that secret has been told to you, for it was not hidden from you by me. (36)
O Goddess, listen as I speak of the principles beginning with Earth;
she of great renown shines resplendent upon a white lotus. (37)
Having meditated on the Earth as possessing such a form— a dark-complexioned woman with the luster of the sun, appearing in the guise of a young girl— one should place her at the two feet. (38)
Through the practice of continuous meditation, he should swiftly destroy all obstacles;
thus the teacher becomes like the earth for all living beings. (39)
Becoming intent on meditation on Śyāmā, one should cause her to reside within oneself;
one should contemplate the wind as being yellow in color in the region of the knees.
By this yoga and by this ritual placement (nyāsa), one who is well-composed attains success;
yogis should always meditate upon space as the eternal form of the earth. 41.

O Great Goddess, at the time of performing the ritual placement (nyāsa), one should contemplate the Ego-principle (ahaṅkāra) as red upon the pair of thighs; likewise, one should place it in the secret place and within the self. 42.
At the time of the ritual placement (nyāsa), one should contemplate [the deity] resembling the rising sun,
with a complexion like saffron-red, four faces, and four arms. (43)
One should contemplate [the deity] illuminating all directions with rosaries;
O Goddess of Devas, at the time of ritual placement (nyāsa), one should perform the placement of the intellect in this manner.
The Prakṛta has been previously explained, as well as the Pauruṣa in particular;
these have been known by you, O Goddess; now hear concerning the Kalās.
Nivṛtti has the luster of white; it extends from the feet up to the hips, illuminating all around with rays as cool as snow.
Pratiṣṭhā, having a yellowish luster, should be meditated upon at the time of ritual placement (nyāsa) from the heart down to the waist; thus, yoga is always produced.

But one should contemplate the Vidyā, O lady of beautiful hips, as being red in color, situated in the heart extending up to the ears, illuminating [everything] at the time of the ritual placement (nyāsa). (48)
One should always perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) for peace as far as the root of the ears,
[visualizing her] resembling moonlight and constantly emitting nectar.
Yogis should meditate on her constantly; at the time of ritual placement (nyāsa), one should contemplate her as being extremely subtle, indeed always to be meditated upon as far as the heart.
At the time of deposition, one should contemplate [the seed-syllable] as resembling the young sun's orb,
blazing with many rays and resting upon the ear of Amṛta.
At the time of depositing [the seed-syllable], one should contemplate it as being like a place sheltered from wind and sun;
it is indeed the digit of nectar, incomparable and free from disease.
O Goddess, by meditating upon her, one is liberated from the bondage of birth and saṃsāra;
indeed, she, the divine, should always be meditated upon by those seeking the conquest of death. (53)
That which is to be known as "Amṛta, Amṛta," the destroyer of old age and death—
by one desiring success, the placement of deities (devatānyāsa) must be performed upon the pericarp (karṇikā).
The form of those great-souled ones has thus been fully described;
for indeed, O Goddess of the gods, they should be recognized as such by the teachers. 55.
The face should likewise be understood and known with diligence.
Listen, O Goddess, as I speak of the placement upon the heart-lotus; I shall describe it to you. (56)
The lotus previously described as infinite is for the one of excellent complexion;
one should contemplate the foot of Dharma as white and Jñāna as red. (57)
They say that detachment is yellow, and sovereignty resembles darkness;
likewise, the limbs here, as well as the coverings, are the same. (58)
The filaments, resembling the color of saffron, should be fashioned from the power (śakti) of the cow;
thus one should contemplate the arrangement of the lotus at the time of sacrifice. 59.
O Goddess of the gods, at the time of initiation one should always contemplate in this manner;
O Goddess, during the ritual placement of the principles (tattvanyāsa), one should then contemplate that very principle.
By him all this reality is pervaded, indeed everything;
all those who have been mentioned whatsoever are known as his splendor.
By its splendor, all principles shine forth; of this there is no doubt.
When each individual placement (nyāsa) has been performed, one should cause each one to be recited by him.
Then all the groups of principles (tattvas), which bestow the fruits of both supernatural powers (siddhi) and liberation (mukti),
as well as the mantras and the constituent parts (kalās), must be understood in their entirety. (63)
Having first performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) in this manner, one gains power in all rites—whether in expulsion, killing, or even striking, O fair-faced one. (64)
With tridents in hand, most terrible, their eyes red with wrath, and their faces made fearsome by frowning brows—such [beings] one should employ for cruel deeds. 65.
O Goddess, one should always contemplate the deity of the mantra as having upward-pointing hair, extremely fierce, black in color, and terrifying, who causes [all things] to wither away. 66.
And those with mallets as weapons in their hands, bearing tridents and skull-topped staffs (khaṭvāṅgas), likewise carrying stones and holding wooden clubs in their hands. || 67 ||
Joined with the syllable *huṃ* at the beginning and illuminated by the syllable *phaṭ* at the end, it performs acts such as killing and utterance; of this there is no doubt. (68)
Listen, O Goddess, as I speak concerning both pacifying and nourishing rites:
[one should visualize] the gentle, white goddess, O Great Goddess, seated upon a white lotus. (69)
All of them held white lotuses and likewise carried water-pots in their hands;
they were gentle, as white as the rays of the moon, and [supported] the temple with their right hands.
O Goddess, in rites for nourishment, pacification, and libation, the deity should be meditated upon;
in rites of subjugation and attraction, she should be visualized as holding a noose and a goad.
All of them should be meditated upon as red in color by the practitioner;
however, for the purpose of paralyzing (staṃbhana), one should always contemplate them as black in color.
Having first performed the *mūrtinyāsa*, one should thereafter commence the [other] *nyāsa*.
O Goddess, this *nyāsa* has been fully described; it is exceedingly difficult to obtain. (73)
But since you are a devoted follower, I have told this to you;
thus has the Nyāsa, the most excellent among all mantras, been declared here.
One is liberated from sins such as the killing of a Brahmin merely by [the rite of] nyāsa;
even after consuming forbidden food or having destroyed the world of moving and non-moving beings. (75)
Even the lowest of men is liberated by performing this ritual deposition (nyāsa); of this there is no doubt.
Having offered gold, having given away cows, and having performed many other burnt offerings (homa), [he is likewise liberated].
O Goddess, by performing this ritual placement (nyāsa), one is liberated at that very moment; of this there is no doubt.
Having thus performed the rite of placement, the preceptor, being well-composed, [proceeds]. (77)
One should liberate [the disciple] by mere sight; no deliberation is required here.
532) If the preceptor performs the sacrifice according to the ritual procedure for the Kālayāga, || 78 ||
O Goddess, I am unable to describe the continuous abundance of its qualities;
even for a single day, that best of practitioners performs the ritual placement (nyāsa) with me.
One who practices this ritual placement (nyāsa) with a concentrated mind for seven days is liberated from the bondage of birth and saṃsāra; of this there is no doubt. (80)
He who contemplates [the deity] at the three junctions of the day shall, within a month, attain Yoga; he quickly leads twenty-one generations of his lineage to the auspicious realms of Śiva.
Whatever dharma one who is disciplined in yoga contemplates in the mind for six months,
he accomplishes all of it, whether it be for the benefit or the harm of the world.
O Lord of Gods, through the practice of repetition for a year, one shall attain equanimity;
there is no doubt that one may then recount the events of the three worlds. (83)
A practitioner who is well-composed and joined in yoga travels through the Lokāloka mountain and the world of moving and non-moving beings within two years; of this there is no doubt.
When the *nidānas* are consumed and the field-sounds (*kṣetranāda*) arise in many ways, the yogi attains accomplishment; there is no doubt here, indeed no uncertainty. || 85 ||
And by applying the remains [of the ointment] between the eyebrows, one gains the power of traveling through the sky;
likewise, there is the staff and the sacred pavitraka made of wood.
Yoga and the accomplishments of men are perfected; of this there is no doubt.
O Goddess, having understood this placement (nyāsa), any other placement is like straw.
Indeed, the lakṣas are to be known right here; the principles (tattvas) are to be known right here, O virtuous one.
Indeed, the Self is to be known right here, and especially the gods as well. (88)
O Goddess of beautiful countenance, this should not be given even to one's own son;
it should be given only to a practitioner and likewise to a teacher. (89)
"May he not cause even the welfare of other wicked mortals to fall.
The Goddess said:
"Tell me the forms of the five Brahmās, Īśa, and the [five] limbs."
Without them, as well as the ancillaries of the Vidyā, one does not attain perfection.
The Lord said: O Supreme Goddess, the five Brahmans are common to the limbs of Śiva. (91)
O Goddess, he is born everywhere endowed with beautiful form and auspicious marks;
O Shobhane, those very forms were previously described in the *Navasūtra*. 92.
The application of the mouth has been fully explained; it must be understood by the teacher.
O fair-eyed one, listen as I shall describe the form of the heart. (93)
Resembling pure crystal and filled with rays of light,
it illuminates both below and above, situated in the region of the heart.
O Goddess, when one is intent on meditation in the heart, it is placed there; of this there is no doubt.
O Goddess, the placement upon the head is the head itself, resembling a pearl necklace, a kunda flower, or the moon. 95.
At the time of the ritual placement (nyāsa), one should contemplate [the deity] illuminating all directions; one should contemplate the goddess Śikhā as resembling ten million moons. 96.
One should meditate upon this flowing stream of nectar as it floods [everything];
by that ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and meditation, the practitioner becomes well-composed. (97)
One succeeds here without doubt, freed from old age and disease;
[this] armor, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns, [should be placed] upon all limbs. 98.
O Goddess, this [mantra], which removes all obstacles and blazes with faces on every side, is perfected through the ritual placement (nyāsa); no doubt should be entertained in this matter. || 99 ||
One should employ the weapon in the region of the hand, but not upon one's own limbs;
O Great Goddess, one should contemplate the obstacles as being terrified. 100.
Having first recited the Astra-mantra ten times ten thousand times, one should thereafter perform the ritual practice (sādhana); thus, one shall attain success free from obstacles. || 101 ||

Having gathered everything by means of that [mantra] in the cardinal and intermediate directions, one should perform the recitation (japa) in the midst of the weapons; then it succeeds, and not otherwise. || 102 ||
Thus, O beautiful one, the ancillaries of knowledge (vidyāṅga) have been described to you;
therein is the Pāśupata weapon, the limb of Śiva known as Ghora. (103)
O Goddess, ten thousand recitations of the ancillary mantra (vidyāṅga) should be performed by those who are well-composed;
then, O Goddess, the supreme practitioner attains success without obstacles. || 104 ||
When the practitioner always contemplates the enclosure wall at the time of recitation, then the practitioner proceeds without obstacles; there is no doubt in this matter. || 105 ||
Being well-composed, one should perform the Jaya-Saṅkarṣaṇa within the limbs of the Vidyā;
having performed the yoga of the five sounds, one should begin the recitation in the center.

The *arghya* should be offered with the eleventh [verse] inserted in the midst of the recitation; the mantra, having been thus recited according to the prescribed measure, should then be properly concluded once again. (107)
Having worshipped according to the rule, one should perform the rite as declared in the Kalpa; then one attains success through the goddess, even from those things fashioned by humans. 108.
The accomplished ministers sport in the sequence previously described;
the glorious one is the performer of all rites through action, mind, and speech.
Having perceived the reality, O fair-faced one, one should recite that reality one hundred thousand times;
thus one attains perfection in yoga, and the mantras become effective, not otherwise.
O Goddess, if one recites it a hundred times at the time of going to bed at night, he shall explain even lost things and various scriptures.
That very God is the impeller and He shall speak; there is no doubt about this.
O Great Goddess, having recognized the Guru, one becomes fit for [liberation]; there is no doubt in this matter. (112)
The Goddess said:
"In which place, moreover, are those [impurities] to be purified—from sound, touch, and the other forms, as well as from the sense organs—by one who knows the single direction? (113)
"O Goddess, listen; O beautiful one, I shall declare that in which [practitioners] attain perfection.
I will tell it to you accordingly; listen with a one-pointed mind. (114)
Earth, water, fire, wind, and space—these five should be properly joined by the high-souled preceptor. 115.
One should purify those qualities which belong to earth and so forth that reside within the earth; likewise for water, fire, and indeed for air as well. (116)
On earth, the subtle element of smell is known as the object called "fragrance";
it resides within the sacrificial oblation of the organs of action and is considered the faculty of the auditory sense-organ. (117)
In this very sequence, the wise one should perform purification;
likewise, Śiva should be purified within Śakti, one by one, in due order.
Likewise, O beautiful one, one should purify the five elements beginning with earth;
then, one should purify the ego-principle as the sixth in the direct order.
This initiation has been explained to you in its entirety, along with the extraction of mantras,
the determination of the kalās, and likewise the determination of the tattvas.
O beautiful one, the meaning of the words has been explained to you in summary.
Having recognized the disciple as being filled with devotion, you should explain the initiation (dīkṣā). (121)
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter of the Niśvāsakārikā.
The Goddess said: "O Lord of the gods, O Master, I have heard everything in detail."
I wish to hear about the partless [Brahman], which stands pervading everything possessed of parts.
The Lord shall hereafter proclaim the eternal Śiva-dharma,
by which one who is liberated and whose soul is devoted to righteousness is called a "preeminent in dharma" (dharmotsanna).
He is eternally independent as a Lord, forever possessed of all auspicious characteristics,
immeasurable, omnipresent, pure, and endowed with the power of all potencies.
Pervading the entire world from Ananta up to Śiva, he remains established;
for he stands in a state of absolute unity, endowed with the power of Śiva (Śiva-śakti). || 4 ||
At the beginning, that Lord Śiva, the immutable,
rules over the entire universe through his sovereign powers, by means of his great yoga, his yoga of power, and his rays of light.
And he is established in the twentieth [tattva], because of his being the observer through his own powers,
due to his tranquility, his status as the agent, his possession of power, and his great majesty.
By means of their power of instruction and pacification, those powers of the Great-Souled One bestow grace upon the individual soul (kṣetrajña) and bring about the entire universe.
Since the entire world, including all that is moving and unmoving, is presided over by Śiva—who is of every form yet formless, incomparable and free from affliction—[he is the supreme reality]. (8)
Pervading all things with all his arts, subtle, having attained identity with that [reality],
consisting eternally of the splendor of mantra, inconceivable, he is Supreme Śiva. (9)
Standing far beyond all means of valid cognition, he is beyond the fourth state (turyātīta), both supreme and non-supreme;
pure in speech, the supreme light, his own splendor is the firm object of perception.
Immeasurable, indescribable, incomparable, and free from disease;
exceedingly subtle, imperishable, and eternal—the cause, the supreme light. (11)
That splendor, condensed thousands of times by the brilliance of the moon, the sun, and fire,
remains pervading ten million parārdhas of lightning flashes.
The lightning, the moon, the sun, the stars, and the fire—all shine with his splendor; he is remembered as the one of great luster. || 13 ||
Like a gem [containing] a gem, he is surrounded by his own splendor;
thus disciplined, the Supreme God is the splendor even of all splendors. (14)
Abiding in the void, eternal like the void, possessing a form with qualities similar to the void;
resembling a spotless mirror, with a luster like autumnal water. || 15 ||
Like the simultaneous rising of many suns,
they illuminated the ten directions with upward-shining light that utterly destroyed all darkness.
Having reflected in various ways upon the Lord, who is imperceptible, of inconceivable form, eternal, omnipresent, subtle, immutable, immovable, and firm; (17)
All-pervading, the doer of all, the all, the dweller in all, the omniscient Lord;
the self of all beings, abiding in all beings, the supreme ether, Śiva, the imperishable. || 18 ||
The food, the eater, and the giver—all these have their supreme essence in Śiva; having ascertained this, Śiva is the Lord of all beings, both the agent and the non-agent. (19)
There are thousands of various Śivas and tens of millions of Padmas,
all of whom are pure and eternal, abiding within the sphere of Śiva.
All possess the radiance of ten million suns and are pure by their very nature;
yet that which has been described as having distinct forms was spoken by practitioners who contemplate the scriptures. (21)
He is the great abode and the great knowledge, as well as the great departure;
he possesses great splendor, great prosperity, great majesty, and great fame. || 22 ||
It is beyond reasoning and unknowable, firmly established in its own nature;
it is ungraspable, abiding in all beings, and likewise unshakeable and immutable.
It is soundless and indeed voiceless, to be personally realized, immutable,
established within the self, to be known as formless and without support. (24)
He is without affliction and indeed imperishable, all-encompassing and of pervasive form; unborn and of infinite forms, he has no lineage, father, or mother.
Indeed, it is a body without bones, sinews, blood, or skin;
it is a frameless form, without beginning, middle, or end, immovable, unshakable, and eternal.
Unextended yet vast, uninterrupted on all sides,
equal toward all beings, and with its body perpetually spread throughout.
It is all that is external and internal, the abode of all yet without an abode;
it is stainless, devoid of ego, and free from intellect and the senses.
It is devoid of qualities, immovable, free from conceptual proliferation, and without affliction;
it is eternally manifest, without appearance, beyond thought-constructs, and free from disease. (29)
It is beyond doubt, incomparable, eternal, and likewise perpetually manifest;
it is neither low nor high, neither crooked nor straight.
It is neither long nor short, neither thick nor thin;
it is neither triangular, nor quadrangular, nor even circular. (31)
It has no form whatsoever, being devoid of all forms and yet devoid of formlessness;
it is neither hidden nor manifest, and there is neither coming nor going.
Neither above nor below, neither in front nor behind;
it is neither existent nor non-existent—what is that which abides everywhere? || 33 ||
The body does not exist as something separate, nor is it established as a single entity;
it is said to be neither a supreme object of cognition nor anything inferior. (34)
Śiva is to be known as subtle and devoid of creation and dissolution;
therein no creation arises, nor does dissolution ever occur. (35)
[He is] without beginning, unproduced, and likewise imperishable; he is the fire, undecaying, fixed, eternal, incomparable, and free from disease. (36)
It is said to be without support and without beginning, unchanging, eternally peaceful, perfectly extinguished, and completely satisfied in every respect. || 37 ||
It is completely free from all existence, devoid of action and time;
it is neither edible nor consumed, and it is transparent and utterly pure.
It is immeasurable and unknowable, omniscient and facing all directions;
it is devoid of the qualities of merit and demerit, and is not dependent upon anything. (39)
It does not shine forth by being thought upon, nor can it be manifested;
for it is stainless, free from passion, pure, auspicious, and sacred.
It is free from both existence and non-existence, devoid of illusion and the subject of illusion;
it is without fault or defect, neither moving nor caused to move.
But it cannot be revealed by means of direct perception and the other instruments of knowledge,
for it is infinite, ungraspable, subtle, and characterized by being beyond all measures.
It is inaccessible to all scriptures, yet it abides both externally and internally;
it possesses the nature of being the cause of all things, yet its characteristic is to transcend all causes. || 43 ||
In this very way, the Great Reality remains established through qualities that are beyond comparison;
yet it cannot be known without its own grace. (44)
And because the author [of the scriptures] is inferred through reasoning and because of the conceptualization found in the scriptures,
that [reality] may be obtained from the mouth of the Guru, who is impelled by that very power.
Since that which is devoid of reality and free from all categories of existence is the supreme reality itself,
he who realizes all this as such has understood everything in its entirety.
In the beginning, middle, and likewise at the end, that pure state which is the reality is proclaimed here through this distinction by means of the mind in the state of Manonmanī.
Pervading all existences, characterized by both purity and impurity, it is the pure reality that is impure; it arises from the state of the nectar of space.
Therefore, it cannot be said that the pure, partless object of knowledge is something to be known; being the supreme self-luminous reality, it does not manifest through anything else. (49)
Just as a man perceives his own objects by means of his own power, so too does that Supreme Lord perceive by means of His own power alone. (50)
He is omniscient, perfectly complete, pure by nature, and auspicious; he is entirely free from all defects and is the source of extraordinary qualities. || 51 ||

This is not the Lord of Pārvatī, who wields the skull-topped trident; nor is this the destroyer of Tripura, whose crest is adorned with the crescent moon. He is devoid of absolute tranquility, yet he is a constant, flowing stream.
The Lord is another Sovereign who is devoid of both anger and favor. || 52 ||
Auspicious in the beginning, auspicious in the middle, and always auspicious at the end—
O Lord, Your body transcends the net of the great collyrium.
Since birth, death, old age, delusion, desire, anger, and the products of worldly existence do not exist for him, his state is therefore peaceful and auspicious (śiva). || 54 ||
Because that state of Śiva is seen even in the lords of causes such as Brahmā,
the auspiciousness of the great-souled Śambhu is eternally celebrated as his Śivatva.
Auspicious, exclusively benevolent, incomparable, and free from disease;
the most auspicious of all auspicious things, eternally bestowing welfare, the propitious one. (56)
But the Arhat, the Lord of Beings, endowed with all ornaments, is to be known as the Teacher of the World and is worthy of worship by the twice-born. (57)
His limbs are smeared with the ashes of compassion; he carries a peaceful khaṭvāṅga staff;
he wears matted hair due to his lack of worldly attachment; and he bears the crescent moon of Śiva as his crown. (58)
He eternally holds the trident of knowledge; the serpent resides at the tip of his tongue of compassion.
With divine vision, he perceives the three worlds as food that is free from all obscuration.
O God, you are the one who has cast off the nature of being driven by desire, adorned with the power of will;
you are immovable, eternal, all-pervading, unborn, constant, and self-existent.
He is inactive yet perfectly restrained; he is the knower, the agent, and eternal.
He is omniscient, the creator of all, and has eyes, heads, and faces on every side.
It is without syllables, unproduced, inexpressible, and free from affliction.
That which eternally illuminates reality is called sovereignty and knowledge;
it stands forever like a witness over the threefold action. (63)
Having pierced through that center of the navel, one should not reflect upon that cycle of existence (saṃsāra),
nor upon whatever movement of the mind there may be, whether auspicious or inauspicious.
Pervading all beings on every side, he is the cognizing nature;
in an instant, he perceives everything—pleasure and pain, the beneficial and the harmful. (65)
One should perceive the entire circle of saṃsāra, abiding in its beginning, middle, and end, all within oneself; yet the all-pervading one does not become attached.
It constantly hears and perceives everything created by all beings, which consists of volition and determination; yet it is not joined to anything anywhere.
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell—both auspicious and inauspicious;
he is the hearer, the speaker, the enjoyer, and the thinker of pleasure and pain. (68)
Seeing and hearing everything, he bestows [liberation] everywhere;
pervading all worlds without exception, he is the one who effects the release from bondage for all.
He is omniscient, the performer of all actions, the agent of creation and dissolution;
without beginning, middle, or end, he is the source and the one who pervades all principles.
The Lord is the master who, through play, is the agent of creation and destruction;
he is omniscient, fully awakened, the primordial light, and likewise the awakener.
He is the protector and the one to be protected, the lord of restraint and favor;
he is the progenitor and the unprocreated, the one to be desired and likewise the ruler.
Perceivable by all the worlds, he is eternal, peaceful, and stainless;
by his will the Lord is possessed of all forms, and by his will he is devoid of parts. (73)
By his will he creates this [world], and by his will he also withdraws it;
he is the adversary of worldly activity, the cause of both destruction and origination. (74)
He is stainless, beyond measure, yet the knower of all measures;
he is the cause of the origin of all things, yet is himself the eternal causeless one.
Sudhāmā is eternal, constant, the source, and the Lord of causes;
he is the nature of all causes and is manifested through his powers.
The Blessed One is by nature the Dharma, characterized by being free from resistance; he is beginningless and endless, immovable, yet the mover of all.
The Supreme Lord is both the enjoyer and the pervader;
the Blessed Śiva is immeasurable through his powers and is eternally satisfied. (78)
He is Akṣobhya (the Immovable) and Vikṣobhya (the Agitator), especially regarding the principles; the Lord whose actions are inconceivable is the sovereign even of those who possess power.
The Lord, who is higher than the highest and preceded by intelligence, is the supreme ether;
therefore, he indeed spat [upon it] through mere knowledge, for he is the impeller.

Just as a medicinal herb acts through its potency, and as the powerful one [acts] by means of his strength; for he is the impeller, indeed both partless (niṣkala) and yet possessing parts (sakalaniṣkala).
O Supreme Goddess, because of her extreme subtlety, her immeasurability, and her sovereignty, the primordial,
utterly pure Śakti is distinguished from [all other] powers and remains unobstructed.
Just as a well-kindled fire burns up dry land and grassy meadows,
so too is the state of having "Bhava" as its tongue-weapon, when it is blazing forth, brought to an end.
The Lord’s characteristic, which consists of the means for bestowing grace, is proclaimed as that which brings about the maintenance and favor of those who have undergone birth and dissolution. 84.
Time, though formless, brings about the gathering of blossoms upon the trees.
And likewise, he observed the falling of the remaining fruits exactly as it occurred. || 85 ||
In the same way, the formless Śambhu is the agent of their arising and destruction;
like the power residing in a magnet, his formless energy performs all actions.
Just as the stainless Śiva-śakti grasps reality below,
so too do the powers, being utterly pure, function under the control of Śaṅkara.
He alone is the creator of the world, and he is also called "Supreme" here;
yet because he does not act by himself, he is therefore described as "quiescent. (88)
For the eternal Lord Sadāśiva is neither the doer nor the instigator, just as [the rain] is not for farmers who follow their own actions. (89)
However, they do not yield fruit without the grace of birth and old age;
thus it is with all actions, including certain recitations and meditations. (90)
Without the grace of Maheśvara, however, they do not bestow fruit;
he transcends all states of being and is devoid of inconceivable qualities. || 91 ||
The eternal one is the creator of all and is the self-nature of all;
yet he cannot be grasped by the senses, nor by the hand, nor by the eye.
The Lord, the Sovereign, who is formless yet possesses all forms, is to be grasped by himself through himself in every way;
he fills everything without exception. (93)
This one alone is the cause of the bondage, liberation, dissolution, and origination of all beings;
hidden and devoid of sound and other qualities, he presides over all creatures. (94)
He is entirely peaceful, omniscient, the Lord, the Sovereign, and imperishable;
having pervaded all things with his powers, he abides as that which is woven warp and woof, without beginning or end.
By his power, he pervades this entire universe of moving and unmoving beings, facing in every direction,
present everywhere within all creatures, both stationary and moving.

Pervading the entire range of all seeds, it remains having permeated everything; because it reveals [the truth] at the beginning—at the commencement of the Śiva-sacrifice—it is called "Agra" (the Beginning) by Śiva. 97.
Because all principles (tattvas) are non-existent, fire indeed faces in every direction;
abiding in the samādhi of the end of all things, it is the object of the internal organ. || 98 ||
That which is perceived as subtle at first by yogis is that which is meditated upon—the Self of all, belonging to all beings, yet devoid of all beings. (99)
The self of all beings, devoid of all beings, the withdrawer of the primary qualities (guṇas)—that is the supreme reality remembered by me. 100.
He is the abode of all the qualities of all beings, the refuge in the secret cave of all beings;
he is established as the self of all beings, omnipresent and imperishable. || 101 ||
Established in his own self, he is pure, with his victorious conduct fully perfected;
thus is the supreme Śiva, the master of his own māyā, who has attained the highest liberation.
Without beginning, middle, or end, free from duality, with all doubts severed—this is the one who has transcended suffering; this is the cause, the bringer of security, the auspicious one. (103)
Free from comparison with objects of transformation, likewise devoid of likeness, and with its conditioned nature cast out from form;
it is distinct from the intellect by virtue of being both non-existence and existence.
Śiva is the cause of all causes, yet he has no other cause. || 104 ||
Since there exists no other such entity anywhere whatsoever, he is Nirvāṇa, the supreme purity, the illusion-free, and the highest Śiva. || 105 ||
This partless God of yours is endowed with parts;
contemplating Him constantly through meditation, one should remember Him with the mind and intellect.
O Mahādevī of virtuous conduct, it has been told to you in the *Kārikā*: "In the supreme *Niśvāsa* Tantra, however, [the deity] is partless (*niṣkala*) with respect to the whole (*sakala*). (107)
This essence of the Śiva-dharma is the most excellent among all tantras;
it should be given to one consecrated in the Śaiva tradition, but it should not be given to one who has received another initiation.
Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter of the Niśvāsakārikā.
The Goddess said:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods of gods, whose banner is marked by the bull!"
O All-Knowing One and Creator of all, be gracious to me, O Lord! || 1 ||
O Maheśvara, O Mahādeva, O Lord, tell me the collective essence of all mantras and the practice of mantra, my master. (2)
O Lord of Gods, please graciously tell me how to perform the five limbs beginning with Vyomavyāpin, as well as those for the Brahmas.
How indeed does the Self abide within the matrices (mātṛkā) as both differentiated and non-differentiated? What is the number of its parts (kalā)? The Lord, possessing sprouts, scatters [them]. (4)
How indeed is the Self established within the number of syllables of the mantras?
Having first established the tenfold Self, [one should proceed] with its limbs in their proper order.
O Lord of Gods, tell me in its entirety and exactly as it is:
what is the number of steps over which the Lord constantly moves? (6)
O Lord of Gods, O Śaṅkara, tell us: how does he who is devoid of internal organs move within all the arts and all mantras? (7)
"O Lord of Gods, O Master, tell me about the internal [nature];
O Goddess, listen to that great knowledge which you have asked about. (8)
It has not been revealed to anyone; I shall tell it to you in its entirety—the sequential course of the movement of all mantras.
O Great Goddess, by the mere knowledge of which one is liberated and also attains success— that movement of mantra is difficult to obtain even for the gods.
O virtuous one, I shall explain, without any doubt and even at the cost of my life, by analyzing each individual word and syllable.
It was previously declared that the number of breaths (*prāṇa*) is twenty-one thousand six hundred, as stated in due order. (12)
O Goddess of the gods, having divided those vital breaths in successive order,
[one should determine] by means of the steps how many breaths there are for each one individually.
And how the embodied soul moves— I shall tell you all of that,
as well as the number of each caste that resides within the Lord.
O Goddess, hear in due order the number of kalās;
one who knows this method of division is said to be "one whose body is divided. (15)
That wise one, eternally on the surface of the earth, shall be a liberator and lead [beings] to Śiva;
for by whatever mantra a man performs an action, [by that he attains his goal]. (16)
And through the state of essential identity (*sāmarasya*), by virtue of its uninterrupted nature, he thus attains the mantra as his very self; there is no doubt in this matter. (17)
In whichever [syllable] one should join the deity of the mantra by means of that very syllable, the knower of mantras should release it through the middle of that; thus he is released. 18.
At whichever specific time the mantra-practitioner becomes one whose body is the mantra, at that very same time the Guru who knows reality should effect liberation. 19.
By whichever caste a man may identify himself, by that very caste he shall liberate [others] and is himself liberated as well. (20)
For by whatever reality one forms the body, O beloved,
by that very same reality one should release it, and thus one is liberated.
As many syllables as there are in the mantras, so many [mental recitations] are prescribed through their meditation.
By means of that, when one sacrifices and offers oblations, one attains success and is even liberated.
As many as are the letters of the Mātṛkā, so many are the paths remembered to be;
by worshipping and offering oblations with them, one succeeds and is even liberated. (23)
All this regarding the mantras has been told to you, O virtuous one;
having understood it all in its entirety, perform the initiation, yoga, and recitation.
Having rendered the syllables and letters auspicious, one should worship them in due order;
those letters which are short or long, and those which are known to be joined with vowels. || 25 ||

Having understood those phonemes as joined with the deities and the principles (tattvas) in their proper order, one should then recognize the words here itself through the various methods of extracting the Praṇava.
The knower of mantras should worship each individual syllable in successive order;
furthermore, the fire sacrifice (homa) previously described for them must be performed by the preceptor.
O Goddess of the gods, if the preceptor performs the sacrifice according to the division of the *kalās*,
he should place them upon the petals of the *kalās* and install them with the mantra at the pericarp (*karṇikā*).

O beautiful lady, the master of adepts who desires spiritual accomplishment must perform the worship, the fire-offering (homa), and all other ritual acts for all [the deities] using their respective mantras. (29)
All of these should not be understood as distinct by those who know the reality;
having worshipped them in this manner according to the rule, the preceptor should perform the initiation.
All this has been explained by me in brief, O fair-faced one;
it should be understood with effort by practitioners who desire liberation. (31)
I shall once again proclaim the unsurpassed nectar of distinction,
by knowing which one is inevitably liberated from the bonds of worldly existence.
This should be understood by the wise through internal application;
beginning from the first, it is to be known for each one in due order. (33)
O sinless one of excellent complexion, having divided [the subject] into eighty-one according to its non-existence, I shall explain it to you in its entirety without any doubt. (34)
When the vital breaths are divided individually for each [limb],
it should be known that there are two hundred breaths, and likewise for those established in the breaths.
Furthermore, O Goddess, the six breaths are known as two *nimeṣas*;
thirty *tṛṣṭis* should be understood as one *lava*, O beautiful lady of the gods. (36)
O Goddess, the Lord moves constantly through each single step;
O Queen of the Gods, this should be understood by those who are well-composed throughout a day and night. (37)
And hear how the Lord moves through the syllables on the left path:
in the case of the syllables pervading the void, sixty vital breaths (prāṇas) are indeed proclaimed. || 38 ||
But devoid of these three, O Goddess, it lasts for half a nimeṣa; such is the thirst of each of the five elements individually, O fair-faced one. (39)
Knowing this, they are indeed liberated from the bonds of all fettered beings (paśus).
Thus it has been told to you, O Goddess of gods, O beautiful one, regarding the syllables of the words.
The Vyomavyāpin has been declared; now I shall tell you about Sadyojāta and the others: namely Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, and likewise Aghora. (41)
O Goddess of gods, I shall explain the nature of Puruṣeśa; listen as to how each one comes to be through the eight immediate kalās.
I shall describe in due order how the Sovereign Lady (Īśānī) eternally moves, consisting of two thousand and seven hundred [verses]. (43)
This must be constantly known by the high-souled yogi who understands the spies;
likewise, O Aghora, it must be understood by the high-souled teacher. 44.
I shall fully proclaim the Vāma [Tantra]; listen with one-pointed mind. It consists of five hundred and thirty-six [verses]. 45.
Furthermore, O Goddess, sixty breaths (prāṇas) must be known by the teacher;
one breath is likewise declared to be equal to one lava. (46)
O Goddess, one-third of that [measurement] should be understood with effort as the *tṛṭi*;
O Goddess, listen as I shall describe it for a man in brief. (47)
Five thousand and four hundred [verses] are to be known;
this, O Goddess, has been fully declared as that which must be understood by one who knows the reality.
I shall tell you of the Lord; listen, O Goddess of excellent complexion, in brief: they are said to be four thousand. (49)
It should be known without doubt that there are three hundred and twenty;
such is the portion (kalā) recorded for each individual Brahman. (50)
O Goddess of the gods, by that number the Lord acts perpetually;
thus has the conduct of the *kalās* been fully described in brief, but not in detail. (51)
It should be understood with effort by yogis who contemplate reality.
O beloved, listen attentively as I shall fully explain the limbs of Śiva. 52.
By the mere knowledge of which one would certainly obtain both supernatural power (siddhi) and liberation, that is declared to be the Heart of the Supreme Self, known as the Soul of All. (53)
The six-syllabled mantra becomes equal [in power] through its recitation;
Suśiva is declared to be eight-syllabled—listen to its ultimate limit, O beloved. (54)
Two thousand [lines] for each [chapter] in due order;
seven hundred [lines] are to be known—this must be understood by the teacher. (55)
O fair-faced one, this movement of Suśiva has been explained to you;
O Goddess, listen as I shall now describe that of Jvālinī in brief. (56)
One thousand and nine hundred are proclaimed;
sixty breaths (prāṇas) are to be known, as well as three breaths. || 57 ||
